entries.text:
Security subqueries must be EXPLICITLY workspace-scoped — admin DB handles bypass RLS › Prove it with a test, not by reading
The leak is invisible to a single-workspace test — it only appears when a *second*
workspace's trust row exists. The guard case in
`work-items-admission.integration.test.ts` is therefore mandatory:

* workspace **A** has a remote, un-admitted feature whose `verified_author_github_user_id = X`;
* workspace **B** (only) trusts `X` in its `user_trust_list`;
* assert the predicate (run on the admin handle) **REFUSES** the workspace-A feature.

Without the cross-workspace row the test passes whether or not the subquery is
scoped — so the leak ships green. Security-gate correctness is the test's job, not
the reviewer's eye: write the adversarial cross-tenant case explicitly.

entries.text:
Security subqueries must be EXPLICITLY workspace-scoped — admin DB handles bypass RLS › The fix (shared-pot-trust-admission D-004)
Thread `workspaceId` through the predicate and add the scope yourself; when the
caller cannot supply a workspace, **drop the trust leg entirely** — the gate then
only ever *under*-admits (refuses a legitimately-trusted item) rather than
*over*-admits (the security failure). Fail-safe direction matters: a missed
fast-path is a latency cost; a leaked admission is a breach.

```ts
// work-items-admission.ts — RIGHT: explicit ws scope, leg dropped when unscoped
export function autoPickableWhereSql(sql: OrgSql, workspaceId?: string) {
  const trustLeg = workspaceId
    ? sql` OR (verified_author_github_user_id IS NOT NULL
               AND verified_author_github_user_id IN
                   (SELECT trusted_github_user_id FROM harness_shared.user_trust_list
                     WHERE workspace_id = ${workspaceId}))`
    : sql``;                                 // no ws ⇒ no trust fast-path (fail-safe)
  return sql`(origin = 'local' OR origin IS NULL OR audit_verdict = 'admit'${trustLeg})`;
}
```

The JS twin (`isAutoPickable`, fed by `loadTrustedGithubUserIds(workspaceId)`) and
the per-id reader (`isWorkItemAutoPickable`, whose own trust SELECT is ws-scoped)
follow the same discipline. The producer side (`verified_author_github_user_id`,
stamped only from a **verified + non-revoked device attestation** — never a
self-claimed id) is what makes the trusted set meaningful; a NULL verified id
never satisfies the leg.
entries.description: Security subqueries must be EXPLICITLY workspace-scoped — admin DB handles bypass RLS › The fix (shared-pot-trust-admission D-004)

entries.text:
Security subqueries must be EXPLICITLY workspace-scoped — admin DB handles bypass RLS › The rule
> **Any security-sensitive subquery that runs on an admin/superuser handle and
> references a workspace-scoped table MUST carry its own explicit
> `workspace_id = $ws` predicate. Never rely on RLS for isolation when the
> handle can bypass it.**

RLS is a backstop for RLS-respecting handles, not a substitute for scoping in
code that runs as admin. Treat "this table has RLS" as *irrelevant* the moment
you're on `getOrgPg()`.
entries.description: Security subqueries must be EXPLICITLY workspace-scoped — admin DB handles bypass RLS › The rule

entries.text:
Security subqueries must be EXPLICITLY workspace-scoped — admin DB handles bypass RLS › The trap
`harness_shared.user_trust_list` ships with RLS (`migration 276`,
`POLICY user_trust_list_workspace_isolation` keyed on `workspace_id`). It is tempting to lean on
that policy for isolation and write the trust fast-path of the G2 admission
predicate as:

```sql
-- WRONG — relies on RLS to scope the trust list
... OR (verified_author_github_user_id IS NOT NULL
        AND verified_author_github_user_id IN
            (SELECT trusted_github_user_id FROM harness_shared.user_trust_list))
```

That is a **cross-workspace privilege-escalation leak.** The admission predicate
(`packages/operator-core/lib/work-items-admission.ts` — `autoPickableWhereSql` /
`isAutoPickable` / `isWorkItemAutoPickable`) runs at every claim/place chokepoint
(`claimWorkItem`, `claimNextWorkItem`, `fleet:place_batch` gather, replica claim).
**Those callers hold the `getOrgPg()` admin handle, which BYPASSES RLS.** So the
subquery above sees `user_trust_list` rows from *every* workspace. A workspace-**A**
feature whose verified author is trusted only in workspace-**B** then satisfies the
trust leg and is **auto-admitted** — i.e. un-screened foreign code runs without the
auditor, in a workspace whose owner never trusted that author.

This is the single sharpest failure mode of the whole gate: the gate exists
precisely to keep remote/un-admitted work from auto-running, and an RLS-reliant
trust leg quietly re-opens that hole for any author trusted *somewhere*.
entries.description: Security subqueries must be EXPLICITLY workspace-scoped — admin DB handles bypass RLS › The trap

entries.text:
Attention push-notification delivery › Extending it
* **New attention source:** call `notifyAttention({ kind, title, body,
  harnessSlug, importance })` at the write site. Add the kind to
  `AttentionNotifyKind` + `MOBILE_KIND` if it needs a distinct mobile route.
* **The desktop native notification needs a cargo rebuild** of
  `papercusp-desktop` to pick up `tauri-plugin-notification` + the
  `show_attention_notification` command. The toast + mobile push work without
  it; the native OS notification is a no-op (caught) until the rebuild.
* End-to-end delivery (APNs/FCM, native OS notification) is **not
  headless-testable** — verify in the desktop shell. The `notifyAttention`
  fan-out + the gates are unit-tested (`attention-notify.test.ts`,
  `set-status.test.ts`).
entries.description: Attention push-notification delivery › Extending it

entries.text:
Attention push-notification delivery › One helper, two channels, event-driven
Everything funnels through **`notifyAttention()`** in
`packages/operator-core/lib/attention-notify.ts`. Producers call it at the source the
moment a ≥high attention item appears; it fans out to two independently
fail-safe channels (a delivery error is logged and swallowed — it never
propagates into the producer's write path):

1. **Mobile** — `notifyWorkspace(wsId, payload)` →
   `packages/operator-core/lib/device-push-dispatcher.ts` → APNs/FCM to devices paired
   in `harness_shared.mobile_push_tokens`. No-op when none are paired. `data`
   must be string-valued and `kind` a `PushKind` — the helper coerces/maps.
2. **Desktop-native** — emits an `attention.notify` event on the sync SSE bus
   (`notifySyncInvalidate`). The webview's `DesktopAttentionNotifier`
   (`apps/operator/app/_components/`, mounted once at the root, app-level so
   `@papercusp/sync` stays domain-free) shows an in-app **sonner toast**
   always, and in the Tauri shell invokes the **`show_attention_notification`**
   Rust command (`papercusp-desktop`, `tauri-plugin-notification`) for a
   native OS notification. Driven from Rust, so no JS-facing notification
   capability is needed; the command is app-defined → allowed by default.

**No 60s poll.** The old `device-intervention-watcher` (a `setInterval(60s)`
catch-all that SELECTed the three tables) was **deleted** in P-021 — its
triggers now emit at the source.
entries.description: Attention push-notification delivery › One helper, two channels, event-driven

entries.text:
Attention push-notification delivery › The four producer call-sites + their once-per-event gating
`notifyAttention()` is called at exactly the points that *create* a ≥high
attention item — there's no poll, so each must fire **once per genuine event**:

| Source      | Where                                                | Fire condition                                                                                 |
| ----------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| escalation  | `endpoint-route/routes/internal/escalation-event.ts` | `escalation != null` (skip notes-only updates)                                                 |
| smoke-fail  | `endpoint-route/routes/internal/smoke-test-event.ts` | **transition** into failing — reads prior `status`, fires only on `pass→fail` / first fail     |
| plan-review | `internal/plan-review-event.ts`                      | every call (the producer posts once per completed review)                                      |
| needs-human | `plans:set-status`                                   | transition INTO `needs-human` at importance ≥ high (`shouldPushNeedsHuman` + `itemImportance`) |

Why this was safe to do at once: each source is its own chokepoint, so there's
**no double-fire** (the poll that used to also push escalation/smoke/plan-review
is gone). The gating above prevents re-pushing on idempotent re-writes. The
trade vs the old poll: the poll was a catch-all that fired regardless of write
path; source emits only fire from these four sites — if a *new* write path for
those tables appears, wire `notifyAttention` into it too.
entries.description: Attention push-notification delivery › The four producer call-sites + their once-per-event gating

entries.text:
Attention push-notification delivery › The importance map (what the ≥high gate includes)
P-020 pushes only at importance **≥ high**. The per-kind importance lives in
`packages/operator-core/lib/attention/adapters.ts`:

| Kind                   | importance                                                                      |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| smoke-fail             | `high` (fixed)                                                                  |
| plan-review            | `high` (fixed)                                                                  |
| coord escalation       | `severityToImportance(sev)` — blocker→`urgent`, question→`high`, advisory→`low` |
| coord message-to-human | `normal`                                                                        |
| plan item              | the item's own `importance:` keyword                                            |

Note `harness_escalations` (the table the watcher polls) has **no severity
column** — it's a harness-level escalation, distinct from a *coord* escalation.
Treat it as inherently high. Net: the watcher's three triggers are all already
high, so the watcher never pushed low-importance noise to begin with.

The fs-watcher mirror for these three tables is **retired** (see the long

entries.text:
Auto-implement "host-restart" orphans are gateway-deaths, not operator restarts › Don't
* Don't lower `TimeoutStopUSec` further or rewrite the SIGTERM/DBOS-drain path to "fix orphans" — the drain is already fast (15s) and the operator isn't the one dying.
* Don't treat `host-restart-recovery` rows as proof of operator restarts — cross-check the bg-host journal for `infra_loss` first.
entries.description: Auto-implement "host-restart" orphans are gateway-deaths, not operator restarts › Don't

entries.text:
Auto-implement "host-restart" orphans are gateway-deaths, not operator restarts › Evidence (2026-06-24, su-54b32)
The round-3 plan (`infra-perf-reliability-audit-round3-2026-06-19` P-005) framed this as: deploy SIGTERMs the cluster → 90s DBOS drain hang → SIGKILL orphans 78% of dispatches. **That framing is disproven live:**

* `papercup-dev-api`: `NRestarts=0`, **10.5h uptime**, `TimeoutStopUSec` already lowered to **15s** (not 90s). It is not restarting hourly.
* `papercup-bg-host` (the DBOS routines primary) is installed + running, also not flapping.
* `improvement_dispatches` (7d): 130/195 orphans are `host-restart-recovery`, **but** the bg-host journal is full of `[durable-spawn] infra_loss: … returned HTTP 200 but the agent produced no turn (exitCode=1) — agent died before emitting a turn … upstream gateway stall/429 storm killing the agent MID-TURN`, plus repeated `TypeError: fetch failed`.
* Live orphan rate at the time: **0.978** (45/46 in 24h).
entries.description: Auto-implement "host-restart" orphans are gateway-deaths, not operator restarts › Evidence (2026-06-24, su-54b32)

entries.text:
Auto-implement "host-restart" orphans are gateway-deaths, not operator restarts › Mechanism
1. The auto-implement dispatch fires a worker agent (spawned `detached: true` in `orchestrator-runner.ts`; the operator only `killTree`s it on explicit abort/timeout, never on its own shutdown). `fire_result='ok'` — the worker launches.
2. The worker makes \~1-2 model calls, hits a gateway 429/stall, and dies before producing a turn → `infra_loss`. The `EI-404` back-edge never fires (no resolving turn).
3. The boot/periodic orphan-collector (`orphaned-dispatch.ts` `collectOrphanedDispatchSignals` → `isHostRestartVictim`) uses the heuristic **"fired before this process boot ⟹ dead host-restart victim"**, marks it `host-restart-recovery`, releases the claim, rolls the attempt back, and the next implement tick **re-dispatches** — into the same unhealthy gateway → repeat. The `EI-1689` thrash breaker eventually routes the item to a human (`needs-human`).

So the label `host-restart-recovery` is a **misattribution**: the worker died of gateway loss, not a host restart.
entries.description: Auto-implement "host-restart" orphans are gateway-deaths, not operator restarts › Mechanism

entries.text:
Auto-implement "host-restart" orphans are gateway-deaths, not operator restarts › TL;DR
If you see a high **auto-implement dispatch-orphan rate** (`harness_shared.improvement_dispatches.outcome='orphaned'`, dominated by `resolved_by='host-restart-recovery'`), do **NOT** assume the operator is restarting and chase the SIGTERM/DBOS-drain shutdown path. That diagnosis is stale. The real cause is almost always **the dispatched worker agent dying mid-turn on the inference gateway** (`[durable-spawn] infra_loss … agent produced no turn`), which the boot orphan-collector then **misattributes** as a host-restart victim and re-dispatches straight back into the same gateway storm — a churn loop. See `rate-limit-is-usually-account-routing-not-capacity`.
entries.description: Auto-implement "host-restart" orphans are gateway-deaths, not operator restarts › TL;DR

entries.text:
Auto-implement "host-restart" orphans are gateway-deaths, not operator restarts › What actually fixes it
* **Root**: inference-gateway stability (429/stall) — owned by `inference-gateway-stability-ownership-2026-06-23` (durable-spawn misclassification + account-pool routing). The orphan rate cannot reach 0 until gateway-loss stops killing workers mid-turn. Do not duplicate that work here.
* **Misattribution/churn** (`orphaned-dispatch.ts`) — **now landed**, not just proposed. `resolved_by` classifies distinct death causes instead of lumping everything into `host-restart-recovery`: `worker-exit-backedge-env` (rate-limit/auth/connectivity, EI-406) and `worker-exit-backedge-context-overflow` (WI-716, oversized item) are both recognized, and `isLaneBreakageOrphan()` excludes them (plus genuine `host-restart-recovery` rows) from the human-facing "lane broken" signal — so a gateway storm no longer files a self-amplifying cascade of false-alarm EIs (the EI-536/523/512/509 loop). `laneInEnvOutage()` goes further: once ≥2 env-failure deaths land inside a 6h window, even *cause-unknown* orphans (no back-edge ever fired — durable-fire lost, or the worker killed before it reported) are suppressed as outage casualties via `isCauseUnknownOrphan()`, since during an outage they're indistinguishable from env casualties. The `resolved_by` ledger/rollup still counts every row; only the noisy human signal is suppressed.
* **Detection**: the perf/reliability regression rig (`system-health/perf-regression-rig.ts`, watchdog collector `perf-regression`, flag `papercusp-perf-regression-rig`) now tracks **dispatch-orphan-rate** as an SLO (crit at 0.6) so this can never again regress silently — it ran at 91-98% with nothing watching.
entries.description: Auto-implement "host-restart" orphans are gateway-deaths, not operator restarts › What actually fixes it

entries.text:
autoloop-release-readiness — grading runbook
The `autoloop-release-readiness` rubric (releaseGating, 8 criteria, ratingScale
`pass / at-risk / fail / unknown`) is the **composite** public-release gate for the
full autonomous loop product. It COMPOSES the leg rubrics instead of duplicating
them: `blender-release-readiness` grades the blender/scout self-learning leg
(separate grader lane), `pot-coordination-health` is the Kettle's own per-wake
scorecard. Origin: EI-12461 / EI-12455; owner directive
`[owner turn f362a778@2026-07-16T20:31:59Z]` (name elided — release-bundle
identity rule, WI-4419: owner-name tags must use the nameless `[owner …]` form).
entries.description: autoloop-release-readiness — grading runbook

entries.text:
autoloop-release-readiness — grading runbook › blender-leg-health · `blender-leg-scorecard`
Defer to the leg rubric — do NOT re-measure scout internals here.
`scorecards:list { rubricRef: 'blender-release-readiness', limit: 1 }`: complete
(`missingKeys:[]`), fresh ≤6h, no unowned `fail`. Scout rows live under
`harness_slug='@singleton'` (workspace+origin scoping — EI-10520); `routed_at` is

entries.text:
autoloop-release-readiness — grading runbook › capacity-admission · `accounts-capacity`
`accounts:status` (+ gateway stats). `pass` = ≥2 healthy accounts (7d-util \< 0.9) AND
clean no-capacity classification under exhaustion (capacity-storm drill on the current
generation, or organic `gated` ticks). Never blame capacity without a real 429
(owner standing directive). Silent member death on a walled pool = `fail`.

```sql
SELECT status, gate, count(*) FROM harness_shared.scout_ticks
WHERE tick_at > now()-interval '48 hours' GROUP BY 1,2;
```
entries.description: autoloop-release-readiness — grading runbook › capacity-admission · `accounts-capacity`

entries.text:
autoloop-release-readiness — grading runbook › Composite verdict (roll-up)
The rubric is a GATE, so the 8 criterion ratings collapse to ONE decision. Take
the worst rating that applies, in this order:

* **NO-GO** if ANY criterion is `fail`. A composite gate is only as green as its
  weakest leg — one failing stage means the loop is not a shippable product.
* **NO-GO** if ANY criterion is `unknown`. A gate cannot certify what it did not
  measure; `unknown` is a NOT-pass that blocks GO. Resolve it (run the instrument,
  gather the evidence) rather than shipping past an unmeasured leg — never let
  `unknown` round up to `pass`.
* **CONDITIONAL-HOLD** if the worst rating is `at-risk` (no `fail`, no `unknown`):
  the fix is live but its window has not cleared. GO only with explicit owner
  sign-off AND a stated clear-by time in evidence; otherwise hold and re-grade
  when the window clears.
* **GO** only when EVERY criterion is `pass`.

Leg deference is transitive: `kettle-supervision-health` (c3) and
`blender-leg-health` (c4) inherit their leg rubric's verdict — a NO-GO on
`pot-coordination-health` or `blender-release-readiness` is a composite NO-GO,
never overridden by a fresh-but-incomplete leg scorecard.
entries.description: autoloop-release-readiness — grading runbook › Composite verdict (roll-up)

entries.text:
autoloop-release-readiness — grading runbook › cup-execution-health · `cup-keeper-runs`
Rolling 24h run success + restart durability.

```sql
-- NB (corrected 2026-07-16, EI-13024): cup_keeper_runs has terminal_state (NOT exit_code)
-- and NO workspace_id — scope via the instances join.
SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE r.terminal_state='completed')::float/greatest(count(*),1) AS success_rate,
       count(*) AS runs
FROM harness_shared.cup_keeper_runs r
JOIN harness_shared.cup_keeper_instances i ON i.instance_id = r.instance_id
WHERE i.workspace_id='papercusp-workspace' AND r.started_at > now()-interval '24 hours';
```

The table is fed by the gen-0 IQ battery (`beekeeper-gen0-runner.ts`), scheduled monthly via
`bp-singleton-iq-battery-0` (owner budget in `payload_template.budgetUsd`). If the window is
empty, check the singleton's `last_fired_at` and whether the last fire left an instance with
ZERO runs (the EI-13049 silent-failure/dedupe-trap class); a manual fill is
`npx tsx packages/operator-core/lib/iq-battery/beekeeper-gen0-runner.ts --harness=papercusp --cap=25`.

`pass` ≥ 0.80 · `at-risk` 0.60–0.80 · `fail` \< 0.60 or systematic identical failures.
Restart durability: keeper respawn after a death (`cup_keeper_instances` churn) with
the claim resumed, or a passing restart drill.

→ subsequent Kettle scorecard covering the window → blender routed-ledger
(`harness_shared.scout_routed_ideas`; `routed_at` is epoch ms) / outcome update.

Execution evidence (amended 2026-07-16): `cup_keeper_runs` rows exist ONLY for IQ-battery
executions — ORGANIC cup executions live in `harness_shared.spawned_agents`
(`child_role='cup'`; a completed run = `status='done'` with `duration_ms`). Accept either
for the execution hop; requiring a matching `cup_keeper_runs` row for an organic placement
makes the criterion unpassable by construction.

Drill traversals count only when marked `origin='drill'` and run on the current generation.

entries.text:
autoloop-release-readiness — grading runbook › placement-throughput · `pot-throughput-ticks`
Rolling 24h. The Mug must place when frontier is nonempty and cup capacity free.

```sql
SELECT tick_at, frontier_depth, placements, cups_busy, cups_cap
FROM harness_shared.pot_throughput_ticks
WHERE workspace_id='papercusp-workspace' AND tick_at > now()-interval '24 hours'
ORDER BY tick_at;
```

`pass` = no run of ≥3 consecutive stuck ticks (`frontier_depth>0 AND cups_busy<cups_cap AND placements=0`),
excluding ticks where the pool is genuinely walled (see capacity-admission).
`fail` = sustained stuck runs, or zero placements all window with a nonempty frontier.

Three measurement caveats:

* **Instrument history starts 2026-07-16 \~22:42Z.** Every tick before that recorded
  placements/completed/mttc/stuck as 0/null unconditionally — the feeding query threw on
  every tick and was silently caught (EI-13076: drizzle mutated the shared client's date
  serializers). Do NOT read pre-fix ticks as evidence of anything; the first honest window
  opens at the fix's bg-host activation.
* **Ticks fire \~every 30s but placements are sparse by design** — the Mug paces placement
  by ranking/backpressure, so consecutive `placements=0` ticks with free capacity are
  normal cadence, not automatically starvation. Judge the stuck-run predicate over
  30-60min windows (does the frontier DRAIN? do placements appear at all?), and check
  bg-host journal `pool-shed` lines first: a tick GAP is the load-shed guardrail pausing
  the ticker (EI-13108), not a dead Mug.
* **`frontier_depth` is READY depth only from 2026-07-17 \~06:00Z** (EI-12461). Before
  that it was the placeable-SHAPED count — `todo`+unassigned+admissible but *including*
  rows whose `blocked_by` / plan-item chain was unsatisfied. A dependency-chained wave
  therefore ticked `frontier_depth≈14` through \~2.5h of CORRECT zero placement
  (2026-07-17 02:44–05:19Z) and scorecard EI-13660 failed placement-throughput on a
  phantom s

entries.text:
autoloop-release-readiness — grading runbook › The one main procedure
1. **Generation stamp first.** Record the generation you are grading BEFORE
   gathering evidence: `blender:success-metrics { watermarkRef: 'bg-host-restart' }`
   (runningGeneration echo) + `dev:pipeline_position` (release sha on `:3070`) +
   `systemctl --user show papercup-bg-host.service -p ActiveEnterTimestamp`.
   Evidence gathered across a host-restart boundary is invalid — re-gather.
2. **Gather instrument snapshots per criterion** (queries below). Each criterion
   binds ONE instrument (`instrumentKey`); the typed grading path verifies the
   snapshot set against the rubric's instrument contract.
3. **Emit via the typed path** — never prose:
   `scorecards:evaluate { rubricRef: 'autoloop-release-readiness' }` → fill the
   returned skeleton → `scorecards:evaluate { rubricRef, ratings, instrumentSnapshots }`
   (validates + fingerprints) → `scorecards:emit` the canonical result.
4. **Rate honestly.** `unknown` beats invented; a criterion whose fix is live but
   whose window has not yet cleared is `at-risk` with the clearing time stated in
   evidence, not `pass`.
5. **Cadence:** ≤6h between complete scorecards while the rubric is release-gating.

entries.text:
Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op
Bash is \~41% of all tool use on this box. Not because the tools are missing — 690 of them
exist — but because nothing **routes** an agent from the shell command it was about to type
to the tool that already answers the question. The substitution registry is that routing
layer, and this doc is how to work on it.

Read this before you: add a row, promote a row, argue with a gate that blocked you, or ship
a new tool that is meant to replace a bash pattern.
entries.description: Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op

entries.text:
Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › 1. The registry is the single source of truth
One list, three projections. Add a pair to the list and all three follow; edit a projection
by hand and a check fails the build.

```
packages/operator-core/lib/bash-substitution/pairs/*.ts
                    │
                    ▼
              ALL_PAIRS  (pairs/index.ts)
                    │
    ┌───────────────┼────────────────────────────┐
    ▼               ▼                            ▼
equivalence.test  gen:tool-routing         seed:substitutions
 (the verdict)    → CLAUDE.md table    → harness_shared.bash_tool_substitutions
                       (what you read)     (what the PreToolUse gate enforces)
```

* **`ALL_PAIRS`** in `packages/operator-core/lib/bash-substitution/pairs/index.ts` is the
  list. A pair not exported there is neither tested nor enforced; a pair added there is
  automatically both.
* It is **"pairs we have EVIDENCE about", not "pairs we enforce"** — negative results stay in
  the list on purpose. `PROCESS_PAIRS` carries a `not-a-substitute` verdict so the conclusion
  is durable and re-derived on every test run instead of being re-litigated every quarter.
  The routing generator filters those out of `CLAUDE.md`, and the database constraint pins
  them at `observe`.
* **The registry is DATA in Postgres, not logic in a hook** (D-002). The hooks contain no
  patterns; they ask the operator. That is why a row can be added, narrowed, or paused
  without touching a shell script.
entries.description: Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › 1. The registry is the single source of truth

entries.text:
Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › 2. Anatomy of a pair
Defined by `SubstitutionPair` in `packages/operator-core/lib/bash-substitution/types.ts`:

| field                          | what it is                                                                                        |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `id`                           | stable registry id, e.g. `file-read.sed-range`                                                    |
| `intentLabel`                  | the intent an advisory speaks about, e.g. `file-range-read`. **This is the registry KEY** (D-023) |
| `bashPattern`                  | a RegExp matched against ONE normalised atom                                                      |
| `toolName`                     | the tool that should have served it                                                               |
| `advisoryText`                 | the sentence the agent reads at `advise`/`deny`                                                   |
| `routing.{want,use,insteadOf}` | the three `CLAUDE.md` table cells — display fields, deliberately not derived                      |
| `expectedVerdict`              | the verdict this pair is RECORDED as carrying — the anti-rot latch                                |
| `policyTier?`                  | the one authorized way to enter above `observe` (§5)                                              |
| `holdAtObserve?`               | the mirror: pin this row TO `observe`, whatever its verdict. Value is the required reason (§5)    |
| `cover(atom)`                  | **the heart** — models what the tool can ACTUALLY express                                         |

`cover()` is where the honesty lives. It must model the tool's real arguments and real
limits, read from the tool definition — not whether the tool is *nominally related
entries.description: Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › 2. Anatomy of a pair

entries.text:
Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › 4. The verdict and its three honest exits
`deriveVerdict` / `auditPair` in `equivalence.ts` produce one of:

| verdict            | meaning                                                            | max tier  |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------- |
| `equivalent`       | every sampled command has a faithful tool expression               | `advise`  |
| `needs-widening`   | some sampled commands have no tool expression — and it names them  | `observe` |
| `not-a-substitute` | the tool answers a **different question**. Never gate this pattern | `observe` |
| `unaudited`        | no audit has run                                                   | `observe` |

A `needs-widening` verdict has exactly **two** honest exits (D-008): **narrow the PATTERN**,
or **widen the TOOL**. Never lower the coverage bar. Which exit is right is decided by the
*shape of the misses*, not by taste — and in practice the misses cluster on a single axis
that tells you the answer. When every miss is a genuinely different question (socket STATE
vs socket LISTEN), the pattern was over-claiming: narrow it. When the misses are the
intent's *majority* case, the tool is not a substitute at all.

There is a third exit that is not a fix: record `not-a-substitute` and keep the row as a
durable negative result.
entries.description: Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › 4. The verdict and its three honest exits

entries.text:
Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › 5. The tier ladder: observe → advise → deny
Three tiers, reusing what the PreToolUse gate already implements. **Add no fourth
mechanism** (D-003).

* **`observe`** — a **staging** state. Emits nothing: both hooks act only on `advise`/`deny`,
  and `locks:check_command` returns the tier without recording it.
* **`advise`** — ride out as `additionalContext` on an **allow**. Teach, never block.
* **`deny`** — hard block. Reserved for rules that **already existed independently**.
entries.description: Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › 5. The tier ladder: observe → advise → deny

entries.text:
Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › 6. Verify it LIVE — a green suite is not evidence the gate runs
**This is the most important section in this doc.** It is here because the registry spent its
entire first observation window enforcing *nothing*, behind 831 passing tests.

The failure (D-041, `EI-18787146155365536`): both PreToolUse hooks `JSON.parse` the result of
`locks:check_command`. The agent transport serializes a tabular result as **TOON**, not JSON.
The parse threw. The hooks are mandatorily **fail-open**, so the throw silently disabled
every resource hold *and* all 21 substitution rows — on both hook paths — and nothing logged
an error anywhere. The test suites never saw it because they stubbed the operator with JSON,
the one thing the real operator does not send.

Three generalisations, in increasing order of how much they will cost you:

1. **A fail-open client that never declares its wire format becomes a no-op the day the
   server starts compacting.** The fix is one line — `_meta: {'format': 'json'}` on the
   request — and the recurrence guard is a stub that *negotiates* rather than always
   replying JSON, so removing the declaration reds the tests.
2. **A stub that can only reply in one format can never observe a format bug.** If your test
   double is more cooperative than the real thing, it is not a test double.
3. **Seeding a row and reading a green suite is not shipping a rule.** Drive the real client
   against the running operator.
entries.description: Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › 6. Verify it LIVE — a green suite is not evidence the gate runs

entries.text:
Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › 7. Filing a false positive
If a row claimed a command it should not have — you were blocked, or advised, on something
the tool genuinely cannot express:

1. **File it.** `improvements:capture { kind: 'bug' }`, with the **raw command** verbatim,
   the row's `intentLabel`, and what the tool could not express. The raw command matters:
   classification is done on the raw string, and a paraphrase loses the shape that caused
   the match.
2. **The filing pauses that row's promotion.** It does not need anyone's agreement first.
3. **The fix is D-008's two exits** — narrow the pattern (usual) or widen the tool (when the
   miss is the intent's majority case). Never lower the coverage bar, and never special-case
   your one command.
4. **Do not route around a deny.** If the block is wrong, the pattern is wrong; fix the
   pattern. A deny's budget is \~0 false positives, so a real one is a genuine defect and is
   treated as such.
entries.description: Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › 7. Filing a false positive

entries.text:
Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › 8. Definition of done for a NEW tool (D-004)
A tool that replaces a bash pattern is **DONE only with all three artifacts**:

1. **An equivalence-audit entry** proving it covers the real bash corpus it replaces —
   sampled from actual transcripts, not from imagination.
2. **A `bash_tool_substitutions` row**, so the gate advises on the bash form the moment the
   tool exists.
3. **A `CLAUDE.md` routing row**, generated from that same registry row.

The numbers behind this are unusually stark. 690 tools exist and Bash is still 41% of all
tool use. The one tool that had all three artifacts (`dev:pg_query`) sits at \~85% adoption;
the ones with none sit at \~1%. `install:safe` — a documented, mandated command with no
routing row — had **zero uses in seven days** while the unsafe form ran 60× across 15
sessions.

**A mandate with 0% adoption is a comment, not a mandate.** Shipping the tool is the easy
half; routing agents to it is the half that decides whether it exists in practice.

Two corollaries worth stating separately:

* **A mis-routing tool is fixed by making its description tell the truth** — not by widening
  it, and not by fighting the ranking (D-014).
* **A `not-a-substitute` row is never surfaced to an agent** (D-026). If the guidance you
  want to deliver is "do X instead of Y" for a pair that is *not* an equivalence, the
  registry is the wrong channel — that guidance belongs in `CLAUDE.md`.
entries.description: Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › 8. Definition of done for a NEW tool (D-004)

entries.text:
Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › 9. Traps, in the order they will bite you
| trap                                         | what happens                                                                                                                                                         | the rule                                                   |
| -------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `\b`-anchored pattern                        | `atomize` splits inside quoted regexes, so a `grep -E "npm install\|npm ci"` search string becomes an atom that looks like a command; your row denies the diagnostic | anchor on whole-command shape, end-anchored (D-038, D-023) |
| hand-picked fixture                          | you measure your imagination, not the corpus                                                                                                                         | build the sample from the pair's OWN `bashPattern`         |
| `cover()` returning true broadly             | `equivalent` unlocks enforcement, then blocks agents with no alternative                                                                                             | model the tool's REAL argument surface (D-001)             |
| editing `pairs/` and stopping at green tests | the DB rows silently rot; `CLAUDE.md` and the gate disagree                                                                                                          | D-020: both `:check`s, from the repo root                  |
| running seeds from a subdirectory            | `Missing script: seed:substitutions` — the shell's cwd leaks between calls
entries.description: Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › 9. Traps, in the order they will bite you

entries.text:
Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › `equivalent` is not a mandate — a pair may hold itself back
A row can be provably equivalent and still be wrong to enforce: "the tool can express this"
and "the agent should be pushed to use it" are different claims. A pair states that with
**`holdAtObserve`**, whose value is the required reason:

```ts
holdAtObserve: 'D-011: capability:git is a pass-through, so this row offers the SAME answer…',
```

`promoteEarnedRows` skips a held row **and demotes one that has drifted above `observe`**.
That self-heal is not tidiness. D-011 recorded this hold for the git-read row in a decision
body — and a later promotion that selected on `equivalence_verdict` alone swept it into
`advise` anyway, firing the registry's largest advisory (\~2,500 calls/week across 77 of 86
sessions) for a benefit D-011 had already argued was near-zero for the superuser role. The
seeder deliberately never demotes, so nothing would have pulled it back.

> **A constraint that lives only in prose will eventually be violated by someone acting in
> good faith on the data.** Carry it in the data — `holdAtObserve` is the mirror of
> `policyTier` (§5) for exactly this reason.
entries.description: Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › `equivalent` is not a mandate — a pair may hold itself back

entries.text:
Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › `observe` does not observe — `advise` is the observation window (D-042)
P-020 originally said: run at `observe` for 48h, then review hit-rate and false-positive
reports. That window could not work, and it is worth understanding why before you design
another one:

* **Nothing logs an `observe` match.** `pretooluse-bash-resource-gate.sh` acts only on
  `if _stier in ('advise','deny')`; `coord-hook.ts` is the same shape; `locks:check_command`
  computes the tier and records nothing.
* **Hit-rate never depended on the tier.** `bashAtoms` comes from `tool_usage_rollup`,
  attributed at session-ingest by replaying patterns over transcripts (native `Bash` never
  reaches `tool_invocations`, D-012). It accrues identically at any tier —
  `activity:bash-substitution-report` will tell you now.
* **False positives cannot arrive at `observe` at all.** A false-positive report needs an
  agent to SEE a claim and disagree. At `observe` nobody is shown anything, so
  `false_positive_count` is pinned at 0 by construction.

So the window could only ever conclude "48h elapsed, zero false positives" — the same
verdict whether the rules were perfect or catastrophic.

**`advise` is the real window.** It is the first visible tier, and it is safe to observe from
because it cannot block: the shell hook rides it out on an explicit `allow`, and OMP uses the
`followUp` reminder rather than `steer` (which aborts the in-flight tool). The full window and
the zero-false-positive bar still gate `advise → deny` — that is the transition P-020's
precedent is actually about (the shell-write guard false-positiving on a `>` inside a heredoc
**blocked** work).

**Don't wait for evidence you could go and measure.** Instead of a passive window, run the
documented caveats through the live registry and read the verdicts (§6). That is what
promoted these rows: 0/12 false positives across every caveat, `npm ci` sti
entries.description: Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › `observe` does not observe — `advise` is the observation window (D-042)

entries.text:
Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › Pin the model to the real tool
A hand-written `cover()` is a *copy* of the tool's argument surface, and copies rot. Two
guards, both earned the hard way:

* **`expectedVerdict` catches pattern-side drift** — widen the pattern without re-recording
  the verdict and the test fails.
* It does **not** catch **tool-side** widening: the tool grows an argument, the model does
  not, and the pair silently under-claims forever. So a pair that hand-models its tool needs
  a **drift guard** tying the model to the real export (D-015), and that guard pins the
  tool's **argument surface**, not just the constants it copied (D-016). See
  `pairs/model-drift-helpers.ts` and `pairs/model-drift.test.ts`.
entries.description: Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › Pin the model to the real tool

entries.text:
Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › Step 0 — measure first, decide second
Every substantive decision in this registry was made by measurement, and several were made
*against* the intuition that preceded them. Before writing a pattern, get the population:
how many atoms, across how many distinct sessions, and what do the misses have in common?
The corpus helpers (`loadCorpusAtoms`, `sampleDistinct`, `buildFixture`) are in
`packages/operator-core/lib/bash-substitution/corpus.ts`.
entries.description: Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › Step 0 — measure first, decide second

entries.text:
Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › Step 1 — write the pair
Add it to the right family file under `packages/operator-core/lib/bash-substitution/pairs/`
(or a new one, exported from `pairs/index.ts`).

**Anchor the pattern on whole-command shape.** `atomize` splits on `|`, *including* a `|`
inside a quoted regex — so the search string of a `grep -E "npm install|npm ci"` becomes an
atom that looks exactly like a command (D-038). A `\b`-anchored pattern claims it and you
end up denying the mid-incident diagnostic. Patterns should also be **END-anchored** (D-023):
match the whole command shape, not a prefix of it.
entries.description: Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › Step 1 — write the pair

entries.text:
Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › Step 2 — build the fixture from the pair's OWN pattern
The fixture is `fixtures/<pair-id>.sample.json`: `evidenceRef`, `extractedAt`, `totalAtoms`,
`totalSessions`, and a `sample[]` of `{sid, ts, atom}`. Build it by running **the pair's own
`bashPattern`** over the corpus — never by hand-picking commands you know the tool handles.
A hand-picked sample measures your imagination.

`fixtures/deps.unsafe-install.sample.json` and its builder are the template to copy.
entries.description: Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › Step 2 — build the fixture from the pair's OWN pattern

entries.text:
Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › Step 3 — run the audit, read the verdict
```bash
npm run test:file -- packages/operator-core/lib/bash-substitution/equivalence.test.ts
```

Record the computed verdict in `expectedVerdict`. If it is not what you expected, §4 says
which of the honest exits to take — **do not** widen `cover()` until it returns the verdict
you wanted.
entries.description: Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › Step 3 — run the audit, read the verdict

entries.text:
Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › Step 4 — project it
```bash
npm run gen:tool-routing          # WRITE: regenerates the CLAUDE.md routing table
npm run gen:tool-routing:check    # must exit 0
npm run seed:substitutions        # upsert the rows (from the repo ROOT)
npm run seed:substitutions:check  # must exit 0
```
entries.description: Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › Step 4 — project it

entries.text:
Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › The end-to-end check — run this for every row you add or promote
```bash
printf '%s' '{"tool_name":"Bash","tool_input":{"command":"npm ci"}}' \
  | PAPERCUSP_OPERATOR_URL=http://localhost:3170 \
    bash apps/operator/scripts/hooks/cc/pretooluse-bash-resource-gate.sh
```

Reading the result:

| output                                         | meaning                                                             |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| a JSON `hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision` | **the gate actually ran** — read the decision and the advisory text |
| **empty output**                               | **ALLOW** — which is also exactly what a total fail-open looks like |

That ambiguity is the whole trap: an empty response is indistinguishable from a dead client.
So **always run a positive control** — a command you expect the row to claim — and confirm it
produces a decision. Only then are your negative controls (the commands that must *not* be
claimed) meaningful.

Verified against `:3170` on 2026-07-27: `npm ci` → `deny` with the authored advisory;
`npm run install:safe` and `ls -la` → empty (allow).

Use `:3170` (staging), not `:3070`. The Hono host has no file-watch, and `:3070` serves the
green release checkout — your edit is not there yet. `dev:restart { target: 'staging',
confirm: true }` first if you changed server-side code.
entries.description: Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › The end-to-end check — run this for every row you add or promote

entries.text:
Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › The one authorized way past `observe`
`maxTierFor()` **never returns `deny`**. An equivalence score alone can never unlock a
block — no amount of measured coverage authorizes prohibition, because coverage is a *cost*
argument and a block is a *correctness* argument.

`deny` is a separate class: a rule that already existed independently of this registry, for
which the registry supplies a *mechanism* rather than a *judgement*. Such a rule has nothing
to observe — the decision was taken elsewhere, before the pattern was ever measured.

That authorization is carried **in the data**, not in reviewer memory (D-039):

```ts
// pairs/dependency-install.ts — the registry's only deny
intentLabel: 'policy-violation:unsafe-dependency-install',
policyTier: 'deny',
```

`assertPolicyTier()` refuses any pair that sets `policyTier` without the
`policy-violation:` prefix on its `intentLabel`, mirroring migration 665's
`tier_requires_equivalence` CHECK so the invariant is stated in the same terms on both sides
of the wire. A cost argument ("the tool is cheaper") can never reach `deny` this way.

**A deny's false-positive budget is \~0**, so its pattern must be *narrower than its problem*
(D-040) — and narrowed **structurally against the corpus**, not by imagination. The install
deny is the worked example: of 60 install-shaped atoms, 24 were `grep -E "npm install|npm ci"`
fragments (denying those blocks the mid-install diagnostic), and a named-package install may
target a scratch tree `install:safe` cannot reach. One readable rule covers both — the verb,
followed by nothing but flags and redirects.

entries.text:
Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › The one-paragraph model
A **pair** is `(bash pattern → tool)` plus a machine-checkable model of what the tool can
actually express. Pairs live in TypeScript. Each one is audited against real commands
sampled from real transcripts, which yields a **verdict**. The verdict caps the **tier** the
row may be enforced at. Everything an agent ever sees — the routing table in `CLAUDE.md`,
the advisory a PreToolUse hook attaches, the hard block on a policy violation — is a
*projection* of that same list, so prose and enforcement cannot drift apart.
entries.description: Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › The one-paragraph model

entries.text:
Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › The sample floor, and the census escape hatch
`MIN_SAMPLE_SIZE = 20` — but the sample is built with `sampleDistinct`, so it counts distinct
**spellings**, not commands. Read literally, the floor rejected any intent expressed in fewer
than 20 different ways: a statement about *vocabulary*, not evidence. It inverted its own
purpose — `^uptime`, 116 commands across 36 independent sessions, failed as "too rare to
enforce", while a 24-spelling pattern across 30 commands passed.

And low spelling-variety is precisely the property that makes a family worth acting on: an
intent everyone types **identically** is the one a single fixed answer can serve.

So `auditPair(pair, corpus, population?)` takes an optional population, and a pattern backed
by at least `MIN_POPULATION_ATOMS` atoms across `MIN_POPULATION_SESSIONS` (5) distinct
sessions clears the floor on **census** evidence instead of spelling variety (D-036). Use it
for homogeneous families; do not use it to rescue a pattern nobody actually runs.

Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › The three projections, and what guards each
| projection                         | written by                         | guarded by                                                                                      |
| ---------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| the `CLAUDE.md` routing table      | `npm run gen:tool-routing`         | `npm run gen:tool-routing:check` — **fails the build** on drift (no DB needed)                  |
| the `bash_tool_substitutions` rows | `npm run seed:substitutions`       | `npm run seed:substitutions:check` — **advisory**, exits 0 with a notice when PG is unreachable |
| the recorded verdict on each pair  | the pair's `expectedVerdict` field | `equivalence.test.ts` recomputes it from the fixture and asserts equality                       |

`seed:substitutions:check` is deliberately advisory rather than a build gate: it needs
Postgres, and a check that reds the fleet gate every time PG is down gets deleted within a
week — a deleted check catches nothing. **Run it yourself after any edit under `pairs/`.**

> **Standing rule (D-020).** After ANY edit under
> `packages/operator-core/lib/bash-substitution/pairs/`, run BOTH
> `npm run gen:tool-routing:check` and `npm run seed:substitutions:check`. A *new* pair or a
> *flipped verdict* additionally needs `npm run gen:tool-routing` (the WRITE) first, then a
> re-seed. Run them from the **repo root** — the shell's cwd leaks between calls and you will
> get `Missing script: seed:substitutions` from a subdirectory.
>
> D-020 exists because the ungated projection rotted while its gated sibling stayed correct:
> three separate changes updated `CLAUDE.md` (because `--check` fails the build) and updated
> the database not at all (because nothing checked and nothing ran). O

entries.text:
Bash vs tool routing — the substitution registry, and how to add a row without shipping a no-op › Where the numbers come from
The substitution metric is counted **at ingest from transcripts**, never from Postgres
(D-012), and the intent **bucket is matched at ingest**, not derived from a verb at read time
(D-013) — see `packages/operator-core/lib/search/session-ingest.ts` and
`packages/operator-core/lib/bash-substitution/usage-rollup.ts`.

Measure **per-bucket, not in aggregate** (D-006). A bucket that does not move after its row
lands is a signal, and it says which of two things went wrong: the tool is not actually
equivalent (send it back to the equivalence audit), or the advisory text is not landing
(rewrite it). Record which, per bucket. Do not declare success on the aggregate number.

A behavior cutover isn't done when :3070 is fixed — enumerate EVERY process that loads the changed module › Related: the psu-pty-host side already screams on a stale sender
`psu-pty-host.mjs`'s control-message handler treats an incoming `mode:'compact'`
as proof of a stale pre-P-022 sender (since no current code ever sends it) and
drops it **loudly** — an `appendHostEvent('retired-mode-dropped', …)` durable
row plus a `stderr` line naming EI-16190 and telling the operator to find and
restart the stale sender. That fix protects the *receiving* side (the psu-pty
host); the watchdog self-check above protects the *sending* side (bg-host)
from staying stale in the first place. Both matter: a receiver-side loud-drop
only helps if something is watching stderr/host-events; a sender-side boot
self-check surfaces the problem the moment the stale process starts, without
requiring the stale behavior to ever actually fire.
entries.description: A behavior cutover isn't done when :3070 is fixed — enumerate EVERY process that loads the changed module › Related: the psu-pty-host side already screams on a stale sender

entries.text:
A behavior cutover isn't done when :3070 is fixed — enumerate EVERY process that loads the changed module › The added defense: a boot-time self-check on the enforcer itself
Since a human can forget step 1–3 for some future cutover the same way this one
was missed, `compaction-compliance-watchdog.ts` now self-checks at start:

* `WATCHDOG_BEHAVIOR_CUTOVERS` is a small registry of `{ id, atMs, note }` —
  one entry per known behavior cutover this watchdog's code must run at-or-after.
* `staleCutoversForProcessStart(processStartedAtMs, cutovers?)` is a pure,
  exported, unit-tested function: given this process's boot instant, it returns
  which known cutovers it *predates*.
* `startCompactionComplianceWatchdog()` computes its own boot instant
  (`Date.now() - process.uptime() * 1000`), logs a one-line version/boot stamp
  on every start (so a stale host is trivially greppable across every host's
  logs: `journalctl | grep 'compaction-watchdog] starting'`), and — if it
  predates any registered cutover — logs a loud `console.warn` AND raises a
  best-effort advisory coord escalation (deduped per process) naming the exact
  cutover it missed and telling the operator to restart it.

Add a new entry to `WATCHDOG_BEHAVIOR_CUTOVERS` for every future watchdog
behavior change so the *next* forgotten-process class self-flags at boot
instead of running silently for 13 hours until an owner notices garbled
context-usage behavior.

entries.text:
A behavior cutover isn't done when :3070 is fixed — enumerate EVERY process that loads the changed module › The durable checklist for the *next* behavior cutover
Before declaring a behavior cutover complete, enumerate **every process** that
loads the changed module — not just the one a deploy restarts:

1. `rg` the import chain from the changed module outward. For anything reached
   through `dbos/bootstrap.ts`, that means every process that calls the shared
   bootstrap: `:3070` (`papercup-dev-api`), `:3170` (staging), AND standalone
   long-lived hosts like `papercup-bg-host.service` that boot the same
   bootstrap function outside the request-serving process.
2. Also check the gateway / embed-sidecar processes if the change touches
   anything they load — they're the same class of "deploy doesn't restart me"
   process as bg-host.
3. **Restart each one explicitly** as part of the cutover, don't assume the
   deploy pipeline covers it. `dev:restart { target: 'bg-host' }` is the tool
   for bg-host specifically.
4. If a genuinely-independent audit exists for the behavior being retired (like
   `native-compaction-audit.ts`), remember what it actually proves: session
   outcomes, not enforcer freshness. It cannot substitute for step 1–3.

entries.text:
A behavior cutover isn't done when :3070 is fixed — enumerate EVERY process that loads the changed module › TL;DR for the next agent
A deploy that restarts `:3070` is not the same as "every process that runs this
code got the fix." Grep the import chain for every long-lived standalone host
(bg-host, gateway, embed-sidecar) before declaring a cutover done, and restart
each one explicitly. A session-outcome audit (no native compact\_boundary rows)
proves sessions behaved — it does not prove the enforcer is current; you need
both an outcome audit and an enforcer freshness check.

entries.text:
A behavior cutover isn't done when :3070 is fixed — enumerate EVERY process that loads the changed module › What
P-022 (WI-4998, "native `/compact` is retired") shipped, deployed, and *looked*
fully cut over: `:3070` restarted into the new code, every psu Claude child ran
with `DISABLE_COMPACT`, and the zero-invocation transcript audit
(`native-compaction-audit.ts`) found no `compact_boundary` rows in sessions
started after the cutover. Verdict: clean.

Except **`papercup-bg-host.service`** — a separate, long-lived process that also
loads `compaction-compliance-watchdog.ts` (via `dbos/bootstrap.ts`'s
`startCompactionComplianceWatchdog`) — had been running since **2026-07-17
22:26Z**, hours before the P-022 rewrite landed. A deploy restarts `:3070`; it
does **not** restart bg-host. So for \~13 hours, bg-host's watchdog kept
force-injecting the OLD `mode:'compact'` control message into live psu-pty
hosts. The current-code psu-pty-host had no handler for that stale mode
("Unknown command: `/compact`" from the CLI, since `DISABLE_COMPACT=1`), so
the inject silently no-op'd — the agent got a **false** "you were just
compacted" continuation banner while its context stayed exactly where it was.

entries.text:
A behavior cutover isn't done when :3070 is fixed — enumerate EVERY process that loads the changed module › Why the existing audit couldn't catch this
The transcript audit is a **completion-criterion check on sessions**: it scans
Claude project transcripts for `compact_boundary` rows and asserts none exist
post-cutover. That is the right check for *"did any session actually
native-compact,"* but it has no visibility into *"is the enforcer itself
running current code."* A stale enforcer that fails safe (drops the write) or
fails silently (the psu-pty host of 2026-07-17) produces **zero** transcript
evidence either way — the audit reads "clean" while the enforcement mechanism
underneath it is broken. **Session-side auditing and enforcer-side freshness
are orthogonal; you need both.**

peer_connected ✓ but federation dead: the boot→wire-drain ordering trap (EI-521) › Fix — wiring must be idempotent + retryable, attempted on the already-booted path
`ensureSendSideWired(handle)` brings the outbox drain + presence announce online,
marking each step wired **only on success**, coalescing concurrent calls, and
running on **both** the fresh-boot and the `already-booted` paths. A transient
failure then self-heals on the next boot pass (the periodic boot-all reconcile /
`rebootHarness`) instead of staying dead until restart. Wired-state is cleared on
close/reset so a reboot re-wires from scratch.
entries.description: peer_connected ✓ but federation dead: the boot→wire-drain ordering trap (EI-521) › Fix — wiring must be idempotent + retryable, attempted on the already-booted path

entries.text:
peer_connected ✓ but federation dead: the boot→wire-drain ordering trap (EI-521) › Root cause — cache-before-wire + the already-booted short-circuit
In `bootSingleHarness` (`packages/operator-core/lib/sync/hyperbee/boot-all.ts`)
the handle was cached **before** the send-side was wired:

```
handles.set(k, handle);          // ← cached FIRST
try { await wireOutboxForHarness(handle, sql); } catch { /* swallowed + logged */ }
```

So if wiring ever throws (a `getOrgPg()` hiccup on a fresh-VM boot is enough),
the handle is cached **without a drain loop**. And because it's now cached, every
later `bootSingleHarness` hits the `if (handles.has(k)) return 'already-booted'`
short-circuit and **never re-wires**. Federation for that harness is dead until
the process restarts. This is the parsimonious explanation for "peer\_connected ✓
but 0 drain loops" — better than the slug / workspace-id mismatch hypotheses
(both code-refuted: the mig-102 capture trigger stamps `NEW.harness_slug` and the
join boots under that same slug + workspace).

Note what is **not** the cause, to save you the dead ends:

* **Not** `boot-all`'s path-liveness filter (the `existsSync(path)` skip). A
  `join-link` member registers a real clone `path`, and the confirmed repro runs
  **with no restart**, so `boot-all` isn't even on the path.
* **Not** a boot timeout from a slow DHT: `joinHarnessSwarm` does
  `void discovery.flushed()` (fire-and-forget), so swarm connectivity never
  blocks the boot promise.
entries.description: peer_connected ✓ but federation dead: the boot→wire-drain ordering trap (EI-521) › Root cause — cache-before-wire + the already-booted short-circuit

entries.text:
peer_connected ✓ but federation dead: the boot→wire-drain ordering trap (EI-521) › Symptom
Cross-machine pot federation **merge** is dead: a joined member's local write
(feature / issue / coord) is captured into `harness_shared.substrate_outbox` but
**never drains** to the replicated log, so the peer never receives it — while
`[swarm] peer_connected` fires normally. The tell on a live frame:

* `substrate_outbox` has the undrained row (`drained_at IS NULL`),
* `peer_connected ✓` (the swarm joined),
* **0 drain loops** running for that harness.

Connection ≠ federation. The swarm join and the outbox drain are wired
**independently**; the swarm can be up while the drain never started.
entries.description: peer_connected ✓ but federation dead: the boot→wire-drain ordering trap (EI-521) › Symptom

entries.text:
peer_connected ✓ but federation dead: the boot→wire-drain ordering trap (EI-521) › When you see this again
Reach for `wireOutboxForHarness` / `ensureSendSideWired` and ask: did the drain
loop actually start, or did a swallowed wiring failure leave a cached-but-drainless
handle? On a live joined member, `SELECT id, table_name, harness_slug,
workspace_id, drained_at FROM harness_shared.substrate_outbox` + whether a drain
loop is counted pins it. Cross-machine confirmation needs `deb-hetzner-federation.sh`
(the pot flow + `fed_hive_merge_probe`), not a single-box run.

entries.text:
peer_connected ✓ but federation dead: the boot→wire-drain ordering trap (EI-521) › Why the tests didn't catch it (the blind spot to avoid repeating)
Three things were each proven in isolation, but the **seam between them was not**:

* `outbox-drain.integration.test.ts` drives `startOutboxDrain` **directly**.
* `feature-content-federation.integration.test.ts` proves the full A↔B round-trip
  but calls `drainOutboxOnce` **manually**, and boots via `bootHarnessSubstrate`
  directly.
* `join-default-boot-wiring.test.ts` proves the join orchestrator **calls**
  `bootSingleHarness` — but **mocks** it.

So nothing proved the *live* `bootSingleHarness → wireOutboxForHarness →
startOutboxDrain` loop actually comes online. A federation test that **drains by
hand** can never catch a drain loop that never started. The regression guard is
`wire-outbox-drain-online.integration.test.ts`: write a row *after*
`wireOutboxForHarness` and assert it is **auto-drained by the loop** (no manual
`drainOutboxOnce`), plus a negative control for `(workspace, harness)` scoping.

claude-code headless permission model (what --allowed-tools / --permission-mode actually do) › Honest limits (the deny-list alone is not a sandbox)
**Update (`fleet-spawn-sandbox-2026-06-01`, P-013/D-015): there is now a
DEFAULT-ON sandbox layered on top of this deny-list** — claude-code's OWN
built-in sandbox (Linux bubblewrap + socat egress proxy; macOS Seatbelt),
injected via `--settings`, opt-out with `PAPERCUSP_FLEET_SANDBOX=0`. It closes
the two gaps the deny-list cannot: it hides credential dirs
(`FLEET_SANDBOX_DENY_READ` — `~/.ssh`, `~/.aws`, `~/.gnupg`, `~/.config/gcloud`,
`~/.papercusp`, `~/.npmrc`) from sandboxed Bash and confines egress to an
allow-listed set of package registries (`resolveFleetAllowedDomains()`;
strip-all with `PAPERCUSP_FLEET_SANDBOX_DENY_ALL_EGRESS=1`). The bullets below
describe the **deny-list layer in isolation** — i.e. the posture *before* that
sandbox, which is now the default container for those reads/egress.

* **Credential reads are not closed by the deny-list** — the allow-listed `Read`
  tool reaches any path. **Network egress is not closed by the deny-list** —
  `WebFetch` is allow-listed. True containment of those needs a network/fs
  sandbox, not a deny-list — which is what the default-on sandbox above now is.
* **Worktree isolation is conditional** — `invoke.ts` falls back to
  `ctx.projectDir` (the shared main checkout) when there's no feature-worktree,
  so "the worker is contained in a worktree" is not universally true.
* Per-role *tightening* of the built-in dev kit (e.g. deny `Write` to read-only
  roles) is deliberately NOT done — it needs per-role real-spawn verification
  because withholding a needed built-in silently breaks a role mid-pipeline.

entries.text:
claude-code headless permission model (what --allowed-tools / --permission-mode actually do) › How to re-verify (don't trust the docs here)
Test against the real CLI with an **external side-effect** (a file on disk, not
just a `tool_use` block in the stream — a denied call still shows an attempt).
Use a pristine `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` (copy in only `.credentials.json`, no
settings) so a stray `settings.local.json` allow-rule can't confound the result.
Pattern that settled it:

```
claude -p "use a shell command to create file X containing Y" \
  --permission-mode dontAsk --allowed-tools "Read" --output-format json
# then check whether file X exists — exists = the tool ran, absent = denied.
```

entries.text:
claude-code headless permission model (what --allowed-tools / --permission-mode actually do) › The model (all verified, not assumed)
1. **`--allowed-tools` is NOT a whitelist on its own.** It's a *pre-approval*
   list (don't-prompt-for-these). What an *un-listed* tool does depends on
   `--permission-mode`:
   * Under **`bypassPermissions`** the allow-list is **ignored entirely** —
     everything runs. (Verified: Bash wrote a file with only `Read` allow-listed.)
   * Under **`default`** the tool still *runs*, but `default` applies a
     **sandbox** that blocks filesystem-writes-outside-workdir + network.
     (Verified: a CWD write was blocked.) → `default` breaks file-writing roles;
     do not use it for the fleet.

2. **`--permission-mode dontAsk` makes `--allowed-tools` a true default-deny
   whitelist** — an un-listed *gated* tool is denied, the model is told, and it
   continues (no hang). Unlike `default`, `dontAsk` does **not** sandbox the
   allowed tools, so writes/edits work. **This is the posture the fleet uses.**

3. **`dontAsk` gating is NON-uniform.** A class of session-local / "meta"
   built-ins is **exempt** from the allow-list and runs even when omitted.
   Verified: with the exact fleet allow-list, `CronCreate` still created a job
   and `EnterWorktree` still ran. A `claude -p` spawn carries 250+ tools incl.
   `CronCreate/Delete/List`, `Workflow`, `Enter/ExitWorktree`, `RemoteTrigger`,
   `PushNotification`, `Monitor`, `ScheduleWakeup`, `Task`, `Skill`, `LSP`.
   **The allow-list alone is not a complete boundary.**

4. **`--disallowed-tools` is the hard block.** It removes a tool from the spawn
   entirely ("No such tool exists in this environment"), wins over the allow-list
   AND over `bypassPermissions`, and supports command granularity:
   `Bash(git push:*)` blocks `git push` while `echo` still runs. This is what
   closes the dangerous *exempt* tools (#3) and dangerous Bash *commands*.

claude-code headless permission model (what --allowed-tools / --permission-mode actually do) › Update 2026-07-01: `Task` → `Agent` — the fleet's own deny-list was a silent no-op
This doc's own advice ("don't trust the docs here, re-verify") caught a real regression.
The subagent-launch built-in was named `Task` when this doc's model was verified against
claude 2.1.158 (`FLEET_DISALLOWED_TOOLS` denied `'Task'` accordingly). On claude 2.1.198 the
**same tool is named `Agent`** — self-reported by the model, and confirmed live:

```
claude -p "spawn a subagent that writes a marker file" \
  --permission-mode dontAsk --allowedTools "... Agent" --disallowedTools "Task"
# marker file WAS created — denying 'Task' did nothing; the fleet's guard was a no-op.

claude -p "spawn a subagent that writes a marker file" \
  --permission-mode dontAsk --disallowedTools "Agent"
# → "Agent exists but is not enabled in this context." — correctly blocked.
```

So every headless fleet worker had been able to fan out via the (renamed) subagent tool
despite `FLEET_DISALLOWED_TOOLS` explicitly intending to block it — the deny-list looked
complete (the entry was right there) but matched nothing. Fixed by carrying **both** names
in one shared source, `libs/papercusp/packages/orchestrator/src/no-subagent-deny.ts`
(`NO_SUBAGENT_TOOLS_DENY = ['Task', 'Agent']`), reused by `FLEET_DISALLOWED_TOOLS` (fleet/
orchestrator spawns) and mirrored into `psu-launcher.mjs`. Denying a tool name that doesn't
exist in a given CLI build is a no-op, never an error, so carrying both names costs nothing
and survives either generation.

`Task`/`Agent` were not the only fan-out surface. A `psu --resume` session with subagents
denied was still able to fan out via **`Workflow`** — a distinct, top-level multi-agent
orchestration tool, not a rename of the subagent-launch tool, so the `Task`/`Agent` deny
never matched it. `no-subagent-deny.ts`'s shared list is now
`NO_SUBAGENT_TOOLS_DENY = ['Task', 'Agent', 'Workflow']`, so `noSubagentToolsDenyFlag()`

`NO_SUBAGENT_TOOLS_DENY`) both close it too — `FLEET_DISALLOWED_TOOLS` already listed
`Workflow` on its own line (Layer-A), so it now appears twice in the rendered
`--disallowed-tools` argv; a repeated deny entry is harmless (same as denying an
absent tool name — a no-op, not an error).

claude-code headless permission model (what --allowed-tools / --permission-mode actually do) › Update 2026-07-06 (WI-3159): `Bash(rtk git push:*)` — a token-filter hook rewrite evaded the push deny
`Bash(git push:*)` is evaluated against the **post-PreToolUse-hook** `updatedInput` — so
when the `rtk` token-filter hook rewrites the shell command (`git push …` → `rtk git push
…`) before the deny-pattern match runs, the rewritten command no longer starts with `git`
and the `Bash(git push:*)` prefix match never fires (proven live: the non-rewritten
control command was denied correctly, isolating this as pure pattern evasion, not a
broken match). `rtk` is on the dev box `PATH` today (a manual vector), and any fleet

```
--mcp-config <cwd>/.mcp.json --strict-mcp-config
--permission-mode dontAsk
--allowed-tools "mcp__papercusp Read Edit Write Bash Glob Grep WebFetch WebSearch"
--disallowed-tools CronCreate CronDelete CronList ScheduleWakeup \
  EnterWorktree ExitWorktree Workflow Task Agent Workflow RemoteTrigger PushNotification \
  Monitor "Bash(sudo:*)" "Bash(git push:*)" "Bash(rtk git push:*)"
--disallowedTools=Task,Agent,Workflow
```

Allow-list is one space-joined arg (claude splits it); deny patterns are
separate argv elements so internal spaces (`Bash(git push:*)`) survive —
`claudeMcpArgs` is the **tail** of `finalArgv` for claude-code, so the variadic
`--disallowed-tools` swallows nothing unintended. Defers the whole posture if the
user set any permission flag in `AGENT_CMD`.

`FLEET_DISALLOWED_TOOLS` (the `--disallowed-tools CronCreate …` list above) no
longer hardcodes `Task` — it spreads the shared `NO_SUBAGENT_TOOLS_DENY = ['Task',
'Agent']` from `no-subagent-deny.ts`, so both tool-name generations are always
covered here too (belt-and-suspenders with the exec-boundary push below).

The trailing `--disallowedTools=Task,Agent` is a **second, independent** deny
emitted at the exec boundary in `invoke()` itself (`noSubagentToolsDenyFlag()`,
single comma-joined token, camelCase flag — distinct from the space-separated
`--disallowed-tools` Layer-A list above), pushed **unconditionally** for every
claude spawn regardless of `userManagesPermissions` / an explicit
`AGENT_CMD`-supplied deny list. It survives because claude *unions* repeated
`--disallowedTools` occurrences rather than the last one winning (verified
live) — see "Update 2026-07-01" below for why it's split out from the rest of
the posture, which an operator-supplied deny list CAN still override.

The headless fleet (orchestrator `invoke()` → `claude -p`) needs to run
unattended without (a) hanging on a permission prompt or (b) being able to do
anything destructive. The flag semantics that achieve this are **surprising and
contradict the docs in places** — every claim here was tested empirically against
claude 2.1.158 with external side-effects, because a doc-only read sent an
earlier pass down the wrong path. If you're changing the fleet's permissions
(`claudeMcpArgs` in `libs/papercusp/packages/orchestrator/src/invoke.ts`), read

The bench's index-cap probe (`packages/operator-core/lib/memory/bench/index-cap-cli.ts`,

simulation pinned **exactly** to the real script's dry-run output:

| ----------------- | ------- | -------- | --------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| 114 (real corpus) | 113     | 26.3     | 99.1%     | over BOTH caps → projector aborts; index stale              |

one-line hooks), and on an all-durable store the index stops updating

entries.text:
claude-file memory: MEMORY.md is a capped projection — and over-cap it goes silently STALE › The three-layer trap
The Claude Code file memory has **three different visibility layers**, and
they diverge at scale:

1. **Topic files** (`~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/*.md`) — the store.
   The `ClaudeFileMemoryBackend` searches these (full re-read + lexical
   score per query; `archive/` is invisible to it).
2. **`MEMORY.md`** — an auto-generated *projection* of the topic files
   (`~/.claude/scripts/memory-compact.mjs`, a SessionStart hook). This is
   what a booting agent actually loads. Native hard cap **\~24.4 KB** —
   past it Claude silently drops the tail.
3. **`archive/`** — where the projector moves evicted files. Recoverable,
   but **invisible to both the index and the backend's search**.

The gotcha: the projector keeps the index under a **20 KB soft cap** by
**physically archiving** overflow `project`-type files (oldest first;
`user`/`feedback`/`reference` are never auto-evicted). So the cap doesn't
just bound session-start visibility — **one compaction pass shrinks the
searchable store itself**.

When the durable set *alone* renders over the hard cap, the projector has
nothing mechanical left to shed and **ABORTS: it archives nothing and
leaves the existing MEMORY.md untouched — i.e. STALE**. New memories stop
appearing in the index entirely, with only a session-start
`memory-hygiene` notice as the signal. The real store on this box already
hit this state (113 durables → 26.3 KB > 24.4 KB).
entries.description: claude-file memory: MEMORY.md is a capped projection — and over-cap it goes silently STALE › The three-layer trap

entries.text:
claude-file memory: MEMORY.md is a capped projection — and over-cap it goes silently STALE › What to do with this
* **Don't design features assuming the file store scales** — anything
  past a few hundred entries is invisible at boot and, after compaction,
  unsearchable. PG-backed memory (mem0) is the scale path; this is one of
  the falsifiable predictions the memory bench scores (D-006).
* **A stale MEMORY.md is a signal, not a bug in your change** — check the
  `memory-hygiene` SessionStart notice; the fix is deliberate curation of
  durables (merge/retire/tighten), never hand-editing the index.
* **Reproduce / re-measure** with
  `npx tsx packages/operator-core/lib/memory/bench/index-cap-cli.ts --sizes 1000,10000`
  (no PG, no keys needed). The simulation lives in `index-cap.ts` and its
  fidelity to the real script is pinned by `index-cap.test.ts` (auto-skips
  where `~/.claude/scripts/memory-compact.mjs` doesn't exist).

entries.text:
COMMITTED does not mean SETTLED — git-sync splits one logical change across ticks, so a type red can belong to nobody › Rules of thumb
* **Never file a new-file type red on first sight.** Re-run a few minutes later. Cheap; catches this
  whole class.
* **Read the message, not just the count.** A cross-file symbol in the error is the landing-race tell.
* **Do not "fix" a half-landed change by editing the other file** — you will collide with the peer
  whose change is mid-flight, and the tick that follows will resolve it anyway.
* **`git blame` will not tell you whose it is** — git-sync commits the tree under one identity. See
  [attributing-a-change-despite-git-sync-squash](/internal/docs/agent-insights/attributing-a-change-despite-git-sync-squash).
