entries.text:
Claude's ToolSearch cannot select a papercusp colon-form tool name — use tools:find / tools:invoke instead › Re-reported for `session:*` (EI-12618) — same class, no session-specific defect
EI-12618 hit the same wall for `session:carry-drill` and hypothesised "an
activation/indexing gap specific to `session:*` group tools" — noting that even
the CORRECTLY-mangled `select:mcp__papercusp-su__session_carry-drill` returned
"No matching deferred tools found", not just the colon form. Two clarifications
fall out, and there is **no `session:*`-specific defect**:

* **On a full-catalog session, the defer set is EMPTY, so every `select:` fails
  trivially.** ToolSearch only searches tools the client declared with
  `defer_loading`. A non-seeded (frontier-tier) Claude session gets the FULL
  papercusp catalog directly in `tools/list` — nothing is deferred — so
  `select:<anything>` returns "No matching deferred tools found" no matter how the
  name is spelled. The tool is already in your list: just call
  `mcp__papercusp-su__session_carry-drill` directly (or `tools:invoke`).
* **On a SEEDED session, deferred tools aren't in `tools/list` at all** (papercusp
  grows the surface via `tools:find` → `activateTools`, not the API-native defer
  mechanism — see [dynamic-tool-surface](/internal/docs/agent-insights/dynamic-tool-surface)),
  so ToolSearch has nothing to select there either. The path is `tools:find`
  (which activates the match) → call it, or `tools:invoke`.

`session:carry-drill` is verifiably registered, MCP-projected, in the `tools:find`
corpus (exact-name lexical hit), and dispatchable via `tools:invoke` — the whole
group is fine. A regression guard
(`packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/session/carry-drill.test.ts`) locks that
in so the hypothesised "session:\* indexing gap" cannot silently become real.
entries.description: Claude's ToolSearch cannot select a papercusp colon-form tool name — use tools:find / tools:invoke instead › Re-reported for `session:*` (EI-12618) — same class, no session-specific defect

entries.text:
Claude's ToolSearch cannot select a papercusp colon-form tool name — use tools:find / tools:invoke instead › Root cause — a name-space mismatch, not a broken tool
Papercusp's own tool identity — the one every doc, prompt, contract, and
`defineTool({ name: ... })` call uses — is **colon form**: `server:verb`
(`curation:state-of-pot`, `rubrics:search`). That is one of the [four
distinct string encodings a tool identity has](/internal/docs/agent-insights/mcp-tool-rename-four-string-forms)
— colon token, MCP-projection underscore, dot module-path, slash file-path.

Claude Code's **ToolSearch is a client-native mechanism papercusp does not
implement or control** ([dynamic-tool-surface](/internal/docs/agent-insights/dynamic-tool-surface)
— "Claude: native ToolSearch — untouched"). It indexes and resolves tools by
the **client-visible id**, which Claude constructs from the MCP `tools/list`
entry as `mcp__<server-slug>__<name>` with every `:` in `name` replaced by
`_` (so `curation:state-of-pot` → `mcp__papercusp-su__curation_state-of-pot`).
`ToolSearch({query:"select:curation:state-of-pot"})` is therefore the WRONG
INPUT SHAPE for that mechanism — not a defect in the tool, and not something
papercusp can fix by patching ToolSearch (it isn't papercusp's code).

The keyword-search miss is a second, independent symptom: ToolSearch's own
lexical/semantic ranking over \~550 catalog entries did not surface the right
tool for a reasonable-looking natural-language query. That ranking quality is
also entirely client-side and outside papercusp's reach.
entries.description: Claude's ToolSearch cannot select a papercusp colon-form tool name — use tools:find / tools:invoke instead › Root cause — a name-space mismatch, not a broken tool

entries.text:
Claude's ToolSearch cannot select a papercusp colon-form tool name — use tools:find / tools:invoke instead › The fix — the escape hatch already exists; it was just undocumented
Papercusp ships its own hybrid lexical+semantic finder, **`tools:find`**
(`packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/tools/find.ts`), whose lexical leg is
**exact-name-authoritative over the REAL (colon-form) tool identity** — the
same string every doc uses. And **`tools:invoke`** dispatches any catalog
tool server-side by that same real name, entirely sidestepping whatever the
calling client's own id-mangling does. Neither of these needed a code change;
the gap was that nothing told a stuck agent to reach for them instead of
retrying ToolSearch with name variants.

**When a documented colon-form tool name doesn't resolve via ToolSearch
(`select:` or a keyword retry):**

1. `ToolSearch({query:"select:mcp__papercusp-su__tools_find"})` (or a keyword
   search like `"find a tool by intent"`) to load `tools:find` itself.
2. `tools:find({query:"<the colon-form name, verbatim>"})` — resolves
   reliably; its lexical leg matches the real name exactly.
3. If the returned hit still can't be called directly (client didn't grow its
   surface), `tools:invoke({name:"<colon-form name>", args:{...}})` — this
   ALWAYS works, on every client, because it dispatches server-side under the
   tool's real identity.

This is now spelled out directly in `apps/operator/prompts/papercusp-su.claude.md`'s
"Finding a capability" section (the injected system-prompt text every Claude
su session gets), so it no longer depends on an agent independently
rediscovering it mid-task.

Claude's ToolSearch cannot select a papercusp colon-form tool name — use tools:find / tools:invoke instead › What (WI-3930)
Found by the GRADE-iter2 M2 battery, reproduced independently by two sessions
on 2026-07-10: an agent following a documented, prescribed read —
`curation:state-of-pot`, `rubrics:list`, `rubrics:search`, `scorecards:freshness`
(the IDEATE-mode grounding-first list; also written this way in the GRADE mode
contract and the su playbook) — tried:

```
ToolSearch({ query: "select:curation:state-of-pot,rubrics:list,rubrics:search,scorecards:freshness" })
→ "No matching deferred tools found"

ToolSearch({ query: "curation state of pot rubrics scorecards grade idea" })  # keyword retry
```

Bare `tsc --noEmit` reports hundreds of pre-existing errors — treat them as a baseline
import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

This page was written when `next build` was the operator's real
typechecker. **Next.js is now retired** — `apps/operator` has no
`next build`, no `next.config.js`, and no `.next-prod/types/*`. The
operator builds via Vite (`@papercusp/operator-vite`'s `vite build`),
which does **not** typecheck by default, so there is no single "real
typechecker reports zero" oracle anymore. What survives unchanged: bare
`tsc --noEmit` against `apps/operator/` reports a large **pre-existing
baseline** (re-measured at \~379 on 2026-06-08, down from the \~860 below;
the count drifts as the tree changes), `--ignoreDeprecations 6.0` is
still required, and the right move is still to **scope your check to the
files you touched**, not the total. The per-file recipe below still works.
entries.description: Bare `tsc --noEmit` reports hundreds of pre-existing errors — treat them as a baseline

entries.text:
Bare `tsc --noEmit` reports hundreds of pre-existing errors — treat them as a baseline › How to verify your work
Always run `tsc` from `apps/operator/`, but **scope your check to the
files you touched**, not the total:

```bash
cd /home/dev/papercupai-workspace/papercup/apps/operator && \
  ../../node_modules/.bin/tsc --noEmit --ignoreDeprecations 6.0 2>&1 | \
  tee /tmp/tsc.log | grep -cE 'error TS'   # capture baseline

# Then per-file:
for f in path/to/your/file1.tsx path/to/your/file2.ts; do
  n=$(grep -cE "^${f//\//\\/}\(" /tmp/tsc.log)
  printf "  %4d  %s\n" "$n" "$f"
done
```

A clean PR has **zero errors in touched files**, regardless of
project total. The flags matter: `--ignoreDeprecations 6.0` is
required because the repo's `tsconfig.json` uses options newer `tsc`
versions deprecated.

entries.text:
Bare `tsc --noEmit` reports hundreds of pre-existing errors — treat them as a baseline › If you must chase the baseline
Don't. Bare `tsc` is a fast-but-noisy file-level check, not a
project-correctness signal — and since Next's typecheck-on-build is
gone, there is no build step that will independently "report zero" to
chase toward. Verify behavior by running the app via the Tauri dev
shell (`cd papercusp-desktop && npm run dev`) and by the affected test
suites (`npm run test:affected`), and confirm only that your touched
files are `tsc`-clean against the baseline.

entries.text:
Bare `tsc --noEmit` reports hundreds of pre-existing errors — treat them as a baseline › What
Running `tsc --noEmit` directly against `apps/operator/` reports
**hundreds of errors** on a clean checkout (\~379 as of 2026-06-08;
historically \~860). These are a real, persistent pre-existing baseline —
`tsc` is not finding regressions, it's the accumulated debt of a tree
that is built/bundled (Vite) rather than typecheck-gated.

The error count fluctuates as other agents land changes —
don't treat a small delta as a regression in either direction. Establish
the baseline, then check only your touched files against it.

This session, I twice spent meaningful time investigating "new"
errors in `lib/agent-tools/plans/*` that turned out to be the pre-

Turn provenance — verified owner-vs-agent labeling › Per-backend coverage (P-004)
* **Claude** — full: envelope + hook verification. Installed by
  `install-standalone-mcp.sh` (`merge_provenance_hook`) and the desktop

* **Codex** — Layer-1 only: its `hooks.json` fires only Pre/PostToolUse (no
  prompt-submit event), so injected turns carry the visible envelope but no
  ledger-verified stamp. Revisit if codex adds the event.
* **OMP** — deliveries ride the same enrolled wake-executor paths, so the
  envelope is present in the injected text; no prompt-submit hook leg.
* **Native auto-compaction continuations** — cannot be pre-tagged (Claude

entries.text:
Turn provenance — verified owner-vs-agent labeling › The problem: every injected turn impersonates the owner
The model API has only `user`/`assistant` roles. Every papercusp injector —
the wake pump (`events:await` deliveries, coord `wake:` re-invokes), loop
fires, `session:request-compaction` continuations, the compaction-compliance
watchdog's force-compacts, fleet auto-kickoffs — delivers by **typing into
the PTY**, byte-identical to the owner typing. Agents then mis-attribute
machine turns to the owner. Seven compactions later, an agent's own
note-to-self renders as "the owner set an explicit gate" (WI-3532 — the
manufactured-directive class; the same bug pointed at permission instead of
a block manufactures false owner APPROVAL, which is worse). Live evidence:
during the 2026-07-11 wake-pump starve, 12 batched machine wakes all rendered
as user turns.

Ad-hoc labels existed (`[await-event]`, `🔁 Monitor wake`) but are per-site,
unverifiable, and absent for the worst case. **Absence of a label proves
nothing; presence is spoofable.**

entries.text:
Turn provenance — verified owner-vs-agent labeling › The protocol: envelope (Layer 1) + trust ledger (Layer 2)
Core module: `packages/operator-core/lib/turn-provenance/turn-provenance.ts`.
Bash mirror: `apps/operator/scripts/hooks/cc/userpromptsubmit-provenance.sh`
(**lockstep — change them together**). Launcher mirror: `tagKickoffProvenance`
in `apps/operator/scripts/psu-launcher.mjs`.

1. **Envelope** — every enrolled injector prefixes
   `⟦turn-origin:<origin> nonce:<16-hex>⟧` (origins: `wake-pump`,
   `loop-fire`, `self-compaction`, `fleet-kickoff`, `watchdog`,
   `coord-inject:<sender>`).
2. **Ledger** — BEFORE typing, the injector appends
   `{sid, nonce, origin, sha256(normalized payload), ts}` to
   `~/.papercusp/turn-provenance/<sid>.jsonl` (TTL 10 min; env overrides
   `PAPERCUSP_TURN_PROVENANCE_DIR` / `_TTL_MS`, clamp ≥30s).
3. **Classification** — a Claude `UserPromptSubmit` hook classifies every
   submitted prompt and stamps `additionalContext`:
   * envelope + **live nonce row** → `VERIFIED AGENT-ORIGIN (origin: …)` —
     the LEDGER's origin wins over the envelope's claim; a payload-hash miss
     is flagged as PTY mangling, not a demotion (nonce is the primary key);
   * envelope + expired/absent row → `UNVERIFIED ORIGIN CLAIM` (spoof/replay
     — quoted text carrying an envelope mid-prompt does NOT classify: the
     envelope must open the turn);
   * no envelope + live **hash** match → verified (envelope lost in transit);
   * no envelope + no match + a known **machine-surface banner** (a
     CLI-internal notification that self-labels `[SYSTEM NOTIFICATION - NOT
     USER INPUT]`, e.g. a background-task completion) → `MACHINE-GENERATED
     SURFACE` — unenrollable (no envelope, no ledger row) but definitely NOT
     the owner (EI-9904);
   * no envelope + no match → **affirmative `OWNER (interactive)`**.

**D-002 — the ledger decides, never the text.** Corollary: injector
enrollment is MANDATORY. An unenrolled injector's turns stamp as OWNER —
t

entries.text:
Turn provenance — verified owner-vs-agent labeling › Threat model honesty
Same-UID is the boundary (as with the psu-pty control sockets): any process
that can write the ledger can mint "verified" rows. The protocol defends
against *confusion* (the dominant real failure) and casual spoofing (quoted
envelopes, replays past TTL), not against a hostile same-user process. Nonce
rows are not consumed on match — replay inside the 10-min TTL of the exact
bytes re-classifies as verified; acceptable because the typing path is
system-owned.

mechanical leg: a claimed `[owner:…]` directive must trace to a turn stamped
`OWNER (interactive)` (via `sessions:search` on the verbatim transcript). A
directive found only in VERIFIED-agent turns is `[self-imposed]`/`[peer:…]`.

entries.text:
Two federation paths for the same row can't coexist — cut over with mutual exclusion, not parallel writes › Restart-free activation (don't rely on a boot backfill)
A once-per-boot backfill means the flip needs an operator restart on every peer,
and post-boot edits wouldn't capture. Instead wire capture where edits actually
happen and self-baseline on both sides:

* **Send side:** a flag-gated, best-effort, **post-commit** hook in the write
  chokepoint (`with-plan-lock`) — baseline from the *pre-edit* body, then diff the
  new body so only the changed part federates. Post-commit + own-try/catch so a
  capture failure can never roll back the committed write.
* **Receive side:** before applying the FIRST incoming part for a plan, seed the
  full baseline from the local `harness_plans.content`, else recompose produces a
  broken `join({one part})`.
* **Deterministic baseline `fed_ts=0`, `origin='remote'`** (non-federating): every
  peer self-seeds the SAME baseline from the same pre-cutover content, so unchanged
  parts TIE (identical body+ts) instead of racing, and any real edit (`fed_ts=now`)
  wins. No coordinated restart needed.
entries.description: Two federation paths for the same row can't coexist — cut over with mutual exclusion, not parallel writes › Restart-free activation (don't rely on a boot backfill)

entries.text:
Two federation paths for the same row can't coexist — cut over with mutual exclusion, not parallel writes › Tells / how to verify
* A flip that "does nothing" or intermittently loses edits ⇒ suspect two live
  paths sharing one clock.
* Prove it on real PG with both real projections + real triggers (mig 102/125/214
  * the new table's capture): a flag-OFF **clobber control** (shows the gate is
    load-bearing), a flag-ON concurrent-different-item **merge**, a **two-instance**
    (two separate DBs) byte-identical convergence, and a **parts-empty peer** merging
    a lone incoming op. See `__tests__/plan-part-federation-cutover.integration.test.ts`.

Related: [retire-or-add-a-federated-table](/internal/docs/agent-insights/retire-or-add-a-federated-table)
(the coupled op-key / register-all / table-registry edits must land atomically or
the P-011 capture-coverage guard goes red).
entries.description: Two federation paths for the same row can't coexist — cut over with mutual exclusion, not parallel writes › Tells / how to verify

entries.text:
Two federation paths for the same row can't coexist — cut over with mutual exclusion, not parallel writes › The shape that works (one sole writer when the flag is ON)
* **Whole-blob projection → bootstrap-only.** When the flag is ON, `INSERT … ON
  CONFLICT DO NOTHING`: it can create a never-seen plan but never UPDATE an
  existing row. A stale snapshot can't clobber. (`projections/harness-plans.ts`)
* **The fine-grained recompose is the SOLE writer.** It writes content **and**
  re-derives every scalar column the whole-blob path used to federate
  (title/status/owner/… from the recomposed frontmatter — they are NOT
  trigger-derived). One writer ⇒ one `fed_ts` stream ⇒ no interference.
  (`projections/harness-plan-parts.ts`)
* **Make the recompose look like a remote apply to the triggers.** Set
  `origin='remote'` + a *moved* `fed_ts` (the op's wire ts). mig-214's UPDATE
  branch only respects a remote apply when `NEW.fed_ts IS DISTINCT FROM
  OLD.fed_ts` — so a moved fed\_ts → "RETURN NEW verbatim" (no re-stamp), and
  origin='remote' → the mig-125 capture trigger skips re-federating it (no echo
  storm). Guard the UPDATE on `content_hash IS DISTINCT FROM` to skip no-op
  recomposes.
entries.description: Two federation paths for the same row can't coexist — cut over with mutual exclusion, not parallel writes › The shape that works (one sole writer when the flag is ON)

entries.text:
Two federation paths for the same row can't coexist — cut over with mutual exclusion, not parallel writes › What
When you re-grain a federated table — replace a coarse path with a finer one
(the case: `harness_plans` whole-blob `plans-by-slug` → per-part `plan-parts`,
plan `plan-federation-regrain-2026-06-13`) — the obvious plan is "build the new
path alongside the old, flag-gated, flip when ready." **That plan is wrong if
both paths write the same column.** Flipping the flag with both paths live does
NOT fix the bug it was meant to fix — it reintroduces it.
entries.description: Two federation paths for the same row can't coexist — cut over with mutual exclusion, not parallel writes › What

entries.text:
Two federation paths for the same row can't coexist — cut over with mutual exclusion, not parallel writes › Why (the trap)
Both paths LWW-write `harness_plans.content` keyed on the row's single `fed_ts`.
With the flag ON and the whole-blob path still live, a local edit emits BOTH a
whole-blob op (a full stale snapshot of the *other* peer's items) AND the per-part
op. On a remote peer the whole-blob projection still applies the stale snapshot →
**clobbers the per-part merge** — the exact concurrent-different-item clobber the
re-grain exists to kill. Mutual exclusion was the *intent* ("flag ON → per-part
authoritative") but was never implemented as code; "registered both projections
unconditionally" reads as done but isn't.

You cannot fix this by splitting columns across the two paths either: there is
**one `fed_ts` column**, and `mig-214` (`stamp_local_federated_write`) re-stamps it
on *any* content change, so two writers fight over one LWW clock — a content
recompose bumps `fed_ts` and starts dropping legitimate scalar updates.

entries.text:
Ship types-only modules from "draft for review" design memos › See also
* `packages/operator-core/lib/harness/binding-types.ts` — the canonical example.
* `packages/operator-core/lib/harness/binding-types.test.ts` — 15 tests; the unit-test surface for a types-only module is small but real.
* Plan-store entry `dogfood-design-memo-binding-service-api-2026-05-24` — the source memo.
* [`forward-defined-registry-entries`](/internal/docs/agent-insights/forward-defined-registry-entries/) — sister pattern for ahead-of-implementation *registrations*.
* [`verification-signal-on-the-row`](/internal/docs/agent-insights/verification-signal-on-the-row/) — when a memo's wire-format is awkward, the right move can be deviating with diagnosis; types-first lets the implementer make that call with a clean spine to push against.
entries.description: Ship types-only modules from "draft for review" design memos › See also

entries.text:
Ship types-only modules from "draft for review" design memos › The pattern
**Split: types now, behavior on memo-acceptance.**

Extract just the type declarations — `BindingRecord`, the error union, the permission enum, pure helpers like `composeBindingId` / `parseBindingId` / `hasRequiredPermission` — into a `*-types.ts` module. No service implementation, no I/O, no behavior the user would object to.

Example from this codebase: `packages/operator-core/lib/harness/binding-types.ts` (commit `f05997aa`). 120 LOC + 15 unit tests, all pure functions. The eventual `binding-service.ts` (when the memo is accepted) will `import` from here verbatim.
entries.description: Ship types-only modules from "draft for review" design memos › The pattern

entries.text:
Ship types-only modules from "draft for review" design memos › The risk: types that get stale
If the memo never lands (user rejects, scope changes, plan deprecates), the types-only module becomes dead code. Two mitigations:

1. **Cross-link the memo from the types file.** The header comment should name the memo slug. If the memo is deleted, a future cleanup pass greps the types file's references and removes the orphan.
2. **Be honest in the commit message about the dependency.** "Per plan-store entry `dogfood-design-memo-binding-service-api-2026-05-24` (still 'draft for review')." Anyone reading `git log` knows the type spine is provisional.
entries.description: Ship types-only modules from "draft for review" design memos › The risk: types that get stale

entries.text:
Ship types-only modules from "draft for review" design memos › The setup
A common pattern in this codebase: a design memo is `status: draft` ("draft for review") with concrete type signatures + a service interface, but the implementation is gated on user acceptance. Examples:

* The `dogfood-design-memo-binding-service-api-2026-05-24` memo specifies `BindingRecord`, a 5-operation `BindingService` interface, and a 9-variant `BindingServiceError` union. The implementation (Phase 1b P-068) waits on the user's review.
* The `dogfood-design-memo-device-attestation-ux-2026-05-24` memo specifies a 3-screen modal flow. The UI implementation waits on the same review.

You're sitting on hours of safe overnight work and the memo is ready enough to type-check. What do you ship?
entries.description: Ship types-only modules from "draft for review" design memos › The setup

entries.text:
Ship types-only modules from "draft for review" design memos › What NOT to do
Don't ship anything that requires user judgment:

| Safe to ship                                   | Wait for memo acceptance                          |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| Type declarations                              | Service implementations                           |
| Pure functions (parsers, predicates, encoders) | Functions that perform I/O                        |
| Error union variants                           | Error-handling policies (retry counts, backoff)   |
| Constant tables (e.g. required permissions)    | Wiring those tables into UI behavior              |
| Tests for the pure functions                   | Tests that assert behavior the memo hasn't pinned |
| New SQL columns (additive only)                | New SQL tables that imply a new domain            |

The line is: *would the user reading the diff say "that's what I'd have written"?* If yes, ship. If they'd say "wait, that's a decision," wait.

The commit message matters. State clearly: "types-only — implementation gated on memo acceptance." Reviewers should know this is groundwork, not a service launch. Use phrasing that signals reversibility: "If you revise the memo, the types change; downstream consumers get typecheck errors to update."
entries.description: Ship types-only modules from "draft for review" design memos › What NOT to do

entries.text:
Ship types-only modules from "draft for review" design memos › What this is NOT
This is not the same as [`forward-defined-registry-entries`](/internal/docs/agent-insights/forward-defined-registry-entries/) — that pattern is about *registering* something ahead of its full implementation (e.g., a query name mapped before the resolver exists). Types-first is about *publishing the type surface* of an unimplemented service so the eventual implementation has a stable spine.

Both patterns are about decoupling "the user has accepted this" from "the next coder can start." Different mechanisms, same shape.
entries.description: Ship types-only modules from "draft for review" design memos › What this is NOT

entries.text:
Ship types-only modules from "draft for review" design memos › Why it works
Three reasons.

**(1) Types-only is reversible.** If the memo revises (e.g. adds a column to `BindingRecord`, swaps the error code shape), the types-only file changes alongside. Every downstream consumer gets a typecheck error to update. No runtime to break, no DB schema to migrate, no API to deprecate. It's the lightest possible commitment to a design.

**(2) The implementing agent gets a head start.** When the memo lands as accepted, P-068's first commit doesn't have to define the types — they already exist, already pass lint, already have unit tests. The implementer reads "the service surface is `BindingService` from binding-types.ts" and starts wiring methods. Days saved.

**(3) The user reviewing the memo can see types in tree.** "Does the `BindingRecord` shape make sense?" → the user can navigate to the file, scroll through the comments, see how `composeBindingId` encodes things, run the tests. Reviewing a memo with a real types file open is qualitatively different from reviewing a memo with no code at all. The review becomes "is the implementation I see in tree what I want?" — a more concrete question than "is the design as written what I want?"
entries.description: Ship types-only modules from "draft for review" design memos › Why it works

entries.text:
Inbox-WSL wsl.exe hangs forever under ConPTY (wizard pty wedge) › How to discriminate it fast (minutes, not hours)
1. `ssh` into the box, `wsl -d <distro> --exec ps aux` → no trace of
   your command = it never started (rules out slow install).
2. Same exact command via **pipes** from Windows-side node:
   `child_process.spawn('wsl.exe', [...], {stdio:'pipe'})` → works =
   rules out args/quoting/env/distro problems in one shot.
3. Drive the app's own `pty_spawn` over CDP (runbook §14) with a
   trivial `echo` → blank + no exit = the ConPTY leg is the variable.
4. `wsl --version` errors → inbox WSL. Done.

Things that look guilty but are NOT: the empty-env theory
(`portable-pty`'s `CommandBuilder` inherits `std::env::vars_os()` —
and wsl.exe runs fine with an empty env block anyway), `--cd` with a
Linux path (valid), multiline `bash -c` scripts through `--exec`
(argv-preserved, fine).
entries.description: Inbox-WSL wsl.exe hangs forever under ConPTY (wizard pty wedge) › How to discriminate it fast (minutes, not hours)

entries.text:
Inbox-WSL wsl.exe hangs forever under ConPTY (wizard pty wedge) › Resolved: auto-`wsl --update` at onboarding is REJECTED (P-022, validated 2026-06-12)
Tried live on the Windows VM: `wsl --update --web-download` installs
Store WSL 2.7.8 cleanly — and then **WSL cannot start at all** on the
nested-QEMU rig: `wsl: Nested virtualization is not supported on this
machine` + `Wsl/Service/CreateInstance/CreateVm/0x800705b4` on every
distro boot. The inbox WSL runs fine nested; the Store engine refuses
this virtualization profile. Recovery: `wsl --uninstall` (removes the
Store package, reverts to inbox) — distro boots again immediately,
state intact.

Consequences:

* Onboarding must NOT auto-run `wsl --update` — on machines like this
  one it converts a degraded-but-working setup into a fully broken one.
  The shipped mitigation is the pty watchdog + its in-pane
  `wsl --update` hint, which a *real-hardware* user can follow safely.
* On THIS VM, never run `wsl --update`. If someone has: `wsl --uninstall`
  restores the rig.
* Whether Store WSL actually fixes the ConPTY wedge therefore remains
  unverified on this rig (it can't run Store WSL); ecosystem evidence
  (VS Code drives wsl-under-ConPTY broadly on Store WSL) still supports
  the hint's advice for real machines.
entries.description: Inbox-WSL wsl.exe hangs forever under ConPTY (wizard pty wedge) › Resolved: auto-`wsl --update` at onboarding is REJECTED (P-022, validated 2026-06-12)

entries.text:
Inbox-WSL wsl.exe hangs forever under ConPTY (wizard pty wedge) › Root cause
The machine runs the **inbox WSL** (the Windows-feature version, not the
Store/MSI release — `wsl --version` is not a recognized option there;
that's the tell). Inbox `wsl.exe` wedges at the WSL-service handshake
when its stdio is a **pseudoconsole** (ConPTY — what `portable-pty`
allocates). The identical command spawned with plain pipes works
instantly. Modern Store WSL doesn't have this (VS Code drives wsl under
ConPTY all day).

This is also the same WSL generation behind the UTF-16/`WSL_UTF8`
decode edge (§3-adjacent, see the Windows-VM runbook) — inbox WSL on a
box means assume both.
entries.description: Inbox-WSL wsl.exe hangs forever under ConPTY (wizard pty wedge) › Root cause

entries.text:
Inbox-WSL wsl.exe hangs forever under ConPTY (wizard pty wedge) › Symptom
The Setup Wizard's **Install Agent Runtime** (and the sign-in / git pty
panes — anything through `InlinePtyTerminal` → `pty_spawn`) sits on
"Installing…" forever on a Windows machine: the xterm pane stays blank,
no `pty-exit` ever fires, and `ps aux` inside the distro shows **no
process was ever started**. The Windows side shows a live
`wsl.exe --distribution papercup-runtime … --exec bash -c "<script>"`
child that never progresses — hours, if you let it.
entries.description: Inbox-WSL wsl.exe hangs forever under ConPTY (wizard pty wedge) › Symptom

entries.text:
Inbox-WSL wsl.exe hangs forever under ConPTY (wizard pty wedge) › The fix set (landed 2026-06-12)
* **`pty.rs` watchdog**: a wsl-routed pty with zero bytes AND no exit
  after 20s is killed with a red in-pane explanation telling the user to
  run `wsl --update` from an elevated PowerShell. A silent wedge can no
  longer strand the wizard.
* **`InlinePtyTerminal` got `onSpawnError`** and `StepAgents` /
  `AuthSignInCards` / `StepGit` wire it — spawn failures reset the
  busy state instead of sticking on "Installing…"/"Running…".
* Same click-through also surfaced (separate bugs, same pane):
  **`@oh-my-pi/cli` is a dead npm ref** (`oh-my-pi` unpublished
  2026-05-21) — it 404'd and aborted the whole runtime `npm install`,
  taking codex with it (removed from `buildInstallSpec`); and
  **`detectClaude` never probed `~/.local/bin/claude`** — the official
  `claude.ai/install.sh` target — so even successful installs read as
  "No agent backend yet" (`preflight-binaries.ts` candidate added).

entries.text:
Agent kickoffs
A **kickoff** is a curated, task-specific system-prompt brief layered on top of the engineer-collaborator playbook when the operator UI spawns a power-user agent session. The button that launches the session names a *kind*; the server writes the matching brief into a temp file and hands its path to the `psu` launcher via `--launch-context=<path>` (P-032). `psu` parses `--launch-context` itself and appends the brief to the **raw** agent CLI — `--append-system-prompt-file` for claude, `--append-system-prompt` for omp, and per-session `CODEX_HOME/AGENTS.md` materialization for codex. The engineer playbook and superuser MCP are assembled by `bootstrap-su` / `buildLaunchSpec` per launch; the `*-su` wrappers (`claude-su` / `omp-su` / `codex-su`) are retired. The launched session opens already framed for the task.

Per [`plans-newbutton-and-subharness-scope-2026-05-25`](/internal/docs/plans/plans-newbutton-and-subharness-scope-2026-05-25), kickoffs ride the launch-context / system-prompt channel — they are not first-user messages. This keeps them in scope for the whole conversation and matches the existing engineer-collaborator brief and PTY feature-pi brief.
entries.description: Agent kickoffs

entries.text:
Agent kickoffs › Adding a new kickoff kind
Three small edits:

1. **Author the brief.** Drop a markdown file at `apps/operator/prompts/kickoffs/<kind>.md`. Plain prose; if you need server-supplied context (e.g. an active harness slug) reference it as `{{harness_context}}` (or invent a new placeholder) and substitute in the renderer.

2. **Add a body renderer.** In `packages/operator-core/lib/agent-kickoff/prompt-file.ts`, extend the `KickoffKind` type and the `KickoffCtx` discriminated union with the new kind, then add a `renderXxxBody(ctx)` function dispatched from `renderKickoffBody`. For brief-file kinds the renderer just `readFileSync`s the curated MD (from `apps/operator/prompts/kickoffs/`) and stamps in the context. For data-driven kinds (like `feature`) the renderer builds the body from PG / files.

3. **Allowlist the kind.** In `packages/operator-core/lib/agent-kickoff/kickoff-kind.ts`, add the kind to `KICKOFF_KIND_ALLOW` (the allowlist + `validateKickoffKind` validator moved here from the retired `console-launch` route in P-032). The kickoff launch now rides `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/adv/launch-su.ts`, which calls `validateKickoffKind` and `buildKickoffPromptFile`, then hands the file to `psu` via `--launch-context`. `psu` appends it to the raw agent CLI itself (no `*-su` wrapper).

The launch refuses any kind not in `KICKOFF_KIND_ALLOW`; the brief body is curated in-repo and never accepted as a free-text payload (D-003).

Agent kickoffs › Built-in kinds
| Kind       | Brief                                        | Launched from                                                                                    |
| ---------- | -------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `new-plan` | `apps/operator/prompts/kickoffs/new-plan.md` | "New plan" button on PlansClient (`/adv/plans` + `/admin/plans`)                                 |
| `feature`  | Inline-rendered from `harness_features` row  | PTY feature-pi spawn (in-app TUI pane) — uses the same factory but doesn't ride the launch route |

The `feature` kind is *not* in the launch-route allowlist — it's only reachable through the in-process PTY spawn path, where the harness/feature ids are already authenticated.

entries.text:
Agent kickoffs › What gets emitted on the wire
The `psu` argv (`launch-su.ts`) ends up shaped like:

```
psu --no-picker --agent=claude --harness=<slug> --no-plan \
  --launch-context=/dev/shm/papercusp-kickoff-aBcDeF/new-plan.md \
  --role=planner
```

A new-plan kickoff always appends `--role=planner` (launch-su.ts:164) — the launched session *is* the Planner role/persona, so the dock panes it as a typed Planner pane (and the deferred row records `role: 'planner'` for the same reason).

The `--agent=` token reflects the **configured backend** (claude unless `/settings/agent` overrides it) — `--agent=omp` would just be one such pick. The New-plan button sends *no* agent, so the route resolves it via `effectiveBackend(readAgentConfig())` (launch-su.ts:77-78), following the global setting rather than a hardcoded value.

Since WI-1282 (su-context-size-variants), the route also accepts an optional `context_size: 'full' | 'trimmed'` in the launch body, validated by `isSuContextSize` and forwarded as `--context-size=<full|trimmed>` on the `psu` argv (right after `--model=`, before `--resume-session=`). Omitted ⇒ no flag is passed and each client (`claude`/`codex`/`omp`) keeps its own native default. This is orthogonal to kickoffs — it sizes the *superuser tool catalog* the session boots with, not the kickoff brief.

The New-plan button launches with `defer_spawn: true` (PlansClient.tsx:662). Instead of spawning an OS terminal, the server records a pending `adv_sessions` "workbench launch" row carrying this same argv as `launchArgv`, then wakes the pui dock-driver — which reactively opens a pane that *runs* the launcher (launch-su.ts:155-181). The `exec psu …` form below is the non-deferred terminal path:

```
exec psu --no-picker --agent=claude --harness=<slug> --no-plan \
  --launch-context=/dev/shm/papercusp-kickoff-aBcDeF/new-plan.md \
  --role=planner
```

`psu` resolves the engineer playbook + coord wiring itself per agent (via `bootstrap-su` / `buildLaunchSpec`); t

A first-user message would mingle with the user's actual input and get trimmed first under context compaction. entries.text:
FrontierSWE — ultra-long-horizon implementation / perf-eng / ML-research
import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

**FrontierSWE** ([Proximal Labs](https://github.com/Proximal-Labs/frontier-swe);
[leaderboard](https://www.frontierswe.com)) is an *ultra-long-horizon* coding-agent
benchmark — **17 tasks** = **7 implementation / 7 performance-engineering / 3 ML-research**,
with **4–20 h agent budgets per trial**. No model fully solves the
implementation tasks, so it is scored on a **continuous \[0,1]** scale over **5 trials**
per (model, harness) and reported as **mean\@5 / best\@5**; the leaderboard ranks models
by **AVG RANK** (mean position, lower = better) + **dominance** (win rate vs a random
opponent on a task). Plan: `benchmark-suite-frontier-swe-2026-06-18`.

FrontierSWE is **M2 in-container + own-scorer** (the METR-HCAST shape), NOT the SWE-bench
diff-batch (M1) shape. The agent works *inside* the task's Docker container over hours;
each task ships its OWN verifier (`tests/test.sh` → `compute_reward.py` →
`/logs/verifier/reward.txt`). We **do not author a verifier** — every arm hits the
byte-identical task scorer (the fairness invariant).
entries.description: FrontierSWE — ultra-long-horizon implementation / perf-eng / ML-research

entries.text:
FrontierSWE — ultra-long-horizon implementation / perf-eng / ML-research › Fairness (binding)
Every FrontierSWE number passes the **C1–C10 pre-claim audit** in
[Benchmark Fairness Criteria](/benchmarks/fairness-criteria) (use
`buildFairnessAudit` from `@papercusp/bench-metrics`). FrontierSWE-specific points:

* **C1 same denominator** — an empty / no-progress workspace scores **0** (it COUNTS); a
  verifier that *fails to run* (image/OOM/timeout) is a `graderError`, excluded
  *symmetrically* across arms and disclosed — never a vanished row.
* **C3 iso-budget** — cap all arms to the same per-task budget; **wall-clock is a
  first-class cap dimension** here (tasks run hours), alongside calls + `$`.
* **C8** — the native 5-trial protocol satisfies ≥2 seeds; report per bucket.
* **C9** — validate against a published number using a task's `solution/solve.sh` gold
  control (or a reference model) before any cross-arm claim.
entries.description: FrontierSWE — ultra-long-horizon implementation / perf-eng / ML-research › Fairness (binding)

entries.text:
FrontierSWE — ultra-long-horizon implementation / perf-eng / ML-research › Hard gates (read before launching)
* **GPUs** — 5 of 17 tasks need datacenter GPUs (B200: `granite-mamba2-inference-optimization`,
  `inference-system-optimization`; H100: `modular-stack-wan21`, `optimizer-design`,
  `pcqm4mv2-autoresearch`). Not runnable on a CPU host — use `frontier-swe-cpu` (12 tasks)
  there, or run the GPU tasks on a cloud GPU. Note `pcqm4mv2-autoresearch` needs **both** an
  H100 **and** internet, so it is excluded from `frontier-swe-cpu` *and* needs network.
* **Wall-clock + disk** — 4–20 h agent + up to 24 h verifier per trial; per-task images are
  GB-scale (`ghcr.io/proximal-labs/...`), memory up to 128 GB, storage up to 150 GB. Grade
  on a **dedicated volume**, prune between tasks.
* **External APIs** — only two tasks reach the network: `frogsgame-rl` needs `TINKER_API_KEY` +
  internet (and is the only external-API task runnable on a CPU host — `gpus=0`, 8 h agent budget);
  `pcqm4mv2-autoresearch` allows internet but also requires an H100.
* **Reliability (D-009)** — long big-repo trials are the worst case for the slow-but-alive
  heartbeat-reclaim gap; the liveness-conditioned reclaim fix (F-FIX-038 / EI-1293) shipped,
  but infra non-completions are still counted-as-`false` + disclosed symmetrically (C6).
* **License (D-005)** — the repo ships **no LICENSE**: research/eval use only, no
  redistribution of derived data without owner sign-off.

entries.text:
FrontierSWE — ultra-long-horizon implementation / perf-eng / ML-research › Scoring & the headline
Each task's verifier emits a continuous reward in `[0,1]`. Per task we report **mean\@5**
(expected mean of a random 5-subset = the trial mean) and **best\@5** (the unbiased
expected max of a random 5-subset; `best@1 = mean`, `best@n = max`). Across tasks the
suite headline is the **coordination-topology comparison**: per-arm **mean\@5 / best\@5**,
**AVG RANK**, and **dominance**, optionally per bucket (implementation / performance /
research).

The public AVG RANK / dominance are relative to a fixed competitor pool (the `job.yaml`
models: claude-opus-4-6, gpt-5.4, gemini-3.1-pro, qwen, kimi, glm-5). By default we report
the **central-Mug vs distributed-peer vs ensemble vs single-agent** comparison on the
same tasks + same scorers under **iso-budget** — where FrontierSWE's real headroom (no
model fully solves the implementation tasks) makes a topology lift measurable. Reproducing
the absolute public rank requires running that competitor pool (an optional, owner-gated step).

entries.text:
Cookbook › Recipe 2: Migrating an existing `.map()` list to RichGrid Source pattern (anti-pattern in this codebase): ```tsx {items.map((item) => (
{item.id} {item.name} {item.status}
))} ``` Migration: ```tsx import { useMemo } from 'react'; import { RichGrid, type ColumnDef } from '@papercusp/grid-core'; const columns = useMemo[]>(() => [ { key: 'id', header: 'ID', width: 1, sortKey: 'id', render: ({ row }) => row.id }, { key: 'name', header: 'Name', width: 3, sortKey: 'name', render: ({ row }) => row.name }, { key: 'status', header: 'Status', width: 1, sortKey: 'status', render: ({ row }) => row.status }, ], []); return ( rows={items} columns={columns} getRowId={(i) => i.id} inline /> ); ``` Steps in order: 1. Add `import { RichGrid, type ColumnDef } from '@papercusp/grid-core'`. 2. Build a `columns` array, one entry per visible field. Wrap in `useMemo`. 3. Replace the `.map()` block with ``. 4. Move per-row click handler from each row to `onRowClick`. 5. Drop the manual loading + error CSS (RichGrid renders its own header even when rows is empty; provide a sibling empty-state component if you need a friendlier message).

entries.text:
Cookbook › Recipe 3: Adding a new column to an existing Zero-synced table
:::caution\[Per-harness tables are being retired]
The per-harness-table model below predates the consolidation migrations.
The canonical stores are now the `harness_shared.*_consolidated` tables —
writers should target those directly (see the
`COMMENT ON harness_features_consolidated` in `000-baseline.sql`), and Zero
exposes only the `*Consolidated.bySlug` / `*Consolidated.all` queries
(the per-harness named queries — `featuresSheets`, `issuesOrg`, … — were
removed; see the comment in `libs/zero-harness/src/queries.ts`). Add columns
to the consolidated table (Recipe 5) rather than to per-harness tables.
:::

The per-harness table names are **not** uniformly `harness_<table>` —
several (e.g. `feature_audit`, `agent_runs`) carry no `harness_` prefix.
The published per-harness tables are `harness_features`, `feature_audit`,
`harness_issues`, `harness_proposals`, `agent_runs`, `harness_snapshots`
(plus `messages`, `supervisor_notes`); see the publication list in
`bin/scaffold-harness-schema.sh` and `libs/zero-harness/src/schema.ts`.

```sql
ALTER TABLE harness_<slug>.harness_snapshots
  ADD COLUMN new_col text;
```

For each existing harness, repeat. Then:

1. Update the per-harness template SQL (the file `bin/scaffold-harness-schema.sh`
   `sed`-substitutes `{{SCHEMA}}` into and runs) so future harnesses get it —
   the column DDL lives in the template, not in the shell script itself.
2. Update `libs/zero-harness/src/schema.ts` — add `new_col: string()`
   (or the right type — beware TIMESTAMPTZ).
3. The publication already includes the table; the new column flows
   automatically.
4. Restart `zero-cache-harness`.
5. Update consumers (`useSyncQuery` results now include `new_col`).
entries.description: Cookbook › Recipe 3: Adding a new column to an existing Zero-synced table

entries.text:
Cookbook › Recipe 4: Adding a new table to all harnesses
Bigger lift. Steps:

1. Add the `CREATE TABLE` DDL to the **per-harness template SQL** (the
   file `bin/scaffold-harness-schema.sh` renders via `sed
   "s/{{SCHEMA}}/$schema/g"`), and add the table to the publication list
   in the scaffold script's `add_to_zero_publication` array. The script
   itself contains no DDL — it only substitutes the schema name into the
   template and runs it.
2. Run scaffold against every existing harness:
   ```bash
   for slug in $(psql -tAc "SELECT nspname FROM pg_namespace WHERE nspname LIKE 'harness\_%'" | sed 's/^harness_//'); do
     bin/scaffold-harness-schema.sh "$slug"
   done
   ```
3. Add the table to `libs/zero-harness/src/schema.ts` (register it in the
   `createSchema({ tables: [...] })` list).
4. Add a query factory to `queries.ts`.
5. Add a `slugToXxxKey` helper to `queries.ts`.
6. Restart `zero-cache-harness`.
entries.description: Cookbook › Recipe 4: Adding a new table to all harnesses

entries.text:
Cookbook › Recipe 5: Cross-harness consolidated table
When you need to render data across all harnesses (e.g. global feature
list).

1. Create a new base table in `harness_shared`:
   ```sql
   CREATE TABLE harness_shared.harness_<name>_consolidated (
     harness_slug text,
     <column>     <type>,
     -- …
     PRIMARY KEY (harness_slug, <pk>)
   );
   ```

2. For each per-harness source table, add an `AFTER INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE`
   trigger that maintains the consolidated table.

3. Add the consolidated table to the `zero_harness` publication.

4. Register a no-arg named query:
   ```ts
   <name>Consolidated: () => z.query.<name>Consolidated,
   ```

5. Register the table in `schema.ts` and restart zero-cache.

`harness_features_consolidated` is the working example to copy.

entries.text:
Cookbook › Recipe 8: Selected-row highlight
`getRowBg` is called with `(row, rowIndex, isSelected)` — RichGrid already
tracks whether a row is selected (from its own internal state, or from the
controlled `selectedRowIds`/`onSelectedRowIdsChange` pair if you pass them):

```tsx
const [selectedId, setSelectedId] = useState<string | null>(null);

const getRowBg = (row: Row, _rowIndex: number, isSelected: boolean) =>
  row.id === selectedId ? '#1f2937' : undefined;

<RichGrid
  rows={rows}
  columns={columns}
  getRowId={(r) => r.id}
  onRowClick={(r) => setSelectedId(r.id)}
  getRowBg={getRowBg}
  inline
/>
```

Return `undefined` (not `'transparent'`) to fall back to RichGrid's own
default striping/hover background rather than overriding it outright. For a
checkbox-style multi-select rather than a single active row, skip the manual
`selectedId` state entirely: pass `selectable` (or a controlled
`selectedRowIds`/`onSelectedRowIdsChange` pair) and read the built-in
`isSelected` argument in `getRowBg` instead of comparing ids yourself.

`apps/operator/app/adv/harnesses/WorkItemsPanel.tsx` is a current live
example of RichGrid with this exact `getRowBg` selected-row pattern; the
retired `SnapshotsPanel.tsx` (see Reference panels below) shows the older,
pre-dock version of the same idea.

Cookbook › When to pick this pattern over PG-canonical
| Pick PG-canonical (Recipe 1-2) when | Pick PG-mirror (this) when                                                    |
| ----------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| You own every writer                | A third-party process or runtime path writes the JSON and you can't change it |
| The data has no on-disk consumer    | A loader reads the JSON file at runtime by path                               |
| Atomicity of write matters          | The JSON is the operational source of truth and PG is a query-side index      |

Reference implementations:

* `packages/operator-core/lib/plugin-enables-pg.ts` (papercusp CLI is the writer)
* `packages/operator-core/lib/plugin-configs-pg.ts` (substrate plugin loader reads JSON at runtime)

entries.text:
Gotchas, performance, and migration anti-patterns › cmdk groups hide automatically when filtering
When the user types in `<Command.Input>`, cmdk filters items by their `value` prop. If a `<Command.Group>` ends up with zero matching children, cmdk **hides the entire group, including the heading.** This is the right UX, but if you're testing or debugging, your group's heading vanishing is expected behavior, not a bug.

Use `<Command.Group hidden={false}>` to force-show, or check the `[hidden]` attr in DevTools.

entries.text:
Gotchas, performance, and migration anti-patterns › Content disclosure: use `LazyDetails` — native `<details>` has been fully migrated
*(Updated 2026-07-09 — the old "approved native `<details>` sites" list is gone; every listed site migrated.)*

There are **zero native `<details>` blocks left in app UI**. The historical tension — HR6 says use `<Collapsible>`, but Radix Collapsible mounts heavy children eagerly even when collapsed — was resolved by **`app/_components/LazyDetails.tsx`**: a Radix Collapsible wrapper that defers mounting `children` until first open (and keeps them mounted afterward so internal state survives collapse/expand). It is the standard primitive for content disclosure (prose, diagnostic dumps, JSON dumps, debug help text) *and* satisfies HR6, so there is no perf reason to reach for native `<details>` anymore.

* Heavy renderer behind a collapsed section (Monaco, MarkdownPreview, JSON tree, long log dump) → `<LazyDetails summary={…}>…</LazyDetails>`.
* Interactive disclosure that should start mounted (collapsible form sections, per-row expanders needing shared animation/focus) → plain `<Collapsible.Root>`.
* Native `<details>` remains acceptable **only inside rendered markdown content** (content-author markup the React tree can't reach), same as the native-checkbox markdown carve-out in HR2.

Two native-`<details>` niceties are knowingly given up by LazyDetails: Chromium's find-in-page inside collapsed content (`hidden-until-found`) and auto-expand on print. If a surface genuinely needs those, raise it in review rather than silently reintroducing `<details>` — the direction is zero `<details>` in `.tsx`.
entries.description: Gotchas, performance, and migration anti-patterns › Content disclosure: use `LazyDetails` — native `<details>` has been fully migrated

entries.text:
Gotchas, performance, and migration anti-patterns › CSS-token lint catches undefined `var(--X)` references
Every `var(--X)` reference in a `.tsx` file must resolve to a token defined in `app/globals.css`, `app/_semantic.css`, or `app/_brand-primitives.css` — or be in the runtime-allowlist `RUNTIME_TOKENS` (in `app/_lints/css-tokens.test.ts`), a literal enumerated set of tokens a framework/component writes at runtime rather than defining in any CSS source — e.g. `--radix-select-trigger-width` (Radix Select), `--op-chat-w` (the chat sidebar's chrome offset), `--left-sidebar-w`/`--dev-rail-w`/`--pc-env-bar-h` (layout rails that measure themselves in JS), Sonner's per-toast `--toasts-before`/`--lift-amount`/`--front-toast-height`, `--mic-level` (voice input level), `--intro-index`/`--cup-index` (dev swarm identity artwork), and `--xy-handle-tx` (React Flow geometry). It's a literal set, **not** a `--radix-*` wildcard, so a new runtime-written token — Radix or otherwise — still has to be added to `RUNTIME_TOKENS` explicitly.

The lint also satisfies **component-local** custom properties: a `--name:` that is both defined and used inside the same `.tsx` (e.g. inside a styled-jsx `<style>` block) counts as defined without any global definition — the global CSS-source scan can't see definitions that live in a `.tsx`, so the lint collects each file's own `--name:` definitions and treats self-references as resolved.

The lint lives at `app/_lints/css-tokens.test.ts` and runs as part of the operator's unit test suite. When it fails the error message lists every undefined token + the files using it, plus the canonical operator vocabulary to map to (`--bg`, `--bg-2`, `--bg-3`, `--fg`, `--fg-dim`, `--fg-mute`, `--border`, `--accent`, `--good`, `--warn`, `--bad`, etc.).

**Common regressions the lint catches:**

* shadcn vocabulary leaking in: `--card`, `--muted-foreground`, `--foreground`
* Tailwind-aliased semantic names: `--danger`, `--ok`, `--success`
* Inverted re-use of swept
entries.description: Gotchas, performance, and migration anti-patterns › CSS-token lint catches undefined `var(--X)` references

entries.text:
Gotchas, performance, and migration anti-patterns › Floating widgets that pin to a viewport corner are NOT centered Modals
The canonical example is the Deck (`OperatorPanel`, the fixed `.operator-panel` HUD whose wordmark reads "Deck") — a floating, viewport-anchored panel with its own bespoke animations and HUD overlays. It's not a centered modal (Modal would yank it to screen-center and add a backdrop), not an anchored Popover (no trigger to align to), and not a side Drawer (it doesn't slide in from the edge).

For this shape, the correct pattern is landmark/dialog semantics by hand — an `aria-label`ed container using `role="region"` (non-blocking, always-on-screen HUD) or `role="dialog"` (if it genuinely captures a task) — with positioning + animation owned by the component. HR1 doesn't apply here; the rule's intent ("focus management + escape handling come from the wrapper") doesn't fit a panel that lives forever on screen and toggles open/closed via its own state machine. Treat the Deck as the canonical exception; if you add a new floating-corner-widget pattern, document it next to it.

*(History: `OracleDock` and `OperatorChatSidebar` — the "Papercup chat" web sidebar — were the other two examples of this pattern. Both were retired 2026-07-09 (`_retired/legacy-web-chats/`): the only chat surface is the terminal-native pui chat pane in the zellij dock.)*

entries.text:
Gotchas, performance, and migration anti-patterns › Migration anti-patterns
Things we did wrong during the migration and had to back out — don't repeat:

*Historical note: the operator has since migrated off Next.js/Turbopack to a
Vite SPA (TanStack Router) + Hono host. The Turbopack-, `.next/`-, and
`next/dynamic()`-specific items below are kept as migration history; they no
longer describe the live build (use Vite's own dynamic-import / lazy patterns
now), but the non-Next items (the regex/stack-walker and the Radix
`data-state` one) still apply.*

* **Don't write a Python regex that captures `.+?` between `<div>` tags.** Self-closing `<div/>` tags throw off the depth counter. Use a stack-based walker that distinguishes `<div ... />` from `<div ...>`.

* **Don't add a `tsconfig.json` to a sub-package to fix `.js`-extension resolution under Turbopack.** Turbopack doesn't honor sub-package tsconfigs for files outside the project's own `tsconfig.json` `include`. We tried; it didn't help. The actual fix was a local copy at `apps/operator/lib/...` that bypassed the package barrel.

* **Don't delete `.next/` to force a recompile.** The dev server gets wedged because it can't find its build manifests. Touch a source file or restart the server entirely instead.

* **Don't rely on `await import()` to lazy-load.** Turbopack statically traces dynamic imports too. To genuinely defer, you need either (a) the library lazy-loaded via Next.js's `dynamic()`, or (b) a constructed import path (`new Function('s', 'return import(s)')`) — but (b) is fragile and we ended up not needing it.

* **Don't compare `data-state` on Radix Tabs triggers when there's no `<Tabs.Content>`.** Compare `aria-selected`. (Repeating because this is the most subtle one.)
entries.description: Gotchas, performance, and migration anti-patterns › Migration anti-patterns

entries.text:
Gotchas, performance, and migration anti-patterns › Modal overlay click vs ESC
Radix Dialog's outside-click is implemented as a `pointerdown` event on the overlay, not a `click`. If you're writing tests that "click outside to close", dispatch a `pointerdown` event, not a `click`:

```js
const overlay = document.querySelector('[data-state=open][role!=dialog]');
overlay.dispatchEvent(new PointerEvent('pointerdown', { bubbles: true, pointerType: 'mouse' }));
```

ESC works as expected via `keydown`.
entries.description: Gotchas, performance, and migration anti-patterns › Modal overlay click vs ESC
Gotchas, performance, and migration anti-patterns › Native checkbox / radio / range — `accent-color` is the carve-out, NOT the migration

entries.text:
Gotchas, performance, and migration anti-patterns › Native `title=` is fine in grid cells, NOT on actions
The "no native title=" rule is a soft rule, not a hard one.

**Use `<Tooltip label>` for action elements** — buttons, status badges, IconButtons, anywhere the user might hover for a hint about what clicking does.

**Use native `title=` for grid-cell truncation tooltips** — when you have thousands of `<RichGrid>` rows and each cell wants "show full text on hover when truncated". Wrapping every cell in a Radix Tooltip mounts thousands of portals + listeners and noticeably hits scroll performance. Native `title=` is browser-built-in, free, and accessible-enough for data hover.

A tell that you should use native `title=`: the value is dynamic and per-row (`title={row.title}`), not a static label. Static action-button hints almost always belong in `<Tooltip>`.
entries.description: Gotchas, performance, and migration anti-patterns › Native `title=` is fine in grid cells, NOT on actions

entries.text:
Gotchas, performance, and migration anti-patterns › Per-field-settings pages — don't reach for RHF
If you're looking at `/settings/voice`, `/settings/backups`, or any other settings page where each control persists independently (no Submit button, no atomic "save the whole form" gesture), **do not migrate it to `useFormWith`**. That conflates the page's model with what RHF was built for. Use `useDebouncedSave(value, persist)` per field instead — full pattern is in [libraries: Form patterns](/internal/docs/design/libraries#form-patterns--picking-the-right-model).

The inverse is also a trap: `/settings/operator` looks similar but is a genuine atomic form — it uses `useFormWith(ConfigSchema)` with a single `<form onSubmit={submit(onSave)}>` and a "Save prompt + preferences" submit button. Don't "fix" it to per-field auto-save; it's RHF on purpose. The distinction is the save gesture, not the URL.

Symptoms that mean you've picked the wrong pattern:

* You're calling `getValues()` from a "Test microphone" / "Test connection" button just to read the user's current draft.
* You wrote a custom `watch()` + debounce on top of RHF to re-create auto-save semantics.
* `isDirty` is permanently `false` even though the user clearly made changes (because you've manually flushed each one).

If any of those, stop and switch to `useDebouncedSave`. HR1/HR2/HR3/HR6 still apply — the `<Modal>` / `<Checkbox>` / `<Select>` / `<Collapsible>` wrappers are still required. You're only opting out of RHF's central form-state model.
entries.description: Gotchas, performance, and migration anti-patterns › Per-field-settings pages — don't reach for RHF

entries.text:
Gotchas, performance, and migration anti-patterns › Performance budget — what's reasonable
These are the numbers we measured after the original migration. Use them as floors; if your change makes any of these significantly worse, investigate.

| Interaction                                       | Dev mode         | Production target |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ---------------- | ----------------- |
| Cold page load (HTTP `time_total`)                | 0.87 – 1.21s     | \< 200ms          |
| Inner tab switch (e.g., Inbox All → Threads)      | \~150ms          | \~50ms            |
| Command palette open (Dialog mount + cmdk wiring) | \~314ms          | \~100ms           |
| Modal open/close cycle                            | \~100ms          | \~30ms            |
| Memory after 10 modal open/close cycles           | 0 KB heap growth | 0 KB heap growth  |

If you're adding a new modal or a new heavy panel and tab switches start feeling sluggish (>300ms in dev), check:

1. Are you mounting heavy children eagerly when the modal closes? Use lazy / dynamic imports or guard rendering with `{open && <…/>}`.
2. Did you wrap a frequently-rendered grid cell in `<Tooltip>`? See "Native `title=` is fine in grid cells".
3. Did a useEffect get added that runs every render? Check deps.
entries.description: Gotchas, performance, and migration anti-patterns › Performance budget — what's reasonable

entries.text:
Gotchas, performance, and migration anti-patterns › Radix Select doesn't allow empty-string values
`<Select value="">` is reserved by Radix Select to mean "no value selected" — same as `<Select value={undefined}>`. If your business logic uses `''` as a real value (e.g., "default mode"), Radix Select will display the placeholder when you actually mean to display "default".

**Fix:** translate at the boundary.

```tsx
<Select
  value={mode || '_default'}
  onChange={(v) => setMode(v === '_default' ? '' : v)}
  options={[{ value: '_default', label: 'default' }, { value: 'ceo', label: 'ceo' }]}
/>
```

Use a papercup like `'_default'` that's guaranteed not to collide with a real value, and translate in `onChange`.
entries.description: Gotchas, performance, and migration anti-patterns › Radix Select doesn't allow empty-string values
Gotchas, performance, and migration anti-patterns › The `data-state` vs `aria-selected` trap (Radix Tabs)

entries.text:
Gotchas, performance, and migration anti-patterns › Tooltip needs real pointer events to fire
When testing tooltips programmatically, synthetic `MouseEvent('mouseenter')` doesn't trigger Radix Tooltip's open state. You need real pointer events from a browser-driver (Playwright `page.hover()` works; `verdict hover @e18` works).

This is a Radix design choice (focus on real input intent, not synthetic dispatches) — there's no workaround beyond using a real driver.

entries.text:
Gotchas, performance, and migration anti-patterns › When the agent population is large
Multiple agents working on the same files concurrently is normal here. The harness is the substrate's most-edited surface. Best practices:

1. **Run an audit before you start.** `grep -lE "from './Tooltip'"` etc. tells you which files use which library. If your file isn't in the list and the pattern says it should, that's a regression to fix.

2. **Run an audit after you finish.** Re-grep. If a file you edited dropped its `Tooltip` import while you were adding new functionality, you reintroduced native `title=` or stripped a wrap by accident.

3. **Don't blanket-replace.** A Python script that mass-removes `<Tooltip>` wrappers (because some IDE auto-import suggested them as redundant) will silently revert dozens of files. We've seen this happen.

4. **When in doubt, look at a working example.** The "where to look" table on the [overview page](/internal/docs/design) lists a canonical example for each pattern.

entries.text:
Library reference › 1. Single-submit form
The user fills N fields, clicks one Submit button, the whole form is validated and persisted as one atomic transaction. Use **`react-hook-form` + `useFormWith(zodSchema)`** (or `makeAjvResolver` for plugin JSON Schemas).

*Canonical sites:* `/login`, `/signup`, `/installed/templates/<slug>/edit`, `/snapshots/<id>/fork`.

See [`react-hook-form` below](#react-hook-form--hookformresolvers--ajv--zod) for the wrappers, schema dialect choice, and migration recipe.
entries.description: Library reference › 1. Single-submit form
Library reference › 2. Per-field auto-save settings page

entries.text:
Library reference › 3. Wizard flow
Multi-step with progress, each step its own slice of state, the whole flow persisted at the end (or in chunks at step boundaries). Use **RHF per step**, with the step's local Zod slice, plus a parent state coordinator.

*Canonical site:* `app/_components/SetupWizard`.
entries.description: Library reference › 3. Wizard flow

entries.text:
Library reference › `<Button>` wrapper + native baseline
In-page buttons get a solid/tinted fill, a 1px border, and readable text — **no** embossed bevel, raised drop-shadow/glow, hover-lift, or "sheen" gradient. Hover/active changes colour, not elevation. See [Buttons](/internal/docs/design#buttons) for the recipe and anti-patterns (this is hard rule 9). There is no scoped backstop rule on `/adv` (the `.pc-advshell__*` family no longer exists) — author buttons flat at the source; the top tab strip is exempt.

A native `<button>` baseline and the `.pc-btn-*` variant rules **are present** in `globals.css`: the shared `:where(button, .pc-btn)` block sets fill, a 1px border, `border-radius: 6px`, and hover/focus/disabled states, followed by the per-variant colors (`.pc-btn-accent`, `.pc-btn-primary`, `.pc-btn-destructive`, `.pc-btn-ghost`) and the one size class (`.pc-btn-lg`). So applying a `.pc-btn-*` class to a native `<button>` **does** style it — `Button.tsx` / `SubmitButton.tsx` rely on exactly that. Those rules are all specificity-0 `:where()`, so **source order** decides: the size and variant rules must stay *after* the baseline block.

**What:** The `<Button>` wrapper at `app/harness/Button.tsx` is the styled entry point (it layers on the global native-`<button>` baseline — see the note above). It has **two orthogonal axes**, and every Button emits the `.pc-btn` base class:

`size` — the scale:

* `size="sm"` *(default)* — the 26px chrome/toolbar scale
* `size="lg"` — the 40px page-CTA scale

`variant` — the surface:

* `variant="neutral"` *(default)* — the plain surface
* `variant="accent"` — soft accent tint; the everyday page CTA
* `variant="primary"` — filled accent for the page's primary CTA
* `variant="destructive"` — red tint for delete / clear / forget actions
* `variant="ghost"` — transparent until hovered, for low-emphasis chrome

**When to use which:**

* Action buttons can use the wrapper for variant/icon/spinner affordances — the global baseline a

entries.text:
Library reference › `cmdk`
**What:** Command palette primitive. Built by Paco Coursey (Vercel). Powers the launchers in Linear, Raycast, Vercel's dashboard, and many others.

**Why this one:** Hand-rolling a command palette means re-implementing fuzzy filtering, keyboard nav (↑/↓/Enter/Escape), focus management, group rendering, virtualization, and accessibility. cmdk does all of that out of the box. We pair it with `@radix-ui/react-dialog` for the shell.

**Usage:** `<Dialog.Root><Command label loop shouldFilter><Command.Input/><Command.List><Command.Empty/><Command.Group heading="…"><Command.Item value onSelect>…</Command.Item></Command.Group></Command.List></Command>`. The `value` on each Item is what cmdk fuzzy-searches.

**File:** `CommandPalette.tsx` — the harness ⌘K palette.
entries.description: Library reference › `cmdk`

entries.text:
Library reference › Exceptions (none of the three patterns)
* **Single-textarea chat composers** (`ChatPanel`, `OracleDock`, `SupportAgentPanel`). One field with custom IME/keyboard handling — plain `useState`.
* **Monaco code editors** (`SpecEditor`, `ManifestSpecEditor`). They edit text files, not form fields.

***

entries.text:
Library reference › Form patterns — picking the right model
Three submission models, three corresponding patterns. Pick by **how the page persists**, not "does it have validation."
