entries.text:
Library reference › `lucide-react`
**What:** Icon set. Tree-shakable, ESM-first, \~1500 icons.

**Why this one:** Forked from Feather Icons, actively maintained, consistent stroke-width, easy to swap. Replaces the 100+ inline `<svg>` icons we had before. Each icon is a separate import: `import { Check, X, ChevronRight } from 'lucide-react'`.

**Sizing convention:** `<Check size={11} />` for inline pills, `<Check size={13} />` for buttons, `<Check className="h-3 w-3" />` works too. Use `strokeWidth={1.75}` to match the harness's existing visual weight; the default `strokeWidth={2}` looks slightly bolder.

**Brand logos kept as inline SVG:** Google, Facebook, Apple, Visa, Mastercard, Amex, Discover. Not in lucide; can't be replaced by a generic icon.
entries.description: Library reference › `lucide-react`

entries.text:
Library reference › `motion` + `@formkit/auto-animate`
**What:** The animation stack. Two general-purpose libraries that complement each other (**use them together, not as alternatives**).

* **`motion`** (the rebrand of `framer-motion` — same engine, same author) — the general-purpose React animation lib. WAAPI-backed since v10, so transforms run on the native compositor. \~41 KB gzip.
* **`@formkit/auto-animate`** — purpose-built for one job: animate when children of an element are added, removed, or reordered. Drop-in via `useAutoAnimate()`. WAAPI direct, zero React re-renders. \~3 KB gzip.

**GSAP is not part of the app UI stack.** Do not add `gsap` or `@gsap/react` for operator UI. If an effect needs choreography, use `motion`; if it is a simple open/close, use CSS; if it is list add/remove/reorder, use `auto-animate`.

**The "jump-gate" route warp is testing-only.** `RouteTransitionProvider.tsx` plays the warp overlay via the **Web Animations API** (transform/opacity only — GPU-composited; no gsap), but the app root mounts that provider only when `FLAGS.TESTING` is on. Normal navigation is plain TanStack `<Link>` without a route-transition overlay.

**The rule of three** (memorize this):

| Need                                                                           | Reach for                                                                                   | Why                                                                                                                                     |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Modal / popover / dropdown / tab open + close                                  | **CSS** with `[data-anim="pop"]` / `[data-anim="fade"]` keyed off Radix `
entries.description: Library reference › `motion` + `@formkit/auto-animate`

entries.text:
Library reference › Native checkbox / radio / range — `accent-color` baseline
**What:** Native `<input type="checkbox|radio|range">` are *intended* to get `accent-color: var(--accent)` so the native control's tint (checkmark fill, radio dot, slider track + thumb) recolors to the app accent without breaking the OS rendering or accessibility semantics.

A *global* `:where(input[type="checkbox"], input[type="radio"], input[type="range"]) { accent-color: var(--accent); }` baseline **is present** in `globals.css:675-677`, so native checkbox/radio/range controls pick up the accent tint automatically. Component-scoped `accent-color` rules also exist (`.pc-toggle input`, `.pc-template-manifest-structured input[type="checkbox"]` with a hardcoded `#22d3ee`), but they are no longer the only source. *(An earlier version of this Aside claimed there was no global baseline; it is present.)*

**Why this exists alongside HR2:** the wrapper is still required for harness interactive UI (HR2 explicit). This is the baseline for native controls that *legitimately can't* be wrapped:

* `<input type="checkbox">` inside `MarkdownPreview` (rendered from text — the React wrapper isn't reachable)
* Native radios in low-priority sites (`/settings/backups` cadence/retention pickers, `/settings/agent` backend picker, `SetupWizard` channel selector) — there's no `<RadioGroup>` wrapper because the cost/benefit doesn't justify one for \~5 sites
* `<input type="range">` (voice TTS rate, chat scale, sketch brush size) — bespoke per-site; `accent-color` is the cross-cutting tint

**No wrapper for radios.** Considered. Rejected: \~5 sites, no indeterminate / multi-state need, no a11y issue with native radios, and Radix `react-radio-group` would still need bespoke styling per site to match the harness theme. Native + `accent-color` is enough.
entries.description: Library reference › Native checkbox / radio / range — `accent-color` baseline

entries.text:
Library reference › Native `<input>` + `<textarea>` styling
The `:where(input:not([type]), input[type=text|number|email|search|tel|url|password|date|time|datetime-local], textarea)` baseline **is present** in `apps/operator/app/globals.css:629-655`, and the live operator-vite UI loads it (`apps/operator-vite/src/routes/__root.tsx` imports `@/app/globals.css`). It sets `background: var(--bg-2)`, `color: var(--fg)`, a 1px `var(--border)`, `border-radius: 4px`, `font-size: 12px`, `4px 8px` padding, plus an accent focus ring (`:657-673`). So an *unwrapped* native `<input>` / `<textarea>` **does** pick up the dark theme. The harness wrappers (`TextInput.tsx` `BASE_STYLE`, `Select.tsx` `TRIGGER_DEFAULT_STYLE`) layer leading/trailing affordances on top — they are no longer the only styled path. *(An earlier version of this Aside claimed the baseline had been dropped in the operator-vite migration; it has since been restored.)*

**Intended look** (carried by the wrappers' inline `BASE_STYLE`): `var(--bg-2)` background, `var(--border)` border, `border-radius: 4`, font-size 12, `4px 8px` padding, with an accent-tinted focus ring. This matches the `<Select>` trigger.

**Why a baseline was the goal:** Inputs are scattered across hundreds of sites; migrating every one to a wrapper would be high-churn for low marginal value. A single `:where(...)` specificity-0 rule would fix the visual problem in one place — any site with an inline style or class still winning, so bespoke surfaces (marketplace search, OracleDock composer, etc.) keep their custom look. That `:where(...)` baseline is in place (`globals.css:629-655`), so the visual problem is solved app-wide; reach for the wrapper for leading/trailing affordances, not for basic theming.

**Selector list** (intentionally narrow): `input[type=text|number|email|search|tel|url|password|date|time|datetime-local]`, untyped `<input>`, and `<textarea>`. Excluded: `checkbox`/`radio` (use `<Checkbox>`), `range`/`color`/`file` (bespoke widget
entries.description: Library reference › Native `<input>` + `<textarea>` styling

entries.text:
Library reference › `@papercusp/grid-core` — `RichGrid`, `VirtualGrid`, `GridTable`, `DataGridShell`
**What:** Grid components for tabular data. Pick by what cells need to do — see the [decision matrix](/internal/docs/design#grids--richgrid-vs-gridtable-vs-datagridshell).

**`VirtualGrid` — the default for large/unbounded grids.** A thin wrapper over `RichGrid` that owns the TanStack virtualizer + scroll container, so only the visible window mounts as DOM. Pass an in-memory `rows` array; every other RichGrid prop passes through. Use it for any grid whose row count is unbounded or can exceed a few hundred — **don't cap the fetch to keep render cheap** (on a local desktop app the data is already local; load it all and window the render). Full API + the companion "honest count" (`_meta.total`) pattern: [data-sync/richgrid](/internal/docs/data-sync/richgrid#virtualgrid-the-drop-in-for-large-grids).

**Built-in print + copy support** (RichGrid, default-on):

* **Print fidelity** — RichGrid renders a hidden native `<table>` next to the grid (`data-rg-print-mirror`). On `@media print`, the virtualized div tree is hidden and the table mirror shows. Browser handles pagination + repeating `<thead>`. No virtualization-snapshot truncation, full dataset prints.
* **Ctrl+C → TSV + HTML payload** — when the grid root has keyboard focus, Ctrl+C copies the current row selection (or all rows if none selected) to the clipboard as both TSV (`text/plain`) and `<table>` markup (`text/html`). Excel / Sheets / Numbers paste it as cells; plain text editors get TSV.
* **Ctrl+A** — selects every row (so the next Ctrl+C copies everything).

To make this work, provide a `toCopyText: (row) => string` on each `ColumnDef` whose cell has meaningful text. For columns that are pure affordance (action buttons, icons), omit `toCopyText` — the column copies empty for each row.

If a column's `header` is JSX, also provide `headerText: 'Plain header'` so the print mirror and the TSV/HTML payloads have a s
entries.description: Library reference › `@papercusp/grid-core` — `RichGrid`, `VirtualGrid`, `GridTable`, `DataGridShell`

entries.text:
Library reference › `@radix-ui/react-checkbox`
**What:** Checkbox primitive. Supports `checked={true | false | 'indeterminate'}`.

**Why this one:** Native `<input type="checkbox">` can't render the indeterminate state declaratively (you have to set `el.indeterminate = true` after mount, awkward in React). It also fights the dark theme and uses OS check styling. Radix renders a `<button role="checkbox">` with a `<Checkbox.Indicator>` slot we control.

**Wrapper:** `app/harness/Checkbox.tsx` exports `<Checkbox checked onChange indeterminate>`. We use lucide `Check` for the checked state and `Minus` for indeterminate.

**Grid cells:** When using inside a `RichGrid` row render, wrap with `<span onClick={(e) => e.stopPropagation()}>` so clicking the checkbox doesn't trigger the row's click handler. For a live Checkbox-in-grid example, see `apps/operator-vite/src/components/adv/AdvEvalsTab.tsx`.
entries.description: Library reference › `@radix-ui/react-checkbox`

entries.text:
Library reference › `@radix-ui/react-collapsible`
**What:** Disclosure primitive (single-section show/hide).

**Why this one:** Same Radix family. Native `<details>` works but doesn't share our focus styles or animation system, and doesn't compose with controlled state cleanly. Collapsible takes `open` + `onOpenChange` like the rest of our Radix primitives.

**Usage:** `<Collapsible.Root open={isOpen} onOpenChange={setIsOpen}><Collapsible.Trigger asChild><button>label</button></Collapsible.Trigger><Collapsible.Content>…</Collapsible.Content></Collapsible.Root>`.

**Files (live):** `apps/operator/app/settings/publishing/PublishingClient.tsx`, `apps/operator/app/settings/operator/page.tsx`, `apps/operator/app/harness/FeatureEditor.tsx`, and `apps/operator-vite/src/components/left-sidebar/HiveSteeringTree.tsx`.
entries.description: Library reference › `@radix-ui/react-collapsible`

entries.text:
Library reference › `@radix-ui/react-dialog`
**What:** Modal dialog primitive. Provides focus trap, focus restoration on close, scroll lock, portal rendering, and ESC + outside-click handling.

**Why this one:** Same Radix family. The hand-rolled alternatives we tried (`<div role="dialog" aria-modal>`) consistently lost focus trap on tab cycling, missed scroll lock on iOS, and raced ESC against other listeners. Dialog gives us all four for free.

**Wrapper:** `app/harness/Modal.tsx` matches the harness's centered-modal visual (rgba(0,0,0,0.75) overlay, fixed inset, content centered). The overlay renders at zIndex `z` (default **100** — `const z = zIndex ?? 100`, so the base `OVERLAY_STYLE.zIndex` of 60 is overridden) and the content at `z + 1` (101); the 100 default puts modals above the persistent OracleDock (z:80). Accepts `contentStyle` for sizing, `overlayStyle` to tweak backdrop, `zIndex` to override stacking. Always provide `title` (sr-only renders if `srOnlyTitle`) for screen readers.

**Programmatic close:** `onOpenChange={(o) => { if (!o) onClose(); }}`. To prevent ESC or outside-click closing: `closeOnEscape={false}` / `closeOnOutsideClick={false}`.
entries.description: Library reference › `@radix-ui/react-dialog`

entries.text:
Library reference › `@radix-ui/react-hover-card`
**What:** Rich hover-triggered popover (different from Tooltip — designed for multi-line content, links, badges).

**Why this one:** Same Radix family. If you find yourself wanting a Tooltip but with non-text content, switch to HoverCard.

`@radix-ui/react-hover-card` (`^1.1.15`) is still in `package.json`, but its only reference (`FeatureLink.tsx`) is retired code under `libs/papercusp/_retired/apps-web/`. There is **no live usage** in the operator app today. (This also undercuts the older Tooltip rationale that hover-card is "already in the codebase" — it's installed, not actively used.)
entries.description: Library reference › `@radix-ui/react-hover-card`

entries.text:
Library reference › `@radix-ui/react-select`
**What:** Single-select dropdown primitive. Renders a button trigger + portaled listbox.

**Why this one:** Native `<select>` is OS-themed (white-on-macOS, blue-highlight-on-Windows) and ignores our dark theme. Radix Select gives us full control: themed trigger, portal-positioned listbox that handles viewport edges, proper keyboard search ("type-ahead"), `<optgroup>` analog (`<Select.Group>` + `<Select.Label>`), and `<ItemIndicator>` for the current selection.

**Wrapper:** `app/harness/Select.tsx` exports `<Select value onChange options>` with a flat options array. For grouped options (org/department/coding sections, etc.), inline Radix Select directly using `<Select.Group>` + `<Select.Label>`.

Radix Select reserves `value=""` to mean "no value selected". If your business logic uses `''` as a papercup for "default mode", map to a non-empty string at the boundary: `value={mode || '_default'} onChange={(v) => setMode(v === '_default' ? '' : v)}`. See `apps/operator/app/settings/user/page.tsx` (the "(use workspace default)" option maps `'_default'` ⇄ `''`).
entries.description: Library reference › `@radix-ui/react-select`

entries.text:
Library reference › `@radix-ui/react-tabs`
**What:** Tab primitive. Real ARIA tablist + tab + tabpanel.

**Why this one:** Same Radix family. Handles activation modes (automatic vs manual), keyboard nav (arrows, home/end), and `aria-selected` automatically.

**Two usage patterns:**

1. **Real tabs with content panels** — wrap each panel in `<Tabs.Content value="…">`. Radix sets `data-state="active"` on the trigger when the matching content is open. See `apps/operator-vite/src/components/adv/AdvShell.tsx` and `apps/operator-vite/src/components/admin/AdminShell.tsx`.

2. **Filter pills (shared content)** — render content imperatively based on `Tabs.Root`'s `value` (no `<Tabs.Content>`). Radix only sets `aria-selected="true"` (not `data-state`). See `apps/operator/app/adv/sessions/AdvSessionsClient.tsx`.

If your tabs render content imperatively (no `<Tabs.Content>`), Radix only flips `aria-selected`, not `data-state`. Bridge with `[aria-selected="true"]` selectors in `harness.css`. See [gotchas](/internal/docs/design/gotchas) for the trap.
entries.description: Library reference › `@radix-ui/react-tabs`

entries.text:
Library reference › `@radix-ui/react-tooltip`
**What:** Hover/focus tooltip primitive. WAI-ARIA `tooltip` role, focus-aware, touch-friendly, keyboard-navigable.

**Why this one:** Radix is the de facto standard for headless UI primitives in React. Same family as the other `@radix-ui/*` primitives we use, so peer-deps align automatically. Maintained by WorkOS, used by Vercel, Linear, and most of the React ecosystem. Tiny (\~5 KB gzipped) and tree-shakable.

**Why not `react-tooltip`?** Older, heavier, less accessible. Why not native `title=`? See [gotchas](/internal/docs/design/gotchas) — it has UX problems we lived through.

**Wrapper:** `app/harness/Tooltip.tsx` exports `<Tooltip label={...}>{trigger}</Tooltip>`. Returns the trigger unchanged when `label` is falsy. Trigger receives `asChild` so the underlying button/span keeps its DOM identity.

**Provider:** A root provider is mounted in the Vite SPA root (`apps/operator-vite/src/routes/__root.tsx`) with `delayDuration={150} skipDelayDuration={300}` — opens after 150ms, with consecutive tooltips opening instantly within 300ms of the last close (keeps quick scans fast). These root timings only govern tooltips composed **directly** from `@radix-ui/react-tooltip`.

`app/harness/Tooltip.tsx` wraps **every** tooltip it renders in its own `RT.Provider` with `delayDuration={250} skipDelayDuration={150}`, which shadows the root values. So a tooltip rendered through `<Tooltip label>` actually opens after **250ms** (not 150ms) with a **150ms** skip window (not 300ms). The root provider is therefore not "wrapped once" — and `app/pi/layout.tsx` mounts a third `Tooltip.Provider` (150/300) that the operator-vite `pi.tsx` route notes is redundant. If you need the root timings, compose the primitive directly rather than through the wrapper.
entries.description: Library reference › `@radix-ui/react-tooltip`

entries.text:
Library reference › `react-hook-form` + `@hookform/resolvers` + `ajv` + `zod`
**What:** Form-state management. RHF owns input registration / dirty tracking / submit handling; the resolvers package bridges to Zod (for forms whose schema we control) or Ajv (for forms whose schema is plugin-author-supplied JSON Schema).

**Why this one:** After a freshness pass on the React form-library landscape (rjsf, jsonforms, formily, formisch, autoform, tanstack-form), `react-hook-form` was the clear winner for our constraints — \~33 KB / 11 KB gzip, zero runtime deps, uncontrolled inputs (minimal re-renders), SSR-compatible behind a `"use client"` boundary, and — critically — a first-class Ajv resolver that handles the per-plugin JSON Schemas without forcing plugin authors to migrate to Zod/Valibot. Same library covers both internal forms (Zod schemas we author) and dynamic plugin-config forms (Ajv against third-party schemas), so the team learns one form mental model. See `apps/operator/lib/forms/README.md` for the per-PR migration recipe.

**Wrappers:** `apps/operator/lib/forms/`:

* `useFormWith(zodSchema)` — wraps `useForm` with `zodResolver` and exposes a tighter `{ register, submit, errors, isSubmitting, isDirty, ... }`. Use this for any form whose schema you own.
* `<FormField label error description>` — labelled input wrapper with inline `FieldError`/string error rendering. Matches the existing CSS-variable styling.
* `<SubmitButton pending>` — disabled-while-submitting button bound to `isSubmitting`.
* `makeAjvResolver(jsonSchema)` — pre-registers `ajv-formats` (so `email`, `uri`, `date-time`, etc. resolve). Use with vanilla `useForm`, not `useFormWith`. Required for any form that consumes plugin-author JSON Schema (the per-plugin Config tab, `/settings/plugins`).

**When to use which schema dialect:**

| Schema source                                                                   | Resolver      | Helper

entries.text:
Library reference › `<TextInput>` + `<TextArea>` wrappers
**What:** Canonical text-entry wrappers at `app/harness/TextInput.tsx`. Re-exports `<input>` / `<textarea>` with the baseline style plus first-class `leading` and `trailing` slots.

**Why use the wrapper:**

* You need a leading or trailing element inside the bordered container (icon, prefix, unit, clear-x button).
* You want the canonical class hook (`.pc-text-input`) for future restyling. (Note: there is no `.pc-text-input` CSS *rule* in current source — the wrapper carries its look via inline `BASE_STYLE`; the class is a future hook, not an active style.)
* You want to opt out of any inline-style cascade a parent might be applying.

**Use the wrapper for affordances, not for theming.** A simple `<input type="text" value … onChange …>` **does** pick up the dark-theme look on its own via the global `:where(input, textarea)` baseline (`globals.css:629-655`; see the [native input section](#native-input--textarea-styling)). Reach for `<TextInput>` when you want the wrapper's leading/trailing slots or validation affordances; a bare `<input>` already matches surrounding fields.

**Don't override the canonical look with ad-hoc inline styles.** Applying `style={{ background, border, borderRadius, padding }}` to an `<input>` or `<textarea>` drifts the look away from the wrapper's `BASE_STYLE` (and away from every other input in the harness). If you need a different look in one place, reach for `<TextInput>` and document the deviation; if you need it everywhere, change `BASE_STYLE` in `TextInput.tsx` (or restore + edit the global `globals.css` baseline). A page-local `inputStyleSmall` const that re-states `background: 'var(--bg-3)'` is the failure mode this rule names.

```tsx
import { TextInput, TextArea } from '@/app/harness/TextInput';

<TextInput
  type="number"
  value={n}
  onChange={(e) => setN(Number(e.target.value))}
  min={1}
  max={64}
  style={{ width: 64 }}
/>

<TextInput
  type="search"
  placeholder="f

entries.text:
Library reference › `vaul`
**What:** Drawer primitive (right/left/bottom/top slide-in panels). Drag-to-dismiss, focus trap, scroll lock, ARIA — all handled.

**Why this one:** Built by Emil Kowalski (Vercel design engineer). Drag gestures and momentum are surprisingly hard to get right; vaul does. The live usage is the right-side plan detail drawer (`apps/operator/app/admin/plans/PlanDetail.tsx` — `<Drawer.Root direction="right">`).

**Why not Radix Dialog with `direction`?** Radix doesn't have a slide direction concept; you'd hand-roll the transform. vaul is dialog-equivalent for drawers and shipped specifically for this use case.

**Usage:** `<Drawer.Root open onOpenChange direction="right"><Drawer.Portal><Drawer.Overlay/><Drawer.Content>…</Drawer.Content></Drawer.Portal></Drawer.Root>`. Always include `<Drawer.Title className="sr-only">` for accessibility.
entries.description: Library reference › `vaul`

entries.text:
Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback
:::caution\[Surface superseded — the web mobile app was replaced by a native rebuild]
This memo critiques the old Tauri-WebView mobile app (`apps/operator-mobile`,
loaded at `localhost:1420`) and cites paths like
`apps/operator-mobile/src/screens/Operator.tsx` and
`apps/operator/lib/mobile-operator-actions.ts`. **Neither exists anymore** —
the `apps/operator-mobile` app and the `mobile-operator-actions.ts` helper are
gone. Mobile was revived as a **native** app (`papercup-rust-mobile`, Android +
iOS, a separate repo; see the plan `mobile-apps-revival-redesign-2026-06-05`)
with a redesigned IA: five **Inbox-first** tabs — **Inbox / Operator / Plans /
Fleet / Settings** — replacing the old Operator/Harness/Running/Inbox/Settings
set. The standalone suggestion-card feed is retired; cards now render inline as
actionable chat bubbles in the Operator thread, and the old "Running" tab was
folded into "Fleet". Treat the feature/design observations below as historical
design intent against a surface that no longer ships in this form.
:::

Captured live by loading the mobile app at `localhost:1420`, pairing
against `localhost:3070`, and walking all five tabs (Operator,
Harness, Running, Inbox, Settings). Screenshots in `/tmp/mob-*.png`.

This doc has **two sections**, written for two different agents.
Each section is self-contained — hand them off independently.

***
entries.description: Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback

entries.text:
Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 1.1 Inform/navigate cards collapse "read it" and "skip it" into one button
**Correction from round 1: I previously claimed this was a real-money
safety bug — that was wrong.** Reading
`apps/operator-mobile/src/screens/Operator.tsx:82-110`:

* **Directive** cards already render two buttons: *Dispatch* + *Dismiss*.
* **Inform / navigate** cards render a single *Acknowledge* button,
  which calls `dismissCard()` (not `dispatchCard()`).
* The `dispatchCard()` helper at
  `apps/operator/lib/mobile-operator-actions.ts:89` short-circuits to
  `"advisory; nothing to dispatch"` for non-directive cards anyway.

So "Acknowledge on an inform card" is just dismiss with a softer
label. No money is at risk.

**The actual (smaller) issue** is that "Acknowledge" overloads two
distinct intents on inform/navigate cards:

* *"I read it, hide it from me"* → equivalent to dismiss.
* *"I followed the navigate link"* → no specific affordance.

On desktop, navigate cards have an "Open ↗" action that follows the
link AND dismisses. Mobile has only Acknowledge, which dismisses
without a dedicated way to follow.

**Fix:**

* For `navigate` cards, render *Open ↗* (which navigates + dismisses)
  alongside *Dismiss*.
* For `inform` cards, *Acknowledge* is fine as-is; consider renaming
  to *Got it* — clearer that it's "dismiss after reading."
* Directive cards (Dispatch + Dismiss) are already correct; no
  change needed.

This is medium-priority — clarity, not safety.
entries.description: Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 1.1 Inform/navigate cards collapse "read it" and "skip it" into one button

entries.text:
Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 1.10 Auto-fire countdown not visible
Desktop shows *"Auto-fire pending — 23s"* with cancel affordance.
Mobile shows the same auto-dispatch card as static `pending` with the
same Acknowledge button. A user can't even tell which cards will
auto-fire vs. which need their tap.

**Fix:** for `auto_dispatch && pending` cards, show a countdown chip
(`Auto-firing in 17s`) and replace the action button with *Cancel
auto-fire*.
entries.description: Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 1.10 Auto-fire countdown not visible

entries.text:
Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 1.11 No per-card recipient on mobile
Desktop cards show *"→ sheets"* (target harness). Mobile cards only
show recipient for `navigate` cards. Directive cards don't say which
harness will receive the directive.

**Fix:** show target harness as a chip on every directive card —
*"will send to `sheets`"* — so the user sees the consequence before
tapping.
entries.description: Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 1.11 No per-card recipient on mobile

entries.text:
Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 1.12 Voice STT/TTS shows "Web Speech (local)" with no controls
Settings shows *"STT/TTS: Web Speech (local)"* but you can't change
it from there. The desktop has a full /settings/voice page with
engine selection, voice ID, model, etc. Mobile has just a *Voice
settings ›* link that drops the user out — and the inline label is
read-only.

**Fix:** make the *Web Speech (local)* string a tappable chooser, or
remove the inline preview and let the link page do the work
(consistent with how *Standing approvals* is shipped).
entries.description: Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 1.12 Voice STT/TTS shows "Web Speech (local)" with no controls

entries.text:
Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 1.13 Misleading Settings labels
Settings shows *"Desktop: localhost:1420"* — but `1420` is the
*mobile* dev port. The actual desktop pair target is `localhost:3070`.
Looks like the label is reading the wrong field.

**Fix:** label this as *"Paired with: localhost:3070"* (the desktop
host the JWT was minted for, not the mobile origin).
entries.description: Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 1.13 Misleading Settings labels

entries.text:
Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 1.14 No first-run / orientation
After pairing, the user is dropped into `/operator` with 5 cards and
no orientation. Same complaint as desktop §1.10 in the prior memo —
new users have no idea what tiers, dispatches, or harnesses are.

**Fix:** 3-step coachmark on first visit:

1. *"These are suggestion cards from your operator. Tap a card to
   see detail; use Dispatch / Open / Dismiss."*
2. *"Tap the voice button to talk. Say 'pause' or 'scan' to
   control the operator hands-free."*
3. *"Bottom tabs let you check harness status, what's running, and
   recent notifications."*

***
entries.description: Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 1.14 No first-run / orientation

entries.text:
Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 1.2 No tier / risk indicator
Cards on desktop carry `tier: low | medium | high`, color-coded.
Mobile shows just `#N · inform` and `pending` — no tier. A user has
no way to tell "this is high-risk, careful" from "low-risk, sure" on
their phone.

**Fix:** show tier as a colored dot or chip next to `#N`:
`● #1 · inform` (red dot for high, amber for medium, green for low).
Pair with §1.1 — mobile should ASK before dispatching anything tier
≥ medium.
entries.description: Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 1.2 No tier / risk indicator

entries.text:
Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 1.3 No Pause toggle
The single most natural mobile gesture for the operator is *"pause
from your pocket"* — and there's no UI for it. Settings has *Standing
approvals* and *Unpair*, but no Pause.

**Fix:** add a *Pause / Resume* toggle as a sticky bar at the top of
the Operator tab (or as a header-right button). Tapping pauses the
operator workspace-wide; same FS flag the desktop reads.
entries.description: Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 1.3 No Pause toggle

entries.text:
Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 1.4 Voice button is silent
Bottom-right floating `◉` voice button has no state — same glyph for
idle, listening, connecting, error. On desktop, voice cycles through
mute / connecting / listening / speaking states. Mobile has none of
that visual feedback.

**Fix:** replace `◉` with a state-aware glyph and color:

* Idle: outline `🎙` gray
* Listening: filled `🎙` red, gentle pulse
* Connecting: filled `🎙` amber, spinner
* Speaking: filled speaker `🔊` cyan
* Error: red exclamation, tap to see error toast
entries.description: Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 1.4 Voice button is silent

entries.text:
Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 1.5 Running tab has no controls
`/running` shows *"OPERATOR · SCANNING · 8M · $0.0000"* — clearly a
status dump. No way to **cancel** a running operator scan. No way to
**inspect** what it's actually scanning. The 8-minute scan time + 0
cost is suspicious — looks like the scan is wedged.

**Fix:**

* Add a *Cancel scan* button on running operator entries.
* Make the row tappable → drawer with current substep / progress.
* Show recent completed scans (tap → see resulting cards).
entries.description: Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 1.5 Running tab has no controls

entries.text:
Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 1.6 Inbox doesn't link back to source
Inbox shows entries like *"Dispatched: 8 harnesses have
accept-with-notes plan reviews"* — but tapping doesn't take you to
the originating card. The notification is a dead-end.

**Fix:** every notification that came from a card stores the
`cardId`; tapping should jump to `/operator?card=<id>` (highlighted +
scrolled into view). For dispatched-card notifications, jump to the
running harness if available.
entries.description: Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 1.6 Inbox doesn't link back to source

entries.text:
Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 1.7 Bottom nav has no unread badge
When new operator cards arrive, the *Operator* tab doesn't show a
badge. Same for new notifications on *Inbox*. Push notifications are
the only signal a user gets about new state — and once the
notification is gone, you can't tell at-a-glance there's stuff to
review.

**Fix:** badge on Operator tab when `pending > 0` (count or dot).
Badge on Inbox tab when `unread > 0`. Match the OS-native badge
pattern — small red circle, tab icon.
entries.description: Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 1.7 Bottom nav has no unread badge

entries.text:
Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 1.8 No Scan history tab on mobile
Desktop just shipped a Scan history tab (this session) so users can
review what previous scans suggested. Mobile has no equivalent. A
power user wants to be able to ask their phone *"what did the
operator suggest 2 hours ago?"* and currently can't.

**Fix:** new tab or a `History →` link from `/operator` header → list
of past scans (summary + cards emitted), same shape as desktop.
entries.description: Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 1.8 No Scan history tab on mobile

entries.text:
Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 1.9 No Delegates surface
Desktop has a Delegates section showing background tasks the operator
handed off. Mobile doesn't expose this at all. If the user has 3
in-flight delegates from voice asks, they can't see them on the phone.

**Fix:** add Delegates tab, or fold into Running tab as a sub-row.
Same data, smaller cards.
entries.description: Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 1.9 No Delegates surface

entries.text:
Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 2.1 Visual hierarchy is inverted on cards
On every operator card:

* The cyan `#1 · INFORM` eyebrow shouts (12px uppercase, cyan-400 on
  near-black — high contrast).
* The `pending` pill whispers (10px uppercase, neutral-500 on
  neutral-900 — barely visible).
* The body text speaks at normal volume (14px neutral-300).
* The single `Acknowledge` button is the visually heaviest element
  (full-width, bordered, takes up \~30% of card real estate).

**Result:** the eye lands on `#1 · INFORM` first (which is a
debug-style index + type label), then jumps to the button (which is
the *commit* action), barely registering the body in the middle.
Reading order is upside down.

**Fix:**

* Demote the `#N · type` label to small gray (or drop entirely; no
  user needs the ordinal).
* Promote the lifecycle state (`pending` / `in flight` / etc.) to be
  the most prominent meta — color-coded chip on the right of the card
  head.
* Make the body the visual anchor — slightly larger (15-16px) and
  higher-contrast (neutral-100 or white).
* De-emphasize Acknowledge until the user has read the body — neutral
  outline button, not a heavy filled one.
entries.description: Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 2.1 Visual hierarchy is inverted on cards

entries.text:
Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 2.10 No haptics, no transitions, no native feel
Pure web app feel — taps are flat, navigation between tabs has no
slide animation, no haptic feedback on Acknowledge. On a Tauri /
WebView mobile app there's no excuse not to use native primitives.

**Fix:**

* Tab transitions: slide-and-fade (use Motion / Framer Motion).
* Card actions: light haptic on tap (Tauri has a haptics API; web
  has `navigator.vibrate` as fallback).
* Acknowledge → confirmation animation (checkmark + slide-out).
entries.description: Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 2.10 No haptics, no transitions, no native feel

entries.text:
Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 2.11 Empty states are blunt
Harness tab and Running tab show *"No harnesses currently running."*
in the middle of the screen. No illustration, no guidance, no
"learn more" link.

**Fix:** make empty states:

* Light SVG illustration (don't have to be fancy — simple line art).
* Heading: *"Nothing running yet"*.
* One-line subtitle: *"When the operator dispatches a harness, it'll
  appear here."*
* Optional CTA: *"Run a scan now"* (button) or *"See past scans"*
  (link to /history).
entries.description: Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 2.11 Empty states are blunt

entries.text:
Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 2.12 Dark theme is fine but flat
Pure dark with neutral-900 cards on neutral-950 background. Borders
are `border-neutral-800` — visible but flat. No depth.

**Fix:** very subtle elevation gradient on cards (1-2% lighter at
top edge → original at bottom). Or a faint inner glow on the
*currently-tappable* card. Adds dimension without changing the
palette.

***
entries.description: Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 2.12 Dark theme is fine but flat

entries.text:
Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 2.2 Cards have no title — body is the title
The body text is doing two jobs: it's the lede AND the explanation.
Compare:

```
#1 · INFORM   pending
Non-accept plan verdict surfaces as inform per operator prompt rules.
[Acknowledge]
```

vs. an extracted title:

```
●low   pending  →  
Plan verdict surfaced as inform
Non-accept verdict — see inform rules in operator prompt.
[Acknowledge]
```

The desktop card has `card.title` separate from `card.body`. Mobile
appears to be using only the body — losing the structural advantage.

**Fix:** render `card.title` as the heading (16-18px, semibold);
`card.body` as the explanation below in normal weight.
entries.description: Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 2.2 Cards have no title — body is the title

entries.text:
Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 2.3 Color is doing nothing
Every card is the same color. Tier (the single most consequential
attribute) has no visual representation. The cyan accent on `#1` and
on links is the only color signal — used for two different things.

**Fix:** make tier color-led:

* Low: subtle green left rail (4px) + green dot in head
* Medium: amber left rail + amber dot
* High: red left rail + red dot

This is the strongest mobile-native signal you can deliver. A user
flicking through their phone should see red/amber/green and know
*before reading* whether they need to focus.
entries.description: Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 2.3 Color is doing nothing

entries.text:
Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 2.4 Typography mixes 3 sizes per card
`10px` (pending) / `12px` (eyebrow) / `14px` (body) — three different
sizes inside the same card head + body, plus a 4th for the button
(`14px`). Eye has to context-switch four times per card.

**Fix:** collapse to two sizes per card — `12px` (meta + state +
buttons) and `15px` (title + body). Use weight (semibold vs. normal)
and color (white vs. neutral-400) for hierarchy instead of size.
entries.description: Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 2.4 Typography mixes 3 sizes per card

entries.text:
Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 2.5 Bottom nav glyphs are inscrutable
Current bottom nav:

| Glyph | Label    |
| ----- | -------- |
| `●`   | Operator |
| `⌘`   | Harness  |
| `▶`   | Running  |
| `◆`   | Inbox    |
| `⚙`   | Settings |

`⌘` is the **command key** in user mental models (Mac users will
expect it to invoke a command palette, not navigate). `●` for
"Operator" reads as "currently active" rather than as an icon for the
operator. `◆` is just a diamond.

**Fix:** use proper Lucide / Phosphor / Material icons:

* Operator: brain / scan-search / radar
* Harness: layers / kanban
* Running: play-circle / activity
* Inbox: bell / inbox
* Settings: settings (gear)

Geometric symbols feel placeholder; real icons feel finished.
entries.description: Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 2.5 Bottom nav glyphs are inscrutable

entries.text:
Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 2.6 Voice button is a debug widget
The floating voice button is a small `◉` circle bottom-right. No
label. No state. No animation. No ring. No safe-area inset (could be
under iOS home indicator).

**Fix:**

* Replace `◉` with a recognizable mic icon.
* Add a status ring (or pulsing border) when listening.
* Inset from bottom by `env(safe-area-inset-bottom) + 80px` so it's
  above the bottom nav on notch phones.
* Optional: a "tap to talk / hold to push-to-talk" affordance —
  desktop voice runs always-on; on mobile, push-to-talk often makes
  more sense (battery + accidental wake).
entries.description: Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 2.6 Voice button is a debug widget

entries.text:
Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 2.7 The PAIRING / CONNECTION / VOICE / ABOUT sections are unstyled lists
Settings is a flat plain text list with vertical labels and values.
No visual grouping beyond uppercase section headers. Compare to iOS
Settings (grouped table cells with rounded corners, dividers between
items, chevron-right on tappable rows).

**Fix:** standard mobile grouped-list pattern:

* Card-shaped section wrapper (rounded, border)
* Each row: label left, value or `›` right
* Dividers between rows
* Tappable rows have chevron + tinted background on press
entries.description: Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 2.7 The PAIRING / CONNECTION / VOICE / ABOUT sections are unstyled lists

entries.text:
Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 2.8 Card list could use breathing room
Cards are stacked tight. On desktop, the operator panel has lots of
chrome around cards (sidebars, etc.); on mobile, cards are most of the
screen — they need more space between them, not less.

**Fix:** `gap-3` → `gap-4`. Inner card padding `p-4` → `p-5`.
Header has the count (`5 pending`) — this could be a sticky header
on scroll, with cards beneath using full vertical space.
entries.description: Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 2.8 Card list could use breathing room

entries.text:
Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 2.9 Running tab feels like a `console.log`
```
Now running
OPERATOR
SCANNING
8M
Scan the workspace and surface up to 5 next-action suggestions.
$0.0000
HARNESSES (0)
No harnesses currently running.
```

This is debug output presented as UI. Layout makes it look like a
shell prompt.

**Fix:** make this a proper status card:

```
┌─ Operator ─────────────── ⏹ Cancel ┐
│  Scanning workspace · 8m elapsed   │
│  Pending: 0 spend                  │
│  ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 8/?      │
└────────────────────────────────────┘

  Running harnesses
  None running
```

Each running thing is a card with an icon, status, elapsed time,
metrics, and a cancel control.
entries.description: Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › 2.9 Running tab feels like a `console.log`

entries.text:
Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › Cross-cutting: shared work between feature + design
A few fixes need both agents:

* **Tier color-coding (§1.2 + §2.3):** feature agent surfaces tier
  in the data; design agent renders it as red/amber/green left rail
  and chip.
* **Action confirm flow (§1.1 + §2.10):** feature agent wires up the
  three actions (Dispatch / Open / Dismiss); design agent lays out
  the slide-up confirmation panel.
* **Voice state (§1.4 + §2.6):** feature agent emits the state
  events from the voice client; design agent renders them.

***
entries.description: Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › Cross-cutting: shared work between feature + design

entries.text:
Mobile operator app — feature + design feedback › How I gathered this
* Loaded `http://localhost:1420/operator` in Edge.
* Quick-paired against `localhost:3070`.
* Walked all 5 tabs (Operator, Harness, Running, Inbox, Settings).
* Captured screenshots at `/tmp/mob-{operator,harness,running,
  notifications,settings}.png`.

Local-inference hardware support matrix (provisioner wizard) › Extending the matrix
* **New VRAM threshold or a new tier** → edit `HardwareTier` (recommend-types.ts) +
  `tierOf()` (recommend.ts), then add/update the corresponding row above.
* **New certified combo for an existing tier** → add a `CatalogEntry` to `CERTIFIED_CATALOG`
  (catalog.ts) with `status: 'provisional'` until it clears certification (P-006/P-007), then
  flip to `'certified'`. `recommendCombo()` already picks the biggest model that fits a tier's
  VRAM budget, so a new bigger-but-still-fitting entry is picked up automatically — no wizard
  code changes needed.
* **New backend kind** (beyond `llama-server` / `vllm`) → this is the case D-009 #3 flagged as
  proving out: registration into `harness_shared.local_backends` is backend-agnostic (D-002's
  gateway abstraction), so a third `LocalBackendKind` should need zero gateway-side changes,
  only a new catalog entry + whatever backend-specific provisioning logic
  (see `provisioner/backend-config.ts`).
* **Give AMD its own tier** (today it detects and falls straight through to `cpu-only`/cloud —
  see the AMD row above) → add an `'amd-*'` member to `HardwareTier` (recommend-types.ts), a
  branch in `tierOf()` keyed on `gpu.vendor === 'amd'` (recommend.ts), and at least one
  `CERTIFIED_CATALOG` entry targeting it (catalog.ts) — `hardware-detect.ts`'s `detectAmd()`
  already supplies vendor + best-effort VRAM, so no probe-side work is needed, only the
  tier/catalog wiring.

entries.text:
Local-inference hardware support matrix (provisioner wizard) › What this is
Decision **D-009** (plan `local-concurrent-inference-2026-07-02`) fixed the packaging story
for local model inference and, as part of that, wrote down a **support matrix**: for a given
piece of detected hardware, which backend + model combo the desktop setup wizard should
recommend. This doc is that matrix, published where a human (or a future agent extending the
catalog) can find it — **the code, not this doc, is the source of truth**; this page exists so
the *policy* behind the code is legible in one place instead of buried in a plan decision body.

If you are about to add a new hardware tier, a new catalog entry, or change a VRAM threshold —
edit the code below, then update this doc's table. If they ever disagree, the code wins; file a
doc-drift fix.
entries.description: Local-inference hardware support matrix (provisioner wizard) › What this is

entries.text:
Local-inference hardware support matrix (provisioner wizard) › Where this lives in code (the actual source of truth)
The wizard's hardware-detection → recommendation step is wired straight through this chain —
there is **no separate hardcoded copy of the matrix in the UI**:

1. **`provisioner/hardware-detect.ts`** — read-only hardware probe (GPU vendor/VRAM via
   `nvidia-smi` / `rocm-smi` (AMD) / Metal detection / CPU fallback) → a `DetectedHardware`
   value. NVIDIA detection also captures `computeCap` (CUDA compute capability, e.g. `"8.6"`)
   when `nvidia-smi` reports it — this doesn't feed the tier/recommendation matrix at all; it
   only feeds `provisioner/llama-binary.ts`'s from-source build path (`computeCapToArch`,
   WI-1617) when the headless CLI's `--provision-binary` flag is used. AMD is genuinely
   *detected* (not treated as a probe failure) even though no catalog entry targets it yet —
   see the AMD row above.
2. **`provisioner/recommend-types.ts`** — the `HardwareTier` union
   (`nvidia-24gb-plus | nvidia-mid | nvidia-low | apple-silicon | cpu-only`) that encodes the
   matrix's row boundaries.
3. **`provisioner/recommend.ts`** — `tierOf()` buckets `DetectedHardware` into a `HardwareTier`
   (this is where the `>=24GB` / `>=12GB` thresholds actually live); `recommendCombo()` matches
   the tier against the catalog and returns a `Recommendation` (entry + human-readable reason),
   or an honest "nothing fits, route to cloud" answer when the tier is `cpu-only` or no catalog
   entry targets it yet. Its `RecommendOptions.containerRuntimeAvailable` (D-009 #3) lets a
   caller pass `false` to skip every `backend: 'vllm'` candidate and fall through to the
   next-best (typically `llama-server`) entry for the same tier — the "downgrade when no
   working Docker/Podman runtime" behavior; the default (`undefined`, used by every pre-P-013
   call site) applies no filter.
4. **`provisioner/catalog.ts`** — `CERTIFIED_CATALOG`: the actual list of hardware-tier →

entries.text:
Operations
> **Webapp retired (2026-05-14).** Any `localhost:3055` or `localhost:3070` URL on this page is only reachable while the **Tauri dev shell** is running. Start it with `cd papercusp-desktop && npm run dev`.
entries.description: Operations

entries.text:
Operations › After every plugin manifest or handler edit
```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:3055/api/plugins/host/refresh
```

The projection registry is module-level state. HMR is unreliable for it. If you don't refresh after editing a plugin, you're testing stale code and you won't know.

The endpoint returns the host status:

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "status": {
    "loaded": 15,
    "errors": 2,
    "plugins": [...],
    "loadErrors": [...]
  }
}
```

`errors=2` is the steady-state baseline (two unrelated pre-existing manifest issues). If you push a change and `errors` goes up, your edit broke discovery — read the `loadErrors[]` list.
entries.description: Operations › After every plugin manifest or handler edit

entries.text:
Operations › `/api/plugins/host/refresh` shows error count > 2
Something in your manifest broke discovery. The response body has `loadErrors[]` — read it.

Common causes: `name` collision with an existing tool from a different plugin; `expose.mcp.name` missing the namespace separator (must contain `.` or `:`); orphan handler (manifest declares `tools[].name = 'foo'` but `index.ts` has no `tools.foo` export).
entries.description: Operations › `/api/plugins/host/refresh` shows error count > 2

entries.text:
Operations › Discovery sources
`loadPlugins` searches in this order:

1. `<projectDir>/plugins/<name>/` — for in-repo bundled plugins. The operator wires this via `findBundledPluginsParent()` in `packages/operator-core/lib/plugin-host-runtime.ts`. In dev, `projectDir` isn't an arbitrary repo root: `findBundledPluginsParent()` walks up looking for `libs/papercusp/plugins` and returns `libs/papercusp` itself, so source #1 is concretely `libs/papercusp/plugins/<name>/`. In installed builds where that path doesn't exist it returns `null` and this source is skipped.
2. `~/.papercusp/harnesses/<slug>/plugins/<name>/` — per-harness plugins.
3. `~/.papercusp/global-plugins/<name>/` — globally installed plugins.

Dedupe by `plugin.name` with priority `project > harness > global`. So if you have both `libs/papercusp/plugins/repomix/` and `~/.papercusp/global-plugins/repomix/`, the in-repo one wins.

This is why you don't need to symlink plugins into `~/.papercusp/global-plugins/` during development. Just put them in `libs/papercusp/plugins/` and they'll be discovered.
entries.description: Operations › Discovery sources

entries.text:
Operations › Hot-reload watcher
`watchPluginsForReload` (in `plugin-host-runtime.ts`) sets up a debounced fs.watch over the global-plugins directory. The match regex is `/papercusp\.json$|\/index\.(?:m?js|ts)$|\/dist\/index\.js$/`, so it triggers on changes to `papercusp.json`, `index.js`, `index.mjs`, `index.ts`, or `dist/index.js`. On a hit, it calls `_resetPluginHostForTests()` which clears the host cache; next request to the host re-runs discovery.

**Gotcha:** a compiled `index.cjs` entry is **not** matched (the regex covers `index.js`/`.mjs`/`.ts` and `dist/index.js`, but not `.cjs`). Editing a `.cjs` entry won't trigger auto-reload — POST `/api/plugins/host/refresh` manually.

It's gated behind `PAPERCUSP_DEV_PLUGIN_WATCH=1`. Off by default because filesystem-watch overhead is unwanted on shared hosts. Turn it on for plugin development if you don't want to keep curling `/api/plugins/host/refresh`.
entries.description: Operations › Hot-reload watcher

entries.text:
Operations › Migrations on the system PG
The embedded-postgres-server has a migration runner that walks `libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/*.sql` on boot and applies missing files via `harness_shared.schema_migrations`. The native system PG (`localhost:5432`) **used to have no equivalent boot hook** — every new SQL file required a manual `psql -f` plus a manual `schema_migrations` INSERT, and a missed migration could silently go dark. That gap is closed: `applyPendingMigrationsAtBoot()` (`packages/operator-core/lib/db-boot-migrate.ts`) now runs the **same idempotent runner** against the operator's admin DB on host boot. It's wired into `apps/operator/bin/host-bootstrap.ts` and **awaited before the boot-gate flips**, so a new SQL file is auto-applied on the next operator restart on the native box.

Two caveats:

* **It runs only on the primary host.** The boot apply sits inside the `PAPERCUSP_BACKGROUND_WORKERS`-gated block. A secondary host (`PAPERCUSP_BACKGROUND_WORKERS=0`) **skips** boot migrations entirely — so if you're on a secondary host, a brand-new migration may still need manual application.
* **It's log-and-continue, not fail-loud.** A migration that fails to apply is logged + coord-broadcast and left pending (retried next boot) rather than halting the shared dev-api. So a broken migration won't wedge boot — but it also won't have applied.

Manual application is the fallback when auto-apply hasn't happened (you don't want to restart, or you're on a secondary host):

```bash
PGPASSWORD=harness_admin_pwd psql -h localhost -p 5432 -U harness_admin -d papercusp \
  -f libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/048-my-table.sql

PGPASSWORD=harness_admin_pwd psql -h localhost -p 5432 -U harness_admin -d papercusp \
  -tAc "SELECT to_regclass('harness_shared.my_table')"
```

If your tool depends on a table that doesn't exist, the queries throw, the dispatcher catches and continues, the tool returns 200 with `output` text — and your quota tracking + telemetry are silently dead until the
entries.description: Operations › Migrations on the system PG

entries.text:
Operations › Per-tool migration checklist
When you're moving an existing route to the endpoint system, run through this list. Each step is mandatory; skip any and you ship a broken tool:

1. Grep for UI callers of the legacy route. Decide replace-with-redirect or full-delete.
2. If new PG schema, write the SQL file in `libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/` and apply it manually.
3. Write the typed function with no transport awareness.
4. Write the manifest entry. JSON Schema directly. No `zodToJsonSchema`.
5. `curl` the HTTP transport. Verify status code + body shape.
6. `curl` the MCP transport. Verify the same.
7. `psql` the telemetry row. Verify `status='ok'` and `app.workspace_id` was set.
8. Quota smoke test: fire perChunk+1 → second is 429.
9. Role gate smoke test: wrong role → 403.
10. `curl /api/plugins/host/refresh`. Confirm error count unchanged.
11. Delete the legacy route in the same commit (only if step 1 said zero UI callers).
12. Submodule commit first if you touched `libs/papercusp/`, then bump the parent's submodule pointer in a second commit.
entries.description: Operations › Per-tool migration checklist

entries.text:
Operations › Per-turn commit discipline
When you're working across the operator app and the `libs/papercusp/` submodule:

* Commit the submodule first.
* Bump the parent's submodule pointer in a second commit.

Otherwise the parent commit references a submodule SHA that isn't pushed and the next agent sees a broken checkout. This is observed-from-experience guidance; multiple agents have shipped half-broken trees by inverting the order.
entries.description: Operations › Per-turn commit discipline

entries.text:
Operations › Read the verification audit log
```bash
TOKEN=$(cat ~/.papercusp/superuser-token)
curl "http://localhost:3070/api/admin/spawn-signing/failures?limit=20" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
```

Query params: `limit` (max 1000, default 100), `since` (ISO timestamp), `reason` (filter). Returns `{ rows, summary: { byReason, window } }`.

A non-zero rate of `invalid_signature` outside explicit test runs is a real signal. Correlate `claimed_spawn` with orchestrator spawn IDs to identify the culprit.
entries.description: Operations › Read the verification audit log

entries.text:
Operations › Rotate the signing key
```bash
TOKEN=$(cat ~/.papercusp/superuser-token)
curl -X POST http://localhost:3070/api/admin/spawn-signing/rotate \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
```

Rotates the PG row **and** bumps the operator's in-process cache. Every in-flight signed URL fails its next call with `invalid_signature`. Wrapper script: `bun run rotate:spawn-key`.

Since WI-3190/WI-3194, `rotateSpawnSigningKey()` returns a **blast-radius report** (and logs it loudly) so a rotate is an *accounted-for* revocation, not a silent one — the admin route surfaces it to whoever triggered the rotate. The report distinguishes an operational `rotation_strand` (a previously-authenticated spawn whose key was rotated out from under it — must be re-spawned) from an `unverified` first-seen/malformed/escalation attempt, because a rotation and a forged-URL attack both surface as `invalid_signature` on the next verify. To tell them apart the process remembers the spawns it has successfully verified (`verifiedSpawns`, capped at 4000), so a later signature failure for one of them is definitively a strand, not an attack. The route can also **opt into active remediation** (`RotateSpawnSigningKeyOptions`, WI-3194): stop/relaunch eligible nursery spawns whose verified URL was just invalidated, capped at `ROTATION_REMEDIATION_CAP` (25). Direct unit callers keep the historical rotate-only behavior; the orchestrator re-spawns anything the remediation didn't cover.
entries.description: Operations › Rotate the signing key

entries.text:
Operations › Search-provider env vars don't reach spawned agents
The orchestrator's `invoke()` path (`libs/papercusp/packages/orchestrator/src/invoke.ts`) decrypts search-provider keys from PG via `buildSearchProviderSpawnEnv` (`spawn-env-from-pg.ts`) and attaches them to `InvokeContext.extraSpawnEnv`. They land in every `invoke()` call's spawn env.

The operator harness-launch path does this independently: `packages/operator-core/lib/harness-launch.ts` calls `buildSpawnEnv` from `packages/operator-core/lib/search-provider-credentials.ts`. Both paths are wired; if a worker doesn't see `TAVILY_API_KEY` etc., the keys aren't in PG (check `harness_shared.operator_search_provider_credentials`) or the encryption key is missing (`~/.papercusp/db-encryption-key`).
entries.description: Operations › Search-provider env vars don't reach spawned agents

entries.text:
Operations › Spawn-signing admin endpoints
The HMAC signing scheme (see [Spawn-URL signing](/internal/docs/endpoint-system/spawn-signing)) ships with two admin routes for incident response and observability. Both are gated `auth: { trust: ['trusted'] }` — the gate is the **trust tier**, not the bearer specifically. The documented loopback + superuser-bearer is the canonical way an operator obtains a `trusted` principal (a valid superuser bearer on a loopback request resolves to `kind: 'system'`, `trust: 'trusted'`), but any other `trusted` principal (e.g. a process-internal/system caller) also passes the gate.
entries.description: Operations › Spawn-signing admin endpoints

entries.text:
Operations › Tool returns 200 but `tool_invocations` is empty
Two likely causes:

1. **Workspace GUC not set.** The HOST\_EXTRAS.deps insert calls `SELECT set_config('app.workspace_id', $1, true)` — but if the request didn't include `?workspace=<id>`, `ctx.workspaceId` is `undefined`, and the insert silently fails. Make sure the test request has the workspace param.
2. **Migration not applied.** The table doesn't exist. See above.
entries.description: Operations › Tool returns 200 but `tool_invocations` is empty

entries.text:
Operations › Tool returns 401 `unauthorized` for a tool you expected to work without bearer
You wrote a built-in (`defineTool(...)`) when you needed a plugin. Built-ins require `ctx.principal`; agents over MCP only have URL spawn context, no bearer. Move the tool to `libs/papercusp/plugins/<name>/`.
entries.description: Operations › Tool returns 401 `unauthorized` for a tool you expected to work without bearer

entries.text:
Operations › Tool returns 404 `unknown_tool` after a manifest edit
You forgot to refresh. `curl -X POST /api/plugins/host/refresh`.

Or HMR wiped the registry. Same fix.
entries.description: Operations › Tool returns 404 `unknown_tool` after a manifest edit

entries.text:
Operations › Tool returns 500 `handler_error`
The function threw an unhandled error. Check the `tool_invocations.error_message` for that call. If the message is `spawn <bin> ENOENT`, the binary isn't installed on the machine running the operator (e.g. `code2prompt` not present in dev). Either install it or skip that tool.
entries.description: Operations › Tool returns 500 `handler_error`

entries.text:
Operations › Tool works on dev but agents in spawned subprocesses don't see it
Check the orchestrator's `.mcp.json` URL. In dev (`NODE_ENV=development`) it should point at `http://localhost:3055/api/sse`; in prod, `http://localhost:3070/api/sse`. Override with `PAPERCUSP_OPERATOR_URL` if neither default applies.
entries.description: Operations › Tool works on dev but agents in spawned subprocesses don't see it

entries.text:
Operations › Tool works on MCP but returns "ctx.X is unset" on HTTP
The HTTP catch-all needs the same `ctx.spawn` / `ctx.secret` / `ctx.projectDir` resolvers as MCP. Check that the plugins catch-all (`packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/plugins/catchall.ts`) builds its `HttpToolHostExtras` with `spawn` (`pluginSpawnImpl`), `secret` (`secretImpl`/`makeSecretResolver`), and `resolveHarnessPaths`. If it doesn't, that's a regression of audit-2/3 fixes.
entries.description: Operations › Tool works on MCP but returns "ctx.X is unset" on HTTP

entries.text:
Operations › When to stop and ask
You should stop and ask before doing any of these:

* The component you want to wrap doesn't fit one of the four shipped plugin shapes (subprocess single-tool, HTTP+optional-secret, subprocess multi-tool, HTTP+required-secret-with-schema). Don't invent a fifth shape; the function-as-truth design doc lists which patterns are blessed.
* You want to extend the manifest contract with a new field. Each existing field corresponds to a dispatcher behavior; adding one is an architecture decision, not a cleanup.
* You hit one of the known open issues and need to work around it. The workaround usually masks a real bug — better to surface it and get the framework fix.
* The handler signature you'd want isn't `(input, ctx) => ToolResult`. The framework can't accommodate exotic shapes. If you want a callback-based contract, a multi-response stream, or anything else non-request/response, it doesn't belong here.
* You're tempted to delete a route a UI surface still fetches from. **Always grep for UI callers first.** The legacy Next app-router routes are gone — `apps/operator/app/api` is now an empty leftover directory with no `route.ts` files anywhere under `apps/operator`; everything is now a `defineTool` route under `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes`, served at `/api/plugins/<plugin>/<tool>`. The migration is complete, but the rule stands for any route you're about to remove: switch UI URLs in the same PR, and delete only when zero callers remain.
entries.description: Operations › When to stop and ask

entries.text:
Operations › Where the registry lives
Three module-level Maps in `libs/generic/tooldef/src/tool-projection.ts`:

* `REGISTRY` — keyed by `mcp:<name>` or `http:<path>`, value is the full `ProjectedTool`
* `BY_MCP_NAME` — `Map<string, ProjectedTool>` for `tools/call` lookups
* `BY_HTTP_PATH` — `Map<string, ProjectedTool>` for the catch-all routes

These are populated at startup as a side effect of:

1. Importing `@papercusp/agent-mcp` — every `defineTool(...)` auto-registers into the registry (PR 0c.D extension).
2. The first call to `getPluginHost()` — runs `loadPlugins({ projectDir, harnessSlugs, globalPluginsDir })`, then `registerPluginTools(loaded)` walks each plugin's `toolDefinitions[]` and calls `registerProjectedTool` per entry.

`registerPluginTools` is **idempotent** for same-plugin re-registration: it calls `unregisterProjectedToolsForPlugin(pluginName)` first, then re-registers. This means `/api/plugins/host/refresh` works correctly without producing collision errors. **Cross-plugin collisions still throw** — two different plugins claiming the same MCP name fails with `ToolRegistrationError`.
entries.description: Operations › Where the registry lives
Transports › Cards (interactive mid-run prompts)

entries.text:
Transports › Content-type hints via `.describe()`
Any text-based format works through `z.string()` — XML, CSV, YAML, NDJSON, Markdown, plain logs are all just text-shaped on the wire; the framework doesn't care what the bytes inside the string represent. The producer formats, the consumer parses.

When a tool wants to advertise *which* text format it emits, attach a `.describe()` annotation. It round-trips through `tools/list` as the JSON-Schema `description` field:

```ts
events: {
  diff_patch: z.string().describe('application/xml'),
  log_line:   z.string().describe('text/plain'),
  json_token: z.string().describe('application/json'),
  csv_row:    z.string().describe('text/csv'),
}
```

`tools/list` returns `events.diff_patch = { type: 'string', description: 'application/xml' }`. Clients pick a parser off the description. No wire-format change — the SSE event stays `event: diff_patch\ndata: <text>`.

The MCP transport dual-fires when `name === 'progress'`: every `ctx.emit('progress', ...)` (or `ctx.progress(...)` via the alias) produces *both* `notifications/papercusp/event` and the spec-standard `notifications/progress`. Built-in MCP UIs that watch the standard progress channel still get a signal; Papercusp-aware clients also receive the typed-event payload.
entries.description: Transports › Content-type hints via `.describe()`

entries.text:
Transports › Default exposure
If a manifest entry omits `expose.*`, the framework picks defaults:

* `expose.mcp.name` → `<short-pluginName>.<tool.name>` (drops `@scope/` prefix)
* `expose.http.path` → `/api/plugins/<short-pluginName>/<tool.name>`

So `@papercupai/repomix` plugin's `pack` tool gets `repomix.pack` over MCP and `/api/plugins/repomix/pack` over HTTP. You only declare `expose.*` to override these — for instance, to host the same tool at a non-default URL for backwards compat.

If you only set `expose.mcp` and not `expose.http`, the tool is MCP-only. If only `expose.http`, HTTP-only. The framework requires at least one.
entries.description: Transports › Default exposure

entries.text:
Transports › Desktop IPC: webview is in-boundary
The desktop Tauri app uses a fourth transport — endpoint IPC over a Unix domain socket (Linux/macOS) or named pipe (Windows). The Tauri webview opens a `Channel<T>` through Rust to the Node sidecar's IPC server (`libs/generic/ipc-endpoint-server/src/server.ts`); the round-trip skips localhost HTTP entirely. See [`packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-ipc/PROTOCOL.md`](https://github.com/Papercusp/papercup/blob/main/packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-ipc/PROTOCOL.md) for the wire format.

IPC calls **skip HMAC signature verification**. The trust boundary is different from the signed-URL HTTP path:

* The signed-URL model defends against a spawned subprocess rewriting its own `?role=...` query param. That subprocess is untrusted code (often a prompt-injected worker) running in a separate process.
* The webview is *not* a separate process in the same threat sense — it's spawned by the same Tauri parent that spawned the Node sidecar, runs the same trusted UI code, and lives in the same process tree. Rewriting "its own role" is a category error: the webview is the role.

So the IPC adapter synthesizes a fixed `principal: { role: 'operator', workspaceId: <active-workspace> }` and dispatches without verifying any signature. The same dispatcher (role gates, rolesQuota, telemetry, idle/wall-clock timeouts) still runs — only the cryptographic verification step is bypassed. All other defenses (loopback bind, file modes, `.mcp.json` permissions) continue to apply.

What this does **not** apply to:

* **MCP-spawned agents** (claude-code / omp subprocesses) — they go through `/api/mcp` (Streamable-HTTP; `/api/sse` is disabled) over loopback HTTP with signed URLs. They're untrusted same-UID code, exactly the threat the signing scheme targets.
* **The non-Tauri webapp** (`:3070` test surface, mobile RN clients) — these are not in-boundary; they use HTTP+SSE.

The transport column in `tool_invocations` records which path each call took

entries.text:
Transports › Freshness negotiation — `_meta.delta`
Alongside `format`/`structured`/`idempotencyKey`, an MCP `tools/call` may carry a fourth
`_meta` control: `delta` — a per-call value (`req.params._meta.delta`) that wins over a
connection-level `?delta=` on the MCP URL, mirroring the `?format=` fallback. It lets a
delta-capable tool answer `not_modified` (or a semantic `added`/`updated`/`removed` diff)
instead of replaying an unchanged snapshot, mirroring HTTP `ETag`/`If-None-Match`. The
**harness**, not the model, sets this and owns cursor storage + base-presence tracking —
absent ⇒ no negotiation (serve `full`, today's behavior, byte-identical to a delta-unaware
client). Full contract, cursor format, the base-presence rules, and the production
flag/gate: [Tool result freshness: the delta base-presence contract](/internal/docs/agent-insights/tool-delta-base-presence-contract).
entries.description: Transports › Freshness negotiation — `_meta.delta`

entries.text:
Transports › How HTTP requests reach a function
The catch-all routes are stupidly simple:

1. `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/plugins/catchall.ts` receives the request (the Hono host catch-all — migrated off the retired Next.js `app/api/plugins/[...path]/route.ts`). It's a **two-step** catch-all: it first tries the in-memory plugin-`apiRoutes` registry (`dispatchPluginApiRoute`) — a plugin can register bespoke handlers outside the projected-tool system; a registry hit returns that plugin's `Response` directly and skips everything below. A registry miss (`null`) falls through to projected-tool dispatch.
2. Looks up the tool by `lookupByHttpPath(req.pathname)` — if not found, 404 (a 404 on a path that matches a *registered* route under a different HTTP method is upgraded to 405-with-`Allow`, since the catch-all shadows the global method-not-allowed hook)
3. Validates the HTTP method against the manifest's `expose.http.methods` (default `['POST']`) — if not allowed, 405
4. Builds a `UnifiedToolContext` from URL spawn params + headers + the host's resolver impls (spawn, secret, projectDir resolver). If no `run` param/header was supplied, a fresh `runId` is generated server-side so `ctx.askUser` / `ctx.publishState` can install — they gate on `workspaceId + runId`. SSE callers had this since T2.2; the JSON path got parity in the pass-9 audit.
5. If `Authorization: Bearer ...` present, resolves it to a principal and tx (no-op for plugins; required for built-ins)
6. Hands off to `dispatchProjectedTool`
7. Maps the resulting `DispatchProjectedResult` to status code + JSON body

The streaming path is the same except step 7 — when `Accept: text/event-stream` is on the request, the response is a `ReadableStream` of SSE events. Each `ctx.progress(pct, msg)` call from the function emits one event. **Replay-on-reconnect** (Last-Event-ID + X-Papercusp-Run-Id) is handled in `handleHttpToolRequestStreaming` (http-projection.ts): when both headers are present and th
entries.description: Transports › How HTTP requests reach a function
Transports › How in-process callers reach a function

entries.text:
Transports › How MCP requests reach a function
Slightly more involved because we use `mcp-handler` as a transport library.

1. `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/transport/index.ts` (Hono `/api/:transport`, migrated off the retired Next.js `app/api/[transport]/route.ts`) wires a `createMcpHandler` server (Streamable-HTTP only, SSE disabled) with `tools/list`, `tools/call`, `resources/list`, `prompts/list` etc.
2. `tools/list` iterates `listMcpProjections(role)` — projection registry filtered by the calling role from URL params. Returns `{ name, description, inputSchema }` for every visible tool.
3. `tools/call` looks up by `lookupByMcpName(name)`, builds a `UnifiedToolContext` (similar to HTTP, but the spawn context comes from the connection URL), and calls `dispatchProjectedTool`.
4. The dispatcher returns; the MCP SDK serializes the result into the JSON-RPC envelope.

Streaming on MCP works via `notifications/progress` — when the client sent a `progressToken` in `_meta`, every `ctx.progress(pct, msg)` becomes one notification. mcp-handler routes those over the open Streamable-HTTP response stream.

**Write idempotency / result replay.** Passing `_meta.idempotencyKey` on a `tools/call` persists the result under that key (`storeMcpResult`) and replays the stored outcome (`lookupStoredMcpResult`) on any retry with the same key, instead of re-firing the tool. This is recovery for a write whose response died on a dropped connection — opt-in per call.

**Per-call keepalive + deadline.** A long/blocking `tools/call` holds the Streamable-HTTP event-stream open but silent, which would otherwise trip the \~60s tunnel/client idle timers. The transport emits a spec-legal SSE comment keepalive on a cadence well under that (default 20s, `PAPERCUSP_MCP_KEEPALIVE_MS`) to reset both timers, and enforces a server-side deadline (default 55s, `PAPERCUSP_MCP_DEADLINE_MS`, set under the 60s `maxDuration`) that returns a clean JSON-RPC error rather than a silent tunnel dr
entries.description: Transports › How MCP requests reach a function

entries.text:
Transports › Idle timeout
`idleTimeoutSec` augments the wall-clock `timeoutSec`: the dispatcher aborts the handler when the gap between `ctx.emit` calls exceeds the cap. Catches wedged child processes that have stopped producing output but haven't formally hung. `0` or `undefined` disables.
entries.description: Transports › Idle timeout

entries.text:
Transports › Projection table
| Wire                                           | When emit('delta', payload) is called                                                                                                                                        | When handler returns                              | When handler throws                           |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| **HTTP/SSE** (`z.string()` schema)             | `event: delta\ndata: <payload as raw text>` (one or more `data:` lines per SSE spec for multi-line)                                                                          | `event: done\ndata: <ToolResult.content as JSON>` | `event: error\ndata: { code, message }`       |
| **HTTP/SSE** (object schema)                   | `event: delta\ndata: <JSON.stringify(payload)>`                                                                                                                              | same                                              | same                                          |
| **MCP**                                        | `notifications/papercusp/event { progressToken, event: 'delta', data: payload }` (always JSON-encoded — JSON-RPC carries strings as quoted strings inside the params object) | `tools/call` response with ToolResult             | `tools/call` response with `isError: true`    |
| **In-process (`dispatchProjectedToolStream`)** | `{ kind: 'event', name: 'delta', data: payload }` (handler-supplied; no transcoding)                                                                                         | `{ kind: 'done', result }`                        | `{ kind: 'error', error: { code, message } }` |
entries.description: Transports › Projection table

entries.text:
Transports › Reserved event names
The framework reserves these wire-level names (`RESERVED_EVENT_NAMES` in `tool-projection.ts`); the `defineTool` `events` generic refuses them at compile time (`UserEvents<T>`) and `registerProjectedTool` re-checks at register time so JSON-manifest plugins also fail loudly:

* `done` — framework auto-emits when the handler returns (payload: ToolResult content array).
* `heartbeat` — `@papercusp/sse` emits every 10s for keepalive (the `sseResponse` default; the tool event-stream catch-alls don't override it).
* `result` — pre-2026-05-12 legacy terminal name; reserved for collision avoidance.
* `chunk` — framework auto-emits when the handler returns a result carrying an `outputRef` (large-output scratch ref).
* `card` — framework-emitted `ctx.askUser` card payloads; cards ride the state channel, so reserving the name keeps a plugin from intercepting another tool's askUser flow (see [Cards](#cards-interactive-mid-run-prompts) below).

`progress` and `error` are intentionally *not* reserved. `progress` is user-emittable via the `ctx.progress(pct, msg)` sugar, which itself routes through `ctx.emit('progress', ...)` — tools declare a schema for it so the wire kind is inferred. The framework auto-emits `event: error` on handler throw, but a handler may also `ctx.emit('error', { message })` mid-stream for non-fatal errors. The canonical case is `runAgentChat` yielding `{type:'error'}` events that don't terminate the stream.
entries.description: Transports › Reserved event names

entries.text:
Transports › Result formats — token-efficient serialization
A `ToolResponse.data` is no longer always `JSON.stringify`'d into `content[0].text`. The result serializer (`libs/generic/tooldef/src/serialize-result.ts`, the single source of truth for every transport) picks a **token-efficient format** server-side and labels it. Plan: `token-efficient-tool-result-formats-2026-06-06`.

**Format selection (delivered, not requested).** The model never names a format — efficiency is a deterministic server-side choice:

* **Server default** — the MCP transport (the agent-facing surface, where the LLM reads `content[0].text`) defaults to **compact**; every other transport (HTTP catch-all, in-process, IPC) defaults to lossless **JSON**. "Compact" resolves to the best format the data's shape can be safely rendered in: **TOON** for arrays, JSON for single objects. TOON is a JSON-lossless superset that renders uniform arrays as CSV-style rows — ≈ −20–35% tokens on real list payloads.
* **Eligibility** — when a tool declares an output schema (`defineTool({ result: z.array(...) })`), `@papercusp/result-encoding`'s `analyzeSchema` computes the capability set once at registration: a flat array of scalar-only objects → `{json,toon,csv,tsv,md}`; an array with nested/heterogeneous rows → `{json,toon}`; a non-array → `{json}`. No schema → the TOON runtime auto-encoder still gives a compact path.
* **Negotiation override** — set by the *client process*, not the model. HTTP: `?format=` or `Accept` (`application/toon`, `text/csv`, `application/json`). MCP: `_meta.format` on the `tools/call` params, or `?format=` on the connection URL. The requested format is intersected with the tool's capability set; an unsupported request falls back to the best representable format and labels the downgrade (`_meta.formatFallback`).

**The response contract.** Every compact payload self-identifies so the model never parses an unlabeled one:

* `content[0].text` carries the rendering prefixed with a `format:
