entries.text:
Transports › Slash exposure — the tool catalog as slash commands
`expose.slash` is a third exposure key next to `expose.mcp` / `expose.http` —
but unlike those it is **a catalog projection, not a dispatch transport**
(plan `slash-exposure-tool-catalog-2026-06-12`, D-001). It projects every
MCP-exposed tool onto the MCP **prompts** primitive, so agent clients that
render MCP prompts as slash commands (Claude Code, OMP) surface the whole
session-visible catalog as `/papercusp:tool:<name>` commands. There is no
fifth framing adapter and no new `tool_invocations.transport` value: the
rendered prompt *instructs the agent* to invoke the tool over the session's
existing MCP connection, so role gates, quota, audit, and result formatting
are all inherited from the normal `tools/call` path.

* **Default ON for every MCP-exposed tool** (owner-ratified D-003). Opt out
  per tool with `expose: { slash: false }`, or override naming/description/
  args with an object (`{ slash: { name, description, args } }`). The
  `papercusp-slash-exposure` flag (default enabled) is the global lever.
* **`prompts/list`** serves the static `definePrompt` catalog **plus** one
  dynamic `tool:<mcp-name>` prompt per visible tool — derived from the *same
  role/profile/manifest/allowlist walk `tools/list` uses* (the shared
  `resolveVisibleToolListings` in `_mcp-handler.ts`), so the slash surface
  mirrors the tool surface by construction. The `tool:` prompt-name
  namespace is reserved; `registerPrompt` rejects static prompts there.
* **Arguments**: top-level scalar input fields become MCP prompt arguments
  (advertised `required: false` on the wire so a bare `/command` is always
  invokable; required-ness is annotated in the description). The rendered
  instruction embeds the full input JSON Schema and directs the agent to
  **elicit missing required fields from the user before invoking**, and to
  confirm first for high-tier tools.
* **`prompts/get`** on a `tool:*` name re-checks session visibilit

Transports › Streaming progress

entries.text:
Transports › Strict-streamable
The HTTP catch-all returns `406 Not Acceptable` if a client sends `Accept: text/event-stream` against a tool that doesn't stream. The exact predicate differs by catch-all:

* The **built-in `/api/agent-tools/*` catch-all** admits SSE when the tool has **any** of: declared `events` (typed event channel), declared `state` (state-shaped, see [`ctx.publishState`](./state-tools.mdx)), or `expose.mcp.streaming === true` (explicit opt-in).
* The **`/api/plugins/*` catch-all** admits SSE only on declared `events` or `expose.mcp.streaming === true`. It does **not** check `tool.state` — plugin tools don't use the framework `state` channel, so a state-shaped plugin tool would still 406 there.

Either way, this prevents clients from opening an SSE connection for a one-shot result. The `state` trigger (built-in path) matters because state-shaped tools need a `runId`-bearing ctx (`ctx.publishState` only installs when `workspaceId + runId` are both present), and the SSE branch is the path that injects a fresh `runId` via `searchParams.set('run', ...)`. State tools that fell through this predicate before the pass-9 fix returned 406 in spite of having a perfectly valid wire shape.
entries.description: Transports › Strict-streamable

entries.text:
Transports › The signed URL params
When a request hits an HTTP plugin route or the MCP transport, the framework reads these query params (or equivalent `X-Papercusp-*` headers):

| Param          | Required for             | Purpose                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| -------------- | ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `workspace`    | Always                   | RLS scoping; `app.workspace_id` GUC                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| `harness`      | Path-resolving tools     | Looks up `projectDir` / `stateDir` via `loadHarnessRegistry()`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| `role`         | Plugin-tool role gate    | A canonical `AGENT_ROLES` id (`worker`, `validator`, `scoper`, `architect`, `reviewer`, `debugger`, `operator`, `documenter`, `curator`, `oracle`, `cup`, `mug`, `planner`, `orchestrator`, … through `judge`). The set is **open** — plugins contribute namespaced `<plugin>:<role>` ids (`role-config.ts`). |
| `run`          | All non-worker quotas    | `window_key = 'run:<id>'`
entries.description: Transports › The signed URL params

entries.text:
Transports › The three context types
The codebase has three context types floating around — same field set, different supersets. Knowing which is which helps when tracing types through the dispatcher and transport adapters.

| Type                           | Lives at                                      | Used by                                                                       | Streaming?                                                   |
| ------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `UnifiedToolContext`           | `libs/generic/tooldef/src/tool-projection.ts` | The dispatcher canonical context. All transport adapters build one.           | Yes — `emit`, `progress`.                                    |
| `ToolContext` (plugin-sdk)     | `packages/plugin-sdk/src/index.ts`            | Plugin tool handlers (`PluginToolMap`).                                       | Yes — `emit`, `progress` (mirrored from UnifiedToolContext). |
| `ToolContext` (legacy, engine) | `libs/generic/tooldef/src/types.ts`           | Legacy principal-gated `defineTool` handlers — `{ principal, tx, log }` only. | No — these don't stream.                                     |

When `defineTool({ requirePrincipal: false, … })` is called (role-gated), the handler receives `UnifiedToolContext` directly. When `defineTool({ … })` is used with default `requirePrincipal: true`, the wrapper synthesizes the legacy `ToolContext` from the unified one — `emit`/`progress` are dropped because legacy built-ins don't stream.
entries.description: Transports › The three context types

entries.text:
Transports › The three transports
| Transport           | Used by                                           | Path                                                                    |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **HTTP** (plugin)   | Dashboard fetches, agent HTTP fallback            | `POST /api/plugins/<plugin>/<tool>`                                     |
| **HTTP** (built-in) | Dashboard fetches with bearer                     | `POST /api/agent-tools/<scope>/<verb>`                                  |
| **MCP**             | Spawned agents over `mcp-handler` Streamable-HTTP | `POST /api/mcp`                                                         |
| **In-process**      | Direct TS imports, server actions                 | `dispatchProjectedTool(...)` (gated) or `tool.fn(input, ctx)` (ungated) |

The HTTP, MCP, and gated in-process paths all go through the same `dispatchProjectedTool` in `libs/generic/tooldef/src/dispatch-projected.ts` (`dispatchProjectedToolStream` for the in-process streaming variant). The same role/capability/quota/timeout/telemetry behavior applies. The raw `tool.fn(input, ctx)` call is the one exception — it bypasses the dispatcher entirely (see [In-process callers](#how-in-process-callers-reach-a-function) below).

> **mcp-handler's SSE transport is disabled.** Only `/api/mcp` (Streamable-HTTP) is live; `mcp-handler` is configured with `disableSse: true`, so a request to `/api/sse` short-circuits to HTTP 404. SSE was turned off because mcp-handler's SSE transport requires Redis (`REDIS_URL` / `KV_URL`) for cross-process pub/sub, which the operator doesn't run. Streamable-HTTP needs no Redis. (`packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/transport/_mcp-handler.ts`.)
entries.description: Transports › The three transports

entries.text:
Transports › Trust model
The per-spawn URL params are **HMAC-signed** end-to-end. The orchestrator mints with the shared key in `harness_shared.operator_secrets`; the dispatcher verifies before honoring any role claim. A worker that rewrites `?role=worker` → `?role=operator` produces an invalid signature, the request is rejected with `request_rejected: spawn_sig_invalid_signature`, and the attempt lands in `harness_shared.spawn_sig_verification_failures`. See [Spawn-URL signing](/internal/docs/endpoint-system/spawn-signing) for the full scheme and threat model.

Layered defences still apply:

* The operator binds to `127.0.0.1` (`PAPERCUSP_BIND_HOST` defaults to loopback). Only local processes can hit `/api/plugins/*` or `/api/[transport]`.
* Built-in tools still require a bearer principal when accessed without a spawn ctx. They throw `UnauthorizedToolError` (HTTP 401) when none is present.
* `.mcp.json` is written mode 0600; per-spawn worktree dirs are mode 0700.

The signing scheme defends against prompt-injected workers rewriting URL params. It does **not** defend against same-UID code reading the signing key from PG, replaying another spawn's still-valid URL, or any of the other same-UID escalation paths catalogued in [Spawn-URL signing → Threat model](/internal/docs/endpoint-system/spawn-signing#threat-model). Off-loopback exposure still needs a real principal/auth layer in front; that's separate work.
entries.description: Transports › Trust model
Transports › Typed event streams

entries.text:
Transports › Wire format per event — schema-inferred
The framework inspects each declared event's Zod schema at registration time and picks the on-the-wire encoding:

* `z.string()` → **raw text**. The payload is the text; multi-line content gets split into multiple `data:` lines per SSE spec, joined back by `parseSseStream`. Use for high-frequency token streams (LLM deltas, log lines) — no JSON.stringify on emit, no JSON.parse on consume, smaller bytes per frame.
* Any object/union/etc. → **JSON-encoded**. Use for structured events (suggestions, tool\_calls, cost summaries).

```ts
events: {
  delta:      z.string(),                              // raw on the wire
  tool_call:  z.object({ name: z.string(), input: z.unknown() }),  // JSON
  cost:       z.object({ usd: z.number() }),           // JSON
  suggestion: SuggestionSchema,                        // JSON
}
```

The MCP transport always JSON-encodes (JSON-RPC doesn't have a raw-text channel inside a notification's `params`); the classification only affects the SSE wire. Clients consuming over MCP see `data: '<the text>'` as a string field; over SSE for the same event, they see `data: <the text>` without quotes.
entries.description: Transports › Wire format per event — schema-inferred

entries.text:
Why a curator role
The curator is the harness's memory-compaction role: the one place where noisy
raw observations get distilled into the bounded, durable memory every other
role reads. It is the only role allowed to *delete* memory. Without it, the
append-only observation log grows linearly with iterations and no other role
has the bandwidth to read it.

The design predates the current engine (it was one of the original
bash-harness roles) and survived into the blueprint era nearly unchanged.
entries.description: Why a curator role

entries.text:
Why a curator role › What the curator does (per its persona)
The persona (`libs/papercusp/packages/harness/blueprints/base/prompts/curator.md`,
inherited by `coding-factory`) is explicit and ordered:

1. **Process pending issues first.** Validator findings land as pending
   issues; the curator triages them in two distinct steps. First the
   **operator** runs the dedup against open/acknowledged issues — exact
   `codePointer` match **or** ≥0.85 Jaccard title overlap collapses a finding
   into the existing one (`attempts++`, a "Resurfaced" note, severity
   bump-up); genuinely-new findings get fresh `I-NNNN` ids. Then the
   **curator** itself auto-closes the stale ones: any open/acknowledged issue
   whose `codePointer` is verified passing this round (its feature is `passed`
   and no new pending entry mentions the same pointer).
2. **Merge raw observations into `MEMORY.md`** — the full curated store at
   `.papercusp/memory/MEMORY.md`, deduplicated, bounded at \~200 lines, and
   organized under four fixed headings: `## Decisions`, `## Context`,
   `## History`, and `## Lessons` — the persona flags **Lessons** as the most
   important section (generalized statements future runs can act on).
3. **Re-derive `summary.md`** — `.papercusp/memory/summary.md`, **hard-capped
   at 40 lines / \~800 tokens**, auto-injected into every future role's prompt
   (it rides the cacheable preamble — see
   [Why prompt-cache-dominant](/internal/docs/harness/decisions/prompt-cache)).
   The curator is the **one role that does not** receive the auto-injected
   `summary.md` — it would be self-referential and it changes every pass, so
   the prompt builder excludes it
   (`libs/papercusp/packages/orchestrator/src/prompt-build.ts`). The curator
   instead reads `raw.md` / `MEMORY.md` from disk with a deliberately fresh
   context: "nothing is in your head; everything is on disk."
4. **Truncate `raw.md`** — `.papercusp/memory/raw.md` is the append-only
   one-liner log any role writes t
entries.description: Why a curator role › What the curator does (per its persona)

entries.text:
Why a curator role › When the curator fires
The curator is a role in the `coding-factory` blueprint — the strict
scoper-to-curator spine
(`libs/papercusp/packages/harness/blueprints/coding-factory/blueprint.yaml`).
There it sits at the end of the spine
(`scoper → architect → worker → validator → reviewer → documenter → curator`)
and runs in the finalize recipe on **both** terminal outcomes:
`onDone: [curator, postCuratorOutputs, documenter, archive]` and
`onEscalate: [curator]`. Same contract as the original design: terminal
events always get a curation pass.

A naming note: the 2026-06-18 rename
(\[\[domain-generic-pot-architecture-2026-06-18]] D-011) moved this spine from
the id `coding` to `coding-factory`, and reused `coding` for the Pot (Mug +
coding cups). So the live default `coding` blueprint is now the single-role
Pot operator — it has **no** curator role and no `gates.finalize`; the curator
pipeline lives only in `coding-factory`, which the Pot falls back to per-repo
(`extends: coding-factory`). The blueprint-id aliases deliberately have no
`coding → coding-factory` entry — a bare `coding` resolves to the new Pot
(`libs/papercusp/packages/orchestrator/src/blueprint-aliases.ts`).
entries.description: Why a curator role › When the curator fires

entries.text:
Why a curator role › Where this stands today
Memory compaction is the curator's pipeline job within the `coding-factory`
spine. (After the 2026-06-18 rename the live default `coding` blueprint is the
Pot, which has no curator pass; the curator pipeline ships only where the
spine does.) Curation has also grown an operator-level read surface: the
`curation:*` tools
(`packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/curation/` — `curation:feed`,
`curation:change-feed`, `curation:state-of-pot`) project completed work and
fleet-wide meta-patterns for supervising agents. The same instinct — distill
the noisy stream into a bounded, grounded digest — applied one level up.

Personal/cross-client semantic memory is a separate system (the `memory:*`
tools over the canonical PG store); the curator owns the *harness's* working
memory. See [Memory](/internal/docs/harness/memory) for the full layering.
entries.description: Why a curator role › Where this stands today

entries.text:
Why a curator role › Why compaction is a separate role
Other frameworks bundle memory maintenance into every agent. The result:
workers spend tokens deciding what's worth remembering, different workers
disagree about what matters, and mid-mission deletions churn shared state.
Splitting compaction into one role gives:

* **One place to review** the "what should we remember" prompt.
* **Atomic mutations** — the curator runs, and every subsequent spawn sees the
  new memory.
* **Auditable history** — `raw.md` is the working set; `MEMORY.md` is what the
  curator distilled from it.
* **Bounded growth** — the 40-line summary and \~200-line store mean the
  system can't ingest more than later spawns can afford to re-read.

Any role appends to `raw.md` without coordination; the curator decides where
an observation belongs (mission memory vs cross-mission identity). The worker
flags; the curator files.
entries.description: Why a curator role › Why compaction is a separate role

entries.text:
Decision log (harness design history)
This page preserves the design-decision history of the **first-generation
(bash) harness** — the rationale trail that shaped the current system — and
maps which decisions survive in today's engine. Historical entries are kept
as written; they describe the system *as it was*.

entries.text:
Decision log (harness design history) › A note on the blueprint rename (`coding` is now the Pot)
This page was written when `coding` *was* the per-feature director spine.
The 2026-06-18 domain-generic-pot-architecture rename
(D-011/D-024) shuffled the blueprint ids, so the names mean different
things today:

* The bash-era per-feature spine — scoper → architect → worker → validator
  → reviewer → documenter → curator, with the debugger/crosscheck overlays
  — survives as **`blueprints/coding-factory/blueprint.yaml`** (the retired
  per-feature director loop, lifted into declared spine edges).
* **`blueprints/coding/blueprint.yaml`** is now a different system entirely:
  the **Pot/Mug operator blueprint** (`kind: pot`, roles `operator` and
  `mug`) — the judgment layer over the cup fleet, not a validation spine.

entries.text:
Lifecycle hooks
Lifecycle hooks are user-supplied shell scripts that the harness runs at fixed
pipeline boundaries. Drop an executable script at
`<project>/.papercusp/hooks/<name>.sh` and the engine invokes it when the
matching event fires. The runner is `runHook()` in
`libs/papercusp/packages/orchestrator/src/hooks.ts`: it looks up
`<stateDir>/hooks/<name>.sh`, skips silently if the file is missing or not
executable (any execute bit set — `mode & 0o111`, so owner, group, **or**
other counts), runs it with `cwd` set to the project
directory, captures combined stdout+stderr to
`<stateDir>/logs/hooks/<unix-seconds>-<name>.log`, and logs a non-zero exit as
a warning — a failing hook never halts the mission. On Windows the script
needs `bash` on `PATH` (Git for Windows ships one); the desktop bootstrap
surfaces that prerequisite.
entries.description: Lifecycle hooks

entries.text:
Lifecycle hooks › Environment a hook receives
On top of the event-specific variables in the table, `runHook()` auto-injects
context so scripts can query the operator instead of scraping harness files
(`hooks.ts:105–113`):

* `HARNESS_SLUG` — the current harness slug (defaults to the project
  directory's basename when not passed explicitly)
* `WORKSPACE_ID` — the active workspace, when known
* `OPERATOR_BASE` — operator API base URL; defaults to
  `$PAPERCUSP_OPERATOR_BASE`, then `http://localhost:3070` (the operator API
  port — `:3055` is the Vite content port with no `/api` routes, the EI-113
  wrong-stack default that audit P-038 fixed)

The full process environment is inherited too; the caller's explicit env wins
over the injected values on conflict.

**Hooks must not read harness state from the filesystem.** Files like
`lanes.json` no longer exist at runtime — PG is the runtime store-of-record
(see [Storage policy](/internal/docs/system/storage-policy)). The contract in
`hooks.ts` is: query the operator API instead.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Example: .papercusp/hooks/afterDone.sh — look up feature state via the API
features=$(curl -fsS "$OPERATOR_BASE/api/harness/$HARNESS_SLUG/features")
status=$(echo "$features" | jq -r '.[] | select(.id == "'"$FEATURE_ID"'") | .status')
```

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Example: .papercusp/hooks/on-escalate.sh — page a Slack channel
curl -X POST -H 'Content-type: application/json' \
  --data "{\"text\":\"Mission escalated: $REASON\"}" \
  "$SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL"
```

Make scripts executable (`chmod +x`) — a non-executable file is skipped
without error.
entries.description: Lifecycle hooks › Environment a hook receives

entries.text:
Lifecycle hooks › Hooks that fire today
The legacy bash run-loop fired ten hook events; that loop is retired
(`libs/papercusp/_retired/orchestrator-run-loop/`). In the current DBOS
pipeline, hooks fire from the **finalizer** — the step list that
`planFinalization()` builds when a feature pipeline ends in DONE or ESCALATE
(`packages/operator-core/lib/dbos/orchestrator-finalize.ts`). Two hook names
are wired:

| Hook          | Fires                                                                                      | Event-specific env                                       | Call site                    |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| `on-escalate` | Pipeline finalizes with **ESCALATE**, before the `onEscalate` recipe roles run             | `REASON`, `PROJECT_DIR`, `STATE_DIR`                     | `orchestrator-runner.ts:930` |
| `afterDone`   | Pipeline finalizes **DONE** (and the done-gates pass), after the `onDone` recipe roles run | `TRIGGER=done`, `FEATURE_ID`, `PROJECT_DIR`, `STATE_DIR` | `orchestrator-runner.ts:952` |

A blocked DONE skips the whole finalization step list, hook included.
`planFinalization()` blocks completion on **any** of three conditions: an open
needs-human plan item, a configured smoke gate that ran and failed
(`smokeEnabled && smokePassed === false`), or — for a `human-gate` acceptance
blueprint — an approval that hasn't been granted yet
(`acceptanceKind === 'human-gate' && !acceptanceApproved`). Any of these and
the `afterDone` hook never runs.

The roles that surround the hooks are **declarative**, not hardcoded:
`planFinalization()` resolves the finalize recipe from the harness's
`.papercusp/blueprint.yaml` `gates.finalize`, defaulting to the coding
blueprint's recipe (`onDone`: curator → postCuratorOutputs → documenter →
`[archive]`; `onEscalate`: curator). A no
entries.description: Lifecycle hooks › Hooks that fire today

entries.text:
Lifecycle hooks › Managing hook scripts over the API
`packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/harness/hooks.ts` exposes
CRUD for hook scripts: `GET /api/harness/:slug/hooks` (list known hooks with
content + executable bit), `PUT`/`DELETE /api/harness/:slug/hooks/:name`
(write with `chmod 755` / remove), and
`GET /api/harness/:slug/hook-logs/:logId` to read a hook-run log. The
`hooks:known` tool returns the same name list.

The known-hooks list comes from `getKnownHooks()`
(`packages/operator-core/lib/known-hooks.ts`), which returns the `live` rows of
a static `DBOS_PIPELINE_HOOKS` registry — yielding `['afterDone',
'on-escalate']` (sorted). So the API lists, and accepts writes to,
`afterDone`/`on-escalate` (the two that fire) and **rejects** names that aren't
live, such as the bash-era `pre-worker` (catalogued `status: 'lost'`, not
returned). A drift guard (`known-hooks.test.ts`) greps the live firing sites
under `lib/dbos/` and asserts set equality with the registry's `live` rows, so
adding a `runHook(...)` call without a registry row fails the build.
`runHook()` itself never consults this list, so scripts created directly on
disk run regardless of whether the API would have allowed the name.

(Earlier the registry was instead derived by grepping the now-retired
`main-loop.ts`, which always found nothing and fell back to `['pre-worker']` —
advertising a hook that never fires and hiding the two that do. The static
registry replaced that grep in `papercusp-full-app-audit-2026-06-09` P-016
(EI-94).)
entries.description: Lifecycle hooks › Managing hook scripts over the API

entries.text:
Lifecycle hooks › Plugin hooks fire alongside
User hook scripts are per-harness; **plugins** hook the same lifecycle
globally. At the `afterDone` step the finalizer fires the in-process typed
hook `firePluginLifecycle('afterDone', …)` on every loaded plugin that
declares a handler (one of the FROZEN legacy fire-points —
plugin-system-pot-port D-003), then emits the `pipeline:done:<slug>:<feature>`
event. Plugin hook failures are logged by the host and ignored; plugin hooks
fire whether or not a user hook script ran. (The old per-plugin shell-out via
the `papercusp-fire-hook` CLI was retired 2026-06-12 — plugin-system-pot-port
P-006.) New pipeline integrations should not use typed hooks at all: declare
**event-reaction rules** on the pipeline event vocabulary instead — see
[Plugins](/internal/docs/spec/plugins).

entries.text:
Lifecycle hooks › The `afterDone` builtin
`afterDone` has a TS builtin behind it: when **no** user hook script ran, the
finalizer calls `notifyParentOnDone()`
(`packages/operator-core/lib/dbos/notify-parent-done.ts`), which posts a
`Completion` message to this harness's parent — so a parent that spawned this
harness as a child learns the sub-work is done. The parent slug is read from PG
(`harness_shared.projects.parent_slug`, sealed server-side at scaffold time by
`doScaffoldHarness`), **not** from config. The message fires **only when the
harness's feature queue has fully drained** — every other feature is `passed`
or `deprecated`, excluding the feature that triggered this finalize. A
non-drained queue is a **silent no-op**: the builtin returns a typed reason
(`no_parent` / `queue_not_drained` / `send_failed` / `lookup_failed`) and posts
nothing. A per-harness `hooks/afterDone.sh` **overrides the builtin entirely**
(parity with the retired bash builtin resolver). Plugin hooks fire regardless
(below).
entries.description: Lifecycle hooks › The `afterDone` builtin

entries.text:
Lifecycle hooks › Why hooks instead of in-prompt actions
This is design intent carried over from the first harness generation, and it
still holds: hooks are **out-of-band**. They consume no tokens, add no latency
to any LLM call, and fire **deterministically** — not "if the agent decides
to". Anything you'd otherwise bolt onto a role prompt as "and also send a
Slack message" belongs in a hook, keeping each prompt focused on the role's
one job.
entries.description: Lifecycle hooks › Why hooks instead of in-prompt actions

entries.text:
Smoke-test gate
Validators verify code-level claims; they don't always start the real service
and hit real endpoints. A feature can "pass" — unit test green, contract
documented, migration applied — while the deployed service 500s from config
drift, a missing env var, or a startup race. The **smoke-test gate** exists to
catch that class of failure *before* a pipeline declares DONE. The principle
("quality through truth": verify service startup, don't trust test output
alone) came from the first harness generation and still holds.
entries.description: Smoke-test gate

entries.text:
Smoke-test gate › Related
* [Lifecycle hooks](/internal/docs/harness/hooks) — `on-smoke-pass` /
  `on-smoke-fail`
* [Decision telemetry](/internal/docs/harness/decisions-timeline) — the

entries.text:
Smoke-test gate › The runner shape (and the bash-era gating still awaiting port)
`service-smoke-test.sh` is what the manual endpoint above spawns, and its
behavior is the shape the automatic gate will reuse: read the smoke config
(`urls` of `{ url, expectStatus, expectText? }`, optional `startupCmd` +
`startupWaitSeconds`, default 30), start the service if the first URL isn't
responding, curl each URL, then on all-pass write `smoke-pass.md` (clearing any
`smoke-failure.md`) and on any-fail write `smoke-failure.md` and reopen the
most-recently-passed feature as failing. The config is OFF by default
(`smokeTest.enabled: false`). What did **not** survive the bash→DBOS migration
is the two automatic *gating modes* the bash main loop ran: `onDone` (block
mission completion) and `onFeaturePass` (revert a feature before the documenter
runs, so docs are never generated for a broken state) — these are the Phase F
follow-up the finalizer still passes `smokeEnabled: false` in lieu of.
entries.description: Smoke-test gate › The runner shape (and the bash-era gating still awaiting port)

entries.text:
Smoke-test gate › What is NOT yet wired: the automatic DONE-gate invocation
The manual/on-demand loop above runs and persists a smoke result, but the
durable finalizer never *calls* the smoke runner itself as part of declaring
DONE. The runner call site passes the gate explicitly off
(`packages/operator-core/lib/dbos/orchestrator-runner.ts`:

> "Smoke gate is config-gated-off for \~all harnesses; not yet ported into the
> durable finalizer (`runSmokeTest` is a main-loop-internal). Tracked as a
> Phase F follow-up; pass not-run so it never blocks here."

— `smokeEnabled: false, smokePassed: null`). Because the finalizer always hands
the gate `smokeEnabled: false`, the DONE-gate machinery — which *would* block on
`smokeEnabled && smokePassed === false` — never trips on the automatic path. A
smoke run that fails today still records its papercup + PG row + attention item,
but it cannot, on its own, stop a pipeline from completing until that Phase F
follow-up wires the finalizer to invoke and consume the runner.

In short: **gate machinery live, manual runner wired, automatic gate
invocation pending.** If you need a service-level check on a harness today, run
it on demand (`POST /api/harness/:slug/smoke-test/run`) or lean on the testing
surface (the project's own test/E2E suites — see
[Testing](/internal/docs/testing)).
entries.description: Smoke-test gate › What is NOT yet wired: the automatic DONE-gate invocation

entries.text:
Smoke-test gate › What is wired today
**The gate.** The durable finalizer's planner
(`planFinalization` in
`packages/operator-core/lib/dbos/orchestrator-finalize.ts`) treats the smoke
result as a first-class DONE gate, exactly like an open `needs-human` plan
item: when `smokeEnabled` is set and `smokePassed === false`, finalization is
**blocked** — no curator/documenter recipe runs and the pipeline does not
complete.

**A manual run.** A live, registered route runs the smoke script on
demand: `POST /api/harness/:slug/smoke-test/run`
(`packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/harness/orchestration-actions.ts`,
loopback-auth; flattened into the route table at `routes/index.ts`) spawns
`service-smoke-test.sh`, which writes the `smoke-pass.md` / `smoke-failure.md`
papercups (clearing the failure papercup on pass). It is also reachable
through the device-tier shim `POST /api/device/harnesses/:slug/smoke-test`
(`routes/device/harnesses.ts`). The script then POSTs its aggregated result
to `POST /api/internal/smoke-test-event`, which upserts the
`harness_shared.harness_smoke_test` row and — on a pass→fail *transition*
only — pushes a high-importance `smoke-fail` attention item. So the papercups
`smoke_test_clean` reads are exactly what this live endpoint writes; they are
not only "earlier engines / out-of-band".

**The health signal.** A smoke failure surfaces through two differently-named
composite checks with **different data sources**: `smoke_test_clean` (the
harness-readers composite health in
`packages/operator-core/lib/harness-readers.ts`) fails when the
`smoke-failure.md` FS papercup exists in the harness state dir; `smoke_passing`
(the operator-UI `HealthBadge`) fails when the latest PG `harness_smoke_test`
row has `status: 'fail'` (the "see smoke-failure.md" text it shows is only a
label, not its source). That same `harness_smoke_test` row (written by the
smoke-test-event route above) is also what the Planning attention feed reads to
list failing harnesses

entries.text:
Multi-harness spawning / communication › 1. Goal
Make harness-spawning and cross-harness coordination first-class capabilities of the standard harness substrate, with auth-bound identity from day one.

Concretely:

* Any harness whose role config declares `allowedActions: [..., "scaffold_harness"]` can spawn children.
* Any marketplace template that declares `spawnable: { kind, requires }` can be spawned as a child.
* Children whose `parent_slug` is set automatically report completion back to their parent — no per-template hook authoring required.
* Every orchestrator understands it's running inside Papercusp, can see its parent / children / siblings at a glance, and can pull full state of any other harness on demand via authenticated read APIs.
* Any harness whose role config grants `send_message` can message any other harness, with a declared `reason` recorded in the audit log.
* **Every executeAction call is authenticated against a per-harness shared-secret token; harness identity is derived from the token binding, not from caller-supplied body fields. `parent_slug` and message `from_slug` are derived (not trusted), so spoofing is impossible at the protocol level.**
* The `papercup-org` template is the first template that uses these features, not a special case.

The user-facing demo: drop a directive into the `papercup-org` parent's inbox, manually invoke its director, watch it spawn children with full context of the org, watch them run while the parent can intervene mid-mission, watch completion flow back.

entries.text:
Multi-harness spawning / communication › 2. Scope
Closed-loop manual demo via standard substrate. End-to-end smokes must pass:

* **Smoke A** — papercup-org happy path (directive → spawn → first non-trivial file → completion message in parent inbox)
* **Smoke B** — generic non-`papercup-org` harness can also spawn children (proves the feature is substrate, not template-specific)
* **Smoke C** — neighbor visibility works (a child's prompt sees its parent's status; a parent's prompt sees its children's statuses; cross-harness supervisor message arrives in child's prompt-build)
* **Smoke D** — auth model holds: a request without a valid token, with a token bound to harness X claiming to be harness Y, or with a forged `callingHarness` body field, is rejected with 401/403

Autonomy (routine ticker, coordinator dispatch, auditor cadence) is a **separate plan** — not included here.
entries.description: Multi-harness spawning / communication › 2. Scope

entries.text:
Multi-harness spawning / communication › 3. Non-goals
* Coordinator dispatch — `NEXT_HARNESS` parses but doesn't fire children autonomously.
* Auditor cadence — file exists, no scheduler invokes it.
* `add_directive_summary` — context bounded by prompt-build truncation instead.
* `mark_campaign_published`, `pause_project`, `resume_project` — useful, not needed for the loop.
* Briefings plugin — gone, dropped from manifest until source is restored or rebuilt.
* Many-directive scale, multi-week autonomy, KPI dashboards.
* Cross-machine spawn (parent on machine A, child on machine B).
* Spawn quotas / rate limiting per parent.
* Permission tiers beyond `allowedActions[]` and the auth token.
* Per-role addressing (`to: [<harness>:<role>]`); messages address harnesses, not roles within.
* `dryRun: true` for `scaffold_harness` — defer to v1.5.
* Cache-and-verify idempotency replay — v1 is cache-is-authoritative.
* Token rotation for compromised harnesses — manual reissue only in v1.

entries.text:
Multi-harness spawning / communication › 8. Acceptance criteria
* All 4 verbs implemented and individually green via authenticated curl
* All 4 verbs idempotent on `actionId` replay (cache-is-authoritative documented)
* All requests rejected with 401 if no/invalid bearer token
* All requests rejected with 403 if body claims a harness identity not bound to the bearer token
* `parent_slug` and `from_slug` always derived from the bearer token, never from body
* `papercusp install papercup-org@0.1.1` materializes 7 working harness dirs each with a `harness_token`
* Builtin `afterDone` hook fires for any harness with `parent_slug` set, including non-papercup-org harnesses
* At least one non-papercup-org template has `spawnable: true` and is reachable via `GET /api/marketplace/spawnable`
* `papercup-org` template re-bundled with NO per-dept afterDone scripts
* Every prompt includes the "About Papercusp" preamble + neighbor view (with `spawned_count` + aggregate) + Tier 3 capabilities
* Tier 3 capability is verified to actually work end-to-end (agent can inspect)
* Coding-harness prompt-build includes own bounded inbox; auto-ack only on DONE/NEXT\_\* decisions
* `send_message` requires `reason` ≥10 chars; placeholder regex matches log a quality flag
* `scaffold_harness` enforces slug uniqueness with 409
* `scaffold_harness` 5-minute timeout enforced
* `spinup_project` recursion is transactional (all-or-nothing across schemas)
* Migration script handles broken registry rows: skip + log
* Smoke A passes twice from clean state
* Smoke B passes twice from clean state — no code in either path references "papercup-org" by name
* Smoke C passes twice — neighbor view + cross-harness messaging + auto-ack scoping verified
* Smoke D passes twice — auth model holds against forgery attempts
* No regressions in `sheets` standalone coding-harness flow
* Estimates updated to actuals; deltas analyzed

entries.text:
Multi-harness spawning / communication › Action execution
| Decision                                   | Choice                                                                                           | Rationale                                                                                                |
| ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Endpoint shape                             | Slug-less `POST /api/admin/execute-action` with `targetSlug` in action body                      | Many actions cross harnesses; URL-as-context is the wrong frame                                          |
| Verb dispatch                              | Single endpoint with `op` discriminator                                                          | Matches the deleted `org.ts` contract; matches `actions-block.ts`'s POST shape                           |
| State backend                              | PG (per-harness `harness_<slug>.messages`, `harness_shared.projects`)                            | Universal Schema + Zero sync already in place                                                            |
| Caller-supplied idempotency                | `actionId` (UUID) supplied by caller; server returns same `result` on replay                     | Workers retry on flake; double-spinup is unrecoverable                                                   |
| Idempotency replay semantics               | **Cache-is-authoritative.** Cached response returned without verifying side effects still exist. | Documented as v1 boundary; out-of-band mutations break replay correctness; v1.5 can add cache-and-verify |
| Per-action error shape                     | `{ok, actionId, error?, result?}`; ACTIONS array continues past mid-array failures               | Matches `actions-block.ts

| Per-harness shared secret | `harness_<slug>.config_token` (random 256-bit, base64url) generated at scaffold time, written to `.papercusp/config.json` mode 0600                                                        | Cryptographic identity binding; token serves as both authn and authz |

entries.text:
Multi-harness spawning / communication › Step 0.5 — Action-body + auth contract *(\~2 hours)*
Single 2–3 page document at `apps/operator/app/api/_hono/execute-action.contract.md`:

**Auth model:**

* Per-harness token: 256-bit random, base64url, generated at scaffold time, stored at `.papercusp/config.json:harness_token` mode 0600
* Auth header: `Authorization: Bearer <token>` required on every request
* Identity derivation: server queries `harness_shared.token_index` to derive `<derivedCallingHarness>`; if no match → 401
* Body's `callingHarness`: must equal `<derivedCallingHarness>` or be omitted; mismatch → 403
* Body's `from` (in `send_message`): must equal `<derivedCallingHarness>`; mismatch → 403
* `parent_slug` (in `scaffold_harness`): NEVER body-controlled; always set by server to `<derivedCallingHarness>`

**Tier 3 verification (the inspect\_harness capability):**

* Confirm whether `claude -p` invocations from `run.sh` include `Bash` in `--allowed-tools`.
* If yes: agent can curl Tier 3 endpoints directly. Step 2.5 is just docs.
* If no: ship `mcp__papercusp__inspectHarness` MCP tools in Step 2.5 wrapping the read endpoints.
* Document the chosen mechanism in this contract.

**Endpoint:**

* `POST /api/admin/execute-action`
* Request body:
  ```ts
  {
    actionId: string,        // UUID supplied by caller, idempotency key
    callingHarness?: string, // optional; must match Bearer-derived if present
    callingDept?: string,    // backwards-compat for run.sh (informational only)
    action: { op: '...', ... }
  }
  ```
* Per-verb request fields:
  * `send_message`: `to[], kind, subject, body, parentMessageId?, reason: string` *(`from` derived)*
  * `mark_message_status`: `messageId, status: 'acknowledged' | 'archived'`
  * `spinup_project`: `directiveId, projectName, projectVertical, projectBudgetCents, departments[]`
  * `scaffold_harness`: `projectSlug, template, spec, goal` *(`parent_slug` derived)*
* Response: `{ok, actionId, result?, error?}`
* Idemp

**Auth middleware *(\~0.5d)*:**

* Reject if no `Authorization: Bearer` header (401).

Multi-harness spawning / communication › Step 3 — Read APIs + tiered visibility prompt-build *(\~1.75d)*
#### 3a — Per-harness reads

In `apps/operator/app/api/_hono/harness.ts`:

* `GET /api/harness/:slug/inbox?status=pending&limit=20`
* `GET /api/harness/:slug/outbox?limit=20`
* `GET /api/harness/:slug/supervisor-notes?limit=10`

**Tier 2 — Neighbor view** (depth-1, queried at prompt-build tim

entries.text:
Multi-harness spawning / communication › Step 4.5 — Builtin completion hook *(\~0.5d)*
New file `libs/papercusp/packages/harness/hooks/builtins/afterDone.sh`:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# Built-in: notify parent harness on mission completion.
# Fires only when this harness has parent_slug set in .papercusp/config.json.
# User-supplied .papercusp/hooks/afterDone.sh overrides this entirely.
set -e
PARENT_SLUG="$(jq -r '.parent_slug // empty' .papercusp/config.json 2>/dev/null)"
[ -z "$PARENT_SLUG" ] && exit 0  # no parent, silent success

TOKEN="$(jq -r '.harness_token // empty' .papercusp/config.json 2>/dev/null)"
[ -z "$TOKEN" ] && { echo "afterDone: no harness_token in config; skipping" >&2; exit 0; }

SELF_SLUG="$(jq -r '.slug // empty' .papercusp/config.json 2>/dev/null)"
[ -z "$SELF_SLUG" ] && SELF_SLUG="$(basename "$PWD")"

ACTION_ID="$(uuidgen)"
BASE="${PAPERCUSP_OPERATOR_BASE:-http://localhost:3055}"

curl -sS --max-time 30 -X POST "$BASE/api/admin/execute-action" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d "$(jq -nc \
    --arg id "$ACTION_ID" \
    --arg to "$PARENT_SLUG" \
    '{actionId: $id, action: {op: "send_message", to: [$to], kind: "Completion", subject: "mission DONE", body: "", reason: "afterDone substrate hook: notifying parent of mission completion"}}')" \
  > /dev/null
```

Update `run.sh`'s `run_hook` to scan `${HARNESS_LIB_DIR}/packages/harness/hooks/builtins/` for any matching `<name>.sh` and fall through when no per-harness override exists. Generic resolver, ship one builtin (`afterDone`) for v1.

**Gate:** seed `parent_slug` + `harness_token` in a test harness's config.json, run a short mission to DONE, verify the parent's `harness_<parent>.messages` table has the Completion row with `from_slug = <child-slug>`.

entries.text:
Multi-harness spawning / communication › Step 4.6 — Bounded inbox in coding-harness prompt-build *(\~0.5d)*
Update prompt-build for orchestrator, scoper, and worker so each iteration's prompt includes:

```markdown
## Recent supervisor messages (from parent: <parent_slug>)
- 2026-05-01T14:32 [BudgetIncrease] from papercup-org-business: "raised your budget to $500"
- 2026-05-01T14:18 [Priority] from papercup-org: "focus on auth before dashboard"
```

Drawn from `harness_<self>.messages WHERE to_slug = <self> AND status = 'pending' AND from_slug = <parent_slug> ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 5`.

**Auto-acknowledge scoping:** at end of iteration, if orchestrator decision ∈ `{DONE, NEXT_WORKER, NEXT_VALIDATOR, NEXT_ARCHITECT, NEXT_HARNESS, ...}` (the "happy progression" verbs), mark consumed messages as `acknowledged`. If decision ∈ `{ESCALATE, REVIEW, FEATURE_FREEZE}` or iteration fails non-zero, leave messages pending so the next iteration (after user intervention) sees them again.

**Gate:** drop a `send_message` from a parent harness to a running child; the child's next iteration's prompt includes it; after the iteration completes with `NEXT_WORKER`, the message status flips to `acknowledged`. Repeat with an iteration that `ESCALATE`s; verify message remains pending.

Multi-harness spawning / communication › Step 5a — Re-bundle the papercup-org template *(\~0.75d)*
Build the missing `parent/` directory:

  .papercusp/
    config.json                            ← roles config (below)

Org parent's `.papercusp/config.json`:

```json
{
  "phase": "org",
  "harness_kind": "org",
  "primaryRole": "director",
  "roles": {
    "director": {
      "inboxKinds": ["Directive", "Completion", "Status"],
      "outboxKinds": ["Decision", "Priority", "Budget"],
      "allowedActions": ["spinup_project", "scaffold_harness", "send_message"],
      "model": "claude-opus-4-7",
      "cadence": 60
    },
    "coordinator": {
      "inboxKinds": ["Completion", "Status"],
      "outboxKinds": ["NextHarness"],
      "allowedActions": ["send_message"],
      "model": "claude-haiku-4-5",
      "cadence": 30
    },
    "auditor": {

      "outboxKinds": ["AuditReport"],
      "allowedActions": ["send_message"],

Multi-harness spawning / communication › Step 6 — Four integration smokes *(\~2d)*
#### Smoke A — papercup-org happy path

```
1. Reset state: prune any existing papercup-org* rows + delete project dirs.
2. Reinstall: papercusp install papercup-org.
3. Drop directive into parent inbox via curl POST /api/harness/papercup-org/messages,
   kind=Directive, body="write a single static index.html that says 'hello world'".
4. Manually invoke parent director:
   curl POST /api/harness/papercup-org/invoke?role=director.
5. Wait up to 5 min for the director run to complete.
6. Assert: parent's executed_actions table has at least one spinup_project and one
   scaffold_harness, each with a non-empty `reason`, with caller_slug = papercup-org.
7. Assert: a new child harness slug appears in GET /api/harness/projects with hasState=true,
   hasSpec=true, parent_slug=papercup-org.
8. Assert: the child's harness_<slug> PG schema exists with messages + executed_actions tables
   + a config_token row.
9. Manually invoke the child loop with a generous timeout: papercusp run <child-slug>
   --max-iterations 10.
10. Wait until the child writes its first non-trivial file (an index.html with content)
    OR reaches DONE — whichever comes first, max 5 min.
11. Assert: builtin afterDone hook fired (only if DONE was reached) — executed_actions
    has a send_message op with from_slug=<child-slug>, kind='Completion', reason populated.
12. Assert: parent's GET /inbox shows the Completion message at status='pending'
    (or, if step 10 stopped at "first file written," assert that the child has a real
    file on disk — proves the spawn produced a working harness even if it didn't
    fully complete).
```

```
1. Create a fresh harness "test-spawner-org" via:
   papercusp init test-spawner-org --target /tmp/test-spawner-org.
2. Hand-edit .papercusp/config.json to set:
     harness_kind: 'org'

entries.text:
Plugin + marketplace pipeline — state as of 2026-05-11 › Plugin runtime model + extension axes
*(Added post-snapshot — the runtime surface grew well beyond the action registry described above.)*

Each plugin instance gets a per-(plugin, harness) `ctx` carrying:

* `ctx.actions` — the action registry (`register(...)`'d handlers behind `/api/plugins/[...path]`).
* `ctx.spawn` — capability-gated `compute:exec` with a frozen PATH (`makePluginSpawn`).
* `ctx.kv` — plugin-private, quota'd K/V backed by `harness_shared.plugin_kv` (quota from `manifest.kvQuota`; left `undefined` in test/no-PG contexts, so plugins must tolerate absence).
* `ctx.oauth.token(field)` — acquires a fresh access token, resolving the backing provider from the plugin's manifest `oauth[]` entries.
* `ctx.recordResource(...)` — writes a record to the provision WAL (for in-process plugins that create external resources from a hook handler rather than a setup script).

The **primary** extension surface is no longer the typed lifecycle hooks — it is two manifest-declared axes the host wires at load:

* **Tool axis** (main consumer): `manifest.tools[]` entries are projected as agent tools `<plugin>.<verb>` over both HTTP and MCP (`registerPluginTools`).
* **Event-reaction axis**: `manifest.reactions[]` rules — when a trigger `on` settles, the rule fires one of the plugin's **own** tools through normal capability-scoped dispatch. Each `on` trigger requires an `events:listen:<on>` capability (`registerPluginReactionRules`). Plugin-emitted events (the WASM event sink, `plugins:fire_event`) feed the same reaction registry as synthetic events.

The **RoutineDefinition** and **RoleDefinition** manifest axes were **retired** in the pot port (`collectRoutines`/`collectRoles` deleted, zero callers). The manifest `roles` field stays schema-tolerated as inert data (so existing plugins that declare it still load); routines authors are pointed at blueprint triggers / event-reaction schedules.

The publishable-snapshot / snapshot-**export** pipeline below was **retired**
(retire-snapshots-instance-spec-2026-06-09, shipped). `libs/papercusp-export-state`
moved to `_retired/snapshot-system/papercusp-export-state`; `@papercusp/export-state`,
the `snapshots:*` tools, all `/api/snapshots/*` publish routes, and the Cupboard
`kind=snapshot` were retired (migration 199 drops `snapshot_index`). The fork route
`instantiate.ts` — the **only** non-test caller of `copyGrantsToNewHarness` — now lives
under `_retired/`. The reproducible replacement is the **InstanceSpec** system
(`packages/operator-core/lib/instance-spec/`).

The surviving `/api/harness/:slug/snapshots` route is a **different** feature —
per-harness iteration snapshots (FS rollback of `.papercusp/snapshots/<ts>-iter-<n>/`),
not publishable snapshots.

*Historical (pre-retirement) flow:*

1. **Capture** — `POST /api/snapshots/create` writes a tarball under `<harness>/.papercusp/snapshots/`.
2. **Publish** — `POST /api/snapshots/<id>/publish` uploads to marketplace.
3. **Fork** — `POST /api/snapshots/<id>/instantiate` (or `papercusp snapshot fork`) creates a new harness with schema rename. **Grants carry over (PR #2)**: `copyGrantsToNewHarness` copies every `(plugin, version, capability)` grant on the source harness to the new fork via `INSERT … SELECT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`.
4. **Republish** — *pending*. PR-B paused per `@plugin`'s reply on coord, awaiting v1 plan greenlight (Batch G+1 bumps `SNAPSHOT_SCHEMA_VERSION` to 2).

entries.text:
Performance — rules every agent must follow
> **Webapp retired (2026-05-14).** Any `localhost:3055` or `localhost:3070` URL on this page is only reachable while the **Tauri dev shell** is running. Start it with `cd papercusp-desktop && npm run dev`.

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

This page was written when the operator app was a **Next.js App Router** project, and several rules below were framed around RSC / Server Components / Next-specific tooling. **That framework is gone.** The operator is now a **Vite SPA on TanStack Router** (`apps/operator-vite`, dev server on `:3055`) fronting a **Hono host** (`apps/operator/bin/hono-host.ts`, `:3070`). There is no `next` dependency, no RSC, no Server Components, and `'use client'` is an inert vestige. The `next/*` import surface (`next/image`, `next/dynamic`, `next/link`, `next/navigation`) is satisfied by TanStack-Router-backed shims under `apps/operator/lib/router-compat/{dynamic,link,navigation}.tsx`. RSC-only advice ("ship zero JS", "push `'use client'` to the leaf") does **not** apply to a SPA — read those rules as historical context. The *measured* perf wins (parallelize fs/PG, request-scoped read caches, virtualize/memoize lists, animate only transform/opacity) still hold; only the **named cause** "Next.js dev mode" and any Next-specific tool are stale. See `apps/operator/docs/plans/finish-next-removal-2026-06-01.md` and `apps/operator/docs/plans/operator-vite-migration-2026-05-20.md`.

**Every agent must read this page before changing code in this repo.** "It works" isn't the same as "it's fast." This page captures (a) practices from apps users consider best-in-class — Linear, Notion, Vercel, Figma, Discord, Stripe — and (b) **real anti-patterns we've shipped** that have caused production slowdowns. The "What not to do" section near the bottom is **load-bearing**: it lists specific traps with measured impact and the correct alternative. If a pattern in your change matches one of those traps
entries.description: Performance — rules every agent must follow
Performance — rules every agent must follow › 1. (Historical — RSC no longer applies) Keep the JS you ship small

entries.text:
Performance — rules every agent must follow › 10. Use `useDeferredValue` and `useTransition` for slow updates
If a search input filters a 500-row table, the typing should feel snappy and the filtering can lag a few ms. Wrap the filter in `useDeferredValue(query)`; the input updates immediately, the table updates when there's an idle frame.
entries.description: Performance — rules every agent must follow › 10. Use `useDeferredValue` and `useTransition` for slow updates

entries.text:
Performance — rules every agent must follow › 11. Co-locate slow data fetches with `<Suspense>` boundaries
A page that needs both a fast and a slow data source should stream — the fast part renders, the slow part shows a skeleton. Don't block the whole page on the slowest fetch.

```tsx
<Page>
  <FastHeader />
  <Suspense fallback={<SlowChartSkeleton />}>
    <SlowChart />
  </Suspense>
</Page>
```
entries.description: Performance — rules every agent must follow › 11. Co-locate slow data fetches with `<Suspense>` boundaries

entries.text: Performance — rules every agent must follow › 12. Use the `next/image` shim (`@/lib/router-compat`) for any non-icon image, and always set explicit dimensions The `next/image` import resolves to the router-compat shim (`apps/operator/lib/router-compat`), not Next's optimizer — there is no Next image server in the SPA. Whichever ``/`` you use, **set explicit `width`/`height` (or an aspect-ratio box) and `loading="lazy"` for below-the-fold images.** A bare `` with no reserved box is a guaranteed CLS regression.
entries.description: Performance — rules every agent must follow › 12. Use the `next/image` shim (`@/lib/router-compat`) for any non-icon image, and always set explicit dimensions

entries.text:
Performance — rules every agent must follow › 13. Move heavy CPU work to a Web Worker
Anything > 50 ms of synchronous JS work blocks user input. Examples that should be in a worker, not the main thread:

* Markdown / code highlighting (we currently do this on main thread — known TODO)
* JSON-Schema → form converter for huge schemas
* Search index building
* CSV / large-payload parsing

The pattern: `new Worker(new URL('./worker.ts', import.meta.url), { type: 'module' })`.
entries.description: Performance — rules every agent must follow › 13. Move heavy CPU work to a Web Worker

entries.text:
Performance — rules every agent must follow › 14. Lazy-load above-the-fold-but-not-critical features
Plugin tabs in Config aren't visible until the user clicks Config. Tutorial dock isn't visible until invoked. Use the `dynamic` shim (`@/lib/router-compat/dynamic`) — or plain `React.lazy` + `<Suspense>` — for these:

```tsx
const ProposalsPanel = dynamic(() => import('./ProposalsPanel'), { ssr: false });
```

(The `ssr: false` option is a no-op vestige on the SPA — there is no SSR — but the shim accepts it so call sites don't have to change.) Reduces the initial chunk for the harness route; the lazy chunk loads when needed.
entries.description: Performance — rules every agent must follow › 14. Lazy-load above-the-fold-but-not-critical features

entries.text:
Performance — rules every agent must follow › 15. Prefer CSS `contain` and `content-visibility` for off-screen work
Tabs that are open but not visible (because their `data-state="inactive"`) still cost layout/paint. Tell the browser to skip them:

```css
.h-tab-content[data-state="inactive"] {
  content-visibility: auto;          /* skip rendering when off-screen */
  contain-intrinsic-size: 800px 600px; /* reserve space so scroll position doesn't jump */
}
```
entries.description: Performance — rules every agent must follow › 15. Prefer CSS `contain` and `content-visibility` for off-screen work

entries.text:
Performance — rules every agent must follow › 16. Use the local cache before the network
`useSyncQuery` (`libs/generic/sync`) is a **transport-agnostic** data hook — it works in any transport mode. On the **Zero/WebSocket** transport it gives us local-first, optimistic reads from the replica; on **polling/SSE** transports it falls back to REST. Don't bypass it with a raw `fetch` for data the active transport already serves. Spinners on data we already have locally are a UX bug.

Mutations follow the same split: `useSyncMutate(path, restFallback)` runs **optimistically through the Zero client only on the WebSocket transport** (instant local apply, then server reconcile/rollback); on polling/SSE — where there is no Zero client — it calls your `restFallback`. Pass a stable `restFallback` so the same call site is REST-correct today and becomes optimistic for free once a WS provider is mounted. (Note: no `@rocicorp/zero` dependency is declared in any `package.json` — Zero is one configured transport, not a hard dependency of the hook.)
entries.description: Performance — rules every agent must follow › 16. Use the local cache before the network

entries.text:
Performance — rules every agent must follow › 17. Pre-fetch the next likely route
If clicking the harness picker is going to navigate to a different harness, use a TanStack `<Link>` (via the router-compat shim) so its chunk can be preloaded before the click. TanStack Router preloads on intent (hover/touch) when configured; keep navigation as `<Link>` elements rather than imperative `router.push` / `navigate()`, which don't get the same preload behavior.
entries.description: Performance — rules every agent must follow › 17. Pre-fetch the next likely route

entries.text:
Performance — rules every agent must follow › 18. Cache server responses appropriately
`Cache-Control: max-age=...` on idempotent GET endpoints. SWR semantics where appropriate. Zero takes care of most of this for harness data; keep it consistent for new endpoints.
entries.description: Performance — rules every agent must follow › 18. Cache server responses appropriately

entries.text:
Performance — rules every agent must follow › 19. `preconnect` to cross-origin API hosts
For Anthropic, Cloudflare, Chatwoot, etc., add `<link rel="preconnect" href="https://api.anthropic.com">` in the SPA's root HTML (`apps/operator-vite/index.html` `<head>`, or the root layout component). Buys you 100–300 ms on the first request.
entries.description: Performance — rules every agent must follow › 19. `preconnect` to cross-origin API hosts

entries.text:
Performance — rules every agent must follow › 2. Virtualize any scrollable list of more than \~50 items
Rendering 1000 DOM nodes for a list the user only sees 20 of is wasted work. Use [`@tanstack/react-virtual`](https://tanstack.com/virtual) (already a dependency). `RichGrid` already handles this for the feature/issues lists; copy that pattern for any new long list.

**Anti-pattern**: rendering all rows and relying on `overflow: auto` to "hide" the off-screen ones. The DOM is still there, paint cost is still there.
entries.description: Performance — rules every agent must follow › 2. Virtualize any scrollable list of more than \~50 items
Performance — rules every agent must follow › 20. Avoid layout thrash (read → write → read in the same frame)

entries.text:
Performance — rules every agent must follow › 21. Use `transform: translate3d(0,0,0)` to promote heavy elements to their own layer
Only for confirmed-hot elements (a moving canvas, a live-updating chart). Don't sprinkle it everywhere — too many compositor layers tank GPU memory.
entries.description: Performance — rules every agent must follow › 21. Use `transform: translate3d(0,0,0)` to promote heavy elements to their own layer

entries.text:
Performance — rules every agent must follow › 22. Avoid box-shadows on scrolling elements
Box-shadow forces re-paint on every scroll frame. If you need a shadow on a sticky header, animate via `transform: translateZ(0)` + a static shadow, or use `filter: drop-shadow` which is sometimes composited.
entries.description: Performance — rules every agent must follow › 22. Avoid box-shadows on scrolling elements

entries.text:
Performance — rules every agent must follow › 23. Use React DevTools Profiler before claiming "it's fast"
Record an interaction. Look at:

* Number of components rendered
* Total render time per commit
* Wasted renders (rendered but result was unchanged)

Target: \< 5 ms per commit on the warm path. If it's > 16 ms, you're below 60fps.
entries.description: Performance — rules every agent must follow › 23. Use React DevTools Profiler before claiming "it's fast"

entries.text:
Performance — rules every agent must follow › 24. Run Lighthouse on the harness page weekly
Targets:

* Performance score ≥ 90
* LCP \< 2.5 s
* INP \< 200 ms
* CLS \< 0.1
* TBT \< 300 ms

If any drops, fix it before merging the next feature.
entries.description: Performance — rules every agent must follow › 24. Run Lighthouse on the harness page weekly

entries.text:
Performance — rules every agent must follow › 25. Use the Performance tab for animation issues
When an animation feels janky:

1. Open Performance tab in Chrome DevTools.
2. Record the interaction.
3. Look at the Frames row. Anything not green (i.e. frames > 16 ms) is dropped.
4. Check the Main row for tasks > 50 ms (long tasks block input).
5. Check the GPU row to confirm transforms/opacity are composited.
entries.description: Performance — rules every agent must follow › 25. Use the Performance tab for animation issues

entries.text:
Performance — rules every agent must follow › 26. Bundle analyzer before merging a dep
Run a Vite/rollup bundle visualizer (e.g. `rollup-plugin-visualizer`) against the operator-vite build and look at the route's chunk for unexpected size. Anything > 100 KB on a single route is suspect. (The old `ANALYZE=true npm run build` / `@next/bundle-analyzer` path is gone — `@next/bundle-analyzer` is not installed and the build is no longer a Next build.)
entries.description: Performance — rules every agent must follow › 26. Bundle analyzer before merging a dep
Performance — rules every agent must follow › 3. Memoize list-row components by stable key

entries.text:
Performance — rules every agent must follow › 4. Animate only `transform` and `opacity` (and `filter` sparingly)
These are GPU-composited; the browser handles them off the main thread. Animating `width`, `height`, `top`, `left`, `padding`, `margin`, `font-size`, or any size-affecting property forces layout + paint on every frame and torches your frame rate.

```tsx
// Wrong — animates layout
<div style={{ transition: 'width 200ms', width: open ? 320 : 0 }} />

// Right — animates the GPU-composited transform
<div style={{ transition: 'transform 200ms', transform: open ? 'translateX(0)' : 'translateX(-100%)' }} />
```

If you absolutely need to animate size, use `motion`'s `layout` prop, which uses FLIP under the hood (compute the start/end rects, animate the *transform* between them — not the size).
entries.description: Performance — rules every agent must follow › 4. Animate only `transform` and `opacity` (and `filter` sparingly)

entries.text:
Performance — rules every agent must follow › 5. Never animate inside a `useEffect` that depends on a frequently-changing value
Animation effects with unstable deps trigger re-render storms. If you find yourself writing `useEffect(() => { setTimeout(...) }, [openCount])`, you're about to fire one timeout per render. Use `motion`'s declarative API (`animate` prop) instead.
entries.description: Performance — rules every agent must follow › 5. Never animate inside a `useEffect` that depends on a frequently-changing value

entries.text:
Performance — rules every agent must follow › 6. Keep server-only code out of the browser bundle
> **Reframed for the SPA.** The old wording ("`'use client'` files cannot import server-only code") was a Next.js RSC boundary rule. `'use client'` no longer means anything, and `app/api/` is gone — server endpoints live in the Hono host (`apps/operator/bin/hono-host.ts` + `lib/endpoint-route/`). The underlying hazard is still real on the SPA.

Everything in the operator-vite client tree gets bundled and shipped to the browser. Don't import Postgres clients, credential loaders, `node:fs`, or other host-only modules into a component or a file the client tree reaches — it bloats the bundle and can leak secrets. Keep client/server-only types and functions in separate files and cross the boundary via the Hono API (`fetch`/`useSyncQuery`), not a direct import.
entries.description: Performance — rules every agent must follow › 6. Keep server-only code out of the browser bundle

entries.text:
Performance — rules every agent must follow › 7. Don't add a dependency you'll only use once
A 50 KB lib for a single gradient effect is not a fair trade. Inspect the route's chunk with a Vite/rollup bundle visualizer (e.g. `rollup-plugin-visualizer` against the operator-vite build) before adding any dep over \~5 KB gzip and prove it's worth the cost. (The old `ANALYZE=true npm run build` / `@next/bundle-analyzer` flow is gone with Next — `@next/bundle-analyzer` is not installed, and `apps/operator`'s `build` script just runs the operator-docs Starlight build then the operator-vite Vite build.) If the team has a stalwart utility (e.g. `@formkit/auto-animate` / `motion` for animations, `lucide-react` for icons), use it instead of pulling a parallel one.
entries.description: Performance — rules every agent must follow › 7. Don't add a dependency you'll only use once

entries.text:
Performance — rules every agent must follow › 8. Always test under "Slow 4G" + "4× CPU throttle" in DevTools
What feels fine on your M3 Pro is unusable on a $300 Chromebook. The harness page is an internal tool — most of the audience is on developer hardware — but the muscle memory matters because it surfaces real perf regressions you'd otherwise miss.
entries.description: Performance — rules every agent must follow › 8. Always test under "Slow 4G" + "4× CPU throttle" in DevTools

entries.text:
Performance — rules every agent must follow › 9. `React.memo`, `useMemo`, `useCallback` — only when measured to help
Premature memoization adds maintenance cost and rarely helps. The exceptions:

* Components in a virtualized list (always memo).
* Components that pass props down a deep tree (memo + stable refs).
* Computations > 1 ms (useMemo). Profile first.

For everything else, React's reconciler is fast enough. Don't `useCallback` every event handler "just in case."
entries.description: Performance — rules every agent must follow › 9. `React.memo`, `useMemo`, `useCallback` — only when measured to help
Performance — rules every agent must follow › A1. Don't `await` filesystem operations in a serial `for` loop

entries.text:
Performance — rules every agent must follow › A10. Radix Dialog focus-trap leaks `pointer-events` — guard with `!important`
Radix's Dialog/cmdk/Modal mount sets two inline styles for focus-scope
locking, and **doesn't always remove them on close**:

1. **`pointer-events: auto` on `Dialog.Content`** — meant to override an
   ancestor's `pointer-events: none`. Leftover after close → the closed
   dialog intercepts every click on the page (`<html> intercepts pointer
   events` is the verdict-cli signature).
2. **`pointer-events: none` on `<body>`** — meant to focus-trap users
   inside the dialog. Leftover after close → the *entire page* is
   unclickable until full reload; appears to the user as "totally frozen."

Both have the same fix: `!important` on the override CSS so the
leftover inline style cannot win. We've hit each one separately:

```css
/* Override the dialog-element leak (first incident: .h-cmd) */
.h-cmd[data-state="closed"] { pointer-events: none !important; }

/* Override the body-element leak (second incident, second freeze) */
html, body { pointer-events: auto !important; }
```

Dialogs still trap focus correctly via `aria-modal` / `aria-hidden` on
their portal overlays, so neither override weakens modal UX — they just
unfreeze the page when the lock leaks.
entries.description: Performance — rules every agent must follow › A10. Radix Dialog focus-trap leaks `pointer-events` — guard with `!important`

entries.text:
Performance — rules every agent must follow › A11. Don't fan out from N `useEffect` hooks fetching the same endpoint
The audit captured `/checkpoints` ×2, `/reviews` ×3, `/agents` ×2 in a single dashboard load — one fetch per `useEffect`-mount, no dedup. In the audited environment each request also paid a 1-2s baseline overhead (then under Next.js dev; that named cause is stale now that the API is served by the Hono host on `:3070`). Cumulative: 30-60s of wasted server work on page load. The duplicate-fetch problem is runtime-independent — fan-out from N effects to the same endpoint is wasteful on any backend.

**Pattern to use**: one `useSyncQuery` in a parent component, propagate via context or props. Or migrate to Zero (already wired for many of these tables).
entries.description: Performance — rules every agent must follow › A11. Don't fan out from N `useEffect` hooks fetching the same endpoint

entries.text:
Performance — rules every agent must follow › A12. (Historical — Next removed) Don't carry flag-style config across major framework upgrades
> **No longer applies to this stack.** Next.js has been removed, so there is no `next.config` and no `experimental.*` flags to audit. Kept as a general lesson.

The original incident: `experimental.turbopackFileSystemCacheForDev: false` was set for a Next 15 Turbopack bug; Next 16 didn't recognize it (`⨯ turbopackFileSystemCacheForDev` at boot). The transferable rule: when you bump any build tool across a major version (now Vite/rollup rather than Next), re-audit flag-style config you set to work around an old version's bug and drop anything the new version warns about.
entries.description: Performance — rules every agent must follow › A12. (Historical — Next removed) Don't carry flag-style config across major framework upgrades

entries.text:
Performance — rules every agent must follow › A13. Don't expose unbounded query tools to AI agents
Tools like `query(sql: string)` or `getUsers(ids: int[])` invite N+1 disasters and unbounded cost. Per [the agent-vs-API analysis](https://...), bounded intent-level tools (`getUserActivityForFeature(featureId)`) are strictly better: cost is provable, and agent reasoning about what to do becomes shorter.
entries.description: Performance — rules every agent must follow › A13. Don't expose unbounded query tools to AI agents

entries.text:
Performance — rules every agent must follow › A14. Don't return data without `_meta` annotations on agent-facing endpoints
If an agent calls your endpoint, include observable cost in the response so it can self-correct:

```json
{
  "data": [...],
  "_meta": {
    "tookMs": 47,
    "cacheHit": true,
    "dbRows": 12,
    "hint": "this is the 14th call to /users/<id>/orders this turn — consider /users/orders?ids="
  }
}
```

The `hint` field is the high-leverage one — server has cross-call context the agent doesn't.
entries.description: Performance — rules every agent must follow › A14. Don't return data without `_meta` annotations on agent-facing endpoints
Performance — rules every agent must follow › A15. Don't read the same JSON file repeatedly within one request

entries.text:
Performance — rules every agent must follow › A16. Don't enforce a minimum-visible debounce on a progress indicator
The route progress bar (`@bprogress/react`, driven by `RouteProgressProvider`)
shows a loading bar during route changes. Its timing constants now live in
`apps/operator/app/_components/routePending.ts`:

```ts
// ❌ Wrong — measured: every nav showed the bar 3s minimum, regardless of
//             how fast the route actually loaded. With the old Next.js dev
//             cold-compile (~3s), perceived nav was 6+s.
const ROUTE_PROGRESS_MIN_VISIBLE_MS = 3000;
const ROUTE_PROGRESS_FALLBACK_MS    = 8000;

// ✅ Right — bar reflects actual pending state; gone the instant the
//            route lands. Cuts ~3s off every navigation.
const ROUTE_PROGRESS_FALLBACK_MS = 1500;            // matches routePending.ts
const ROUTE_PROGRESS_GENERIC_MIN_VISIBLE_MS = 0;    // generic routes: no debounce
const ROUTE_PROGRESS_HARNESS_MIN_VISIBLE_MS = 360;  // /harness/* keeps a deliberate floor
```

**Per-target min-visible (the one intentional exception):** the min-visible
debounce is **0ms for generic routes** but **360ms specifically for
`/harness/*`** navigations; `routePendingMinVisibleMs()` picks per target.
So the "always 0" rule below holds for ordinary navigation, with the harness
floor as the documented, deliberate carve-out.

A "minimum-visible debounce" on a progress bar conflates two things:

* **Anti-flicker** (the bar shouldn't appear and disappear within a
  single frame for instant routes) — `bprogress` already debounces
  sub-frame transitions internally, so this isn't the caller's job.
* **Padding the perceived load time** (showing the bar longer than
  reality so the user "feels" something happened) — this is the
  *opposite* of useful. The bar lingering after content lands looks
  like a stuck navigation.

Always let the progress indicator reflect actual state. If you find
yourself adding `MIN_VISIBLE_MS` to a polling/loading UI element,
that's the sme
entries.description: Performance — rules every agent must follow › A16. Don't enforce a minimum-visible debounce on a progress indicator
Performance — rules every agent must follow › A17. Don't fetch the same per-slug data N times in a Promise.all that varies by sub-key
Performance — rules every agent must follow › A18. Don't pin per-process caches to module scope without a globalThis papercup
Performance — rules every agent must follow › A19. Don't shell-walk `/proc` per request without a cache
Performance — rules every agent must follow › A2. Don't open one Postgres pool per slug in a serial loop

entries.text:
Performance — rules every agent must follow › A3. Don't introduce a heavy and a lite endpoint and have hot paths use the heavy one
`/api/harness/projects` does N×PG-pool-open enrichment per project; `/api/harness/projects/lite` returns the same shape minus the enrichment. Audit found **5+ seconds per call**, hit on every harness page load (including SSR) and every 30-second autoloop tick. A `/lite` endpoint is a smell signal: anywhere a callsite uses the heavy version "just in case," it likely doesn't need the enrichment. Default to lite, justify each upgrade.
entries.description: Performance — rules every agent must follow › A3. Don't introduce a heavy and a lite endpoint and have hot paths use the heavy one
