entries.text:
Shared pots — a user's guide
import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

A **pot** is a project several people can work on together. Each person runs
their own Papercusp; the pot's shared state — work items, plans, conversations,
contributor list, file claims, presence — **syncs peer-to-peer** between
everyone's machines and shows up in each person's local app. There is no central
server: the pot is identified by a cryptographic keypair, and every machine
running it is an equal peer.

This page walks a user through the full lifecycle: **create → share → discover →
join → collaborate → moderate → leave**. For the security/trust reasoning behind
it (why GitHub is the authority of record, what's advisory, the threat model) see
[Shared harnesses — trust model](/security/shared-harnesses/). For how code
itself round-trips through git, see [Pot git-sync](/system/pot-git-sync/).

**Pot** = the project (keypair-identified). **Swarm** = one machine running the
pot (yours is a Swarm; each collaborator's is another). **Member** = a harness
inside the pot. A pot federates across its Swarms — each Swarm is a peer.
Identity is anchored to your **GitHub account**.

The **owner** is whoever holds the pot's private key (the Swarm that created
it). Owner-only actions — approving joiners, banning, takedowns, editing the
listing — only work from the owning Swarm. A person who **joined** a pot holds a
*viewer* of it: they federate its content and collaborate, but can't make owner
decisions. Where an action is owner-only, it's called out below.
entries.description: Shared pots — a user's guide

entries.text:
Shared pots — a user's guide › 1. Create a pot
There are two ways to start a pot.
entries.description: Shared pots — a user's guide › 1. Create a pot

entries.text:
Shared pots — a user's guide › 2. Share it — public, invite, or private
Sharing happens at the **pot** level (per-harness sharing was retired). You
publish a pot to the peer-to-peer **directory** so others can find and join it.

* **Tool:** `discovery:set_pot` — args: `hiveId`, `title`, `description`,
  `visibility` (default `public`), `inviteSecret` (required for `invite`),
  `memberLinks` (one-click join links — see step 4). It's an idempotent
  create-or-edit: call it again with the same `hiveId` to edit the title /
  description / visibility.

The three visibilities mean exactly:

| Visibility  | What it does                                                                                               | Who can find it                                              |
| ----------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **public**  | Announced to the **global directory topic**.                                                               | Anyone browsing the directory ([step 3](#3-discover-a-pot)). |
| **invite**  | Announced only on an **invite-scoped topic** derived from a secret you share. **Requires `inviteSecret`.** | Only people you give the invite secret to.                   |
| **private** | **Never announced.** Stays local-only.                                                                     | No one — it doesn't federate on the network at all.          |

A `private` (or never-published) pot doesn't announce on the DHT and **doesn't
federate** — the peer-to-peer machinery is a dormant, zero-risk path until you
publish it `public` or `invite`. Setting a published pot back to `private`
**withdraws** it: it stops being re-announced, and other peers age the listing out
on a TTL. Only a *shared* (public/invite) pot actually syncs to other machines.

A published pot can additionally broadcast a **live status beacon** (a
entries.description: Shared pots — a user's guide › 2. Share it — public, invite, or private

entries.text:
Shared pots — a user's guide › 3. Discover a pot
To find pots other people have shared:

* **Tool:** `discovery:pots` — browse the directory of pots this peer has seen
  announced (title · description · owner · member harnesses). In the desktop app
  this is the **Pots / Network** board.
* The directory is **best-effort gossip** — it's how you *find* a pot, not how
  you're admitted to it. Joining still runs the full admission/attestation flow
  (step 4), so a listing you can see isn't a pot you're automatically in.
* An **invite** pot won't appear in the global directory; you reach it through
  the invite secret / link the owner shared with you.
entries.description: Shared pots — a user's guide › 3. Discover a pot

entries.text:
Shared pots — a user's guide › 4. Join a pot
Joining a pot makes you a peer: you start federating its content, get a
local view of it, and can collaborate.

**How you join** (this is a desktop / link action, not an agent command):

* **One-click join link** — `papercusp://harness?topic=…&github=…&repo_id=…`.
  The owner's listing carries these (`memberLinks`); pasting one into the app (or
  clicking it) joins you to that exact pot. The link pins the swarm **topic** so
  you land on the owner's pot, the GitHub `owner/repo`, and the immutable numeric
  `repo_id`.
* **From the directory** — pick a pot in the Pots / Network board and join it.
* **An invite pot** is joined with the owner's **invite link / secret**
  (`papercusp://pot?pubkey=…&secret=…`). This join is **honest**: if the pot
  hasn't actually announced yet (owner offline, withdrawn, or wrong secret) you're
  told it didn't connect and left subscribed — never handed a fake "joined."

Under the hood, joining wires up four things per member: a swarm federation
handle, a git-sync routine, presence rows, and registry entries (a `remote_hive`
view + the member harnesses). If no peer is reachable the moment you join, the
join lands in a `phase_0_pending` state — that's **not stuck**: it re-federates on
your next boot (or as soon as a peer comes online), so you don't need to redo it.
entries.description: Shared pots — a user's guide › 4. Join a pot

entries.text:
Shared pots — a user's guide › 5. What syncs between members
Once you're a member, the pot's shared state federates over **one topic derived
from the pot's keypair** — all the pot's harnesses ride that one topic.

**Federates (advisory peer-synced state, projected into each member's local DB):**

* Work items / features (the queue + per-item status + claims)
* Plans and plan decisions
* Conversations, threads, and coordination messages
* Pot settings, the contributor list, presence (who's online), and the member
  list

**Does *not* federate:**

* **Pull-request / merge state.** PR status is read live from GitHub per machine,
  not synced — GitHub is the authority for "did it merge."
* Secrets, `.env`, credentials — never leave your machine.

Peer-synced rows are a fast, shared *cache* for coordination and display. Anything
that actually matters — whether code merged, who has write access, whether
something shipped — is **re-derived from GitHub at the point of action**, never
trusted from a peer. That's the core of the
[trust model](/security/shared-harnesses/); it's why the synced state can be
freely shared without it being a security authority.
entries.description: Shared pots — a user's guide › 5. What syncs between members

entries.text:
Shared pots — a user's guide › 6. Collaborate
Working together in a pot uses the same surfaces as solo work — they're just now
shared across Swarms:

* **Shared work items + plans.** Create, claim, and complete work items; they
  show up for every member. Plan items and decisions federate too.
* **File claims.** When agents on different machines might touch the same files,
  the pot serializes contended claims through a single **lock authority** (a
  deterministic function of who's online), so two machines don't stomp each
  other. Git-sync + merge resolution is the data-safety backstop underneath.
* **Coordination.** Messages, conversations, and presence federate, so you can
  see who's active and talk in-thread across machines. **Real-time coordination
  (wakes/receipts/events) crosses machines for POT-SCOPED sends**: a pot-scoped
  `coord:send {wake:'required'}` re-invokes the remote recipient on arrival and
  acks with a delivery receipt (`coord:receipt:<msg_id>` — `events:await` it);
  `events:emit {scope:'pot'}` fires waiters on every machine. Un-scoped sends
  stay machine-local — the send result's `federated:` field tells you which you
  got. Cross-machine wakes are rate-budgeted per sender device.
entries.description: Shared pots — a user's guide › 6. Collaborate

entries.text:
Shared pots — a user's guide › 7. Moderate
Moderation is **owner-gated** and rides the owner-signed pot policy. The flow:

1. **Report** — a member files a report against a piece of content or another
   member with **`pot:report`**. (This only works if the owner enabled member
   reporting in the pot policy.)
2. **Review** — the owner reads the queue with **`pot:moderation_queue`**.
3. **Act** — the owner can:
   * **`pot:takedown`** — hide a piece of content across the pot (adds it to the
     owner-signed takedown list; honest peers honor it as a tombstone). Pass
     `restore: true` to un-hide.
   * **`pot:ban_member`** — ban a repeat abuser by their numeric GitHub id. This
     **denies re-join in every mode** and revokes their devices. (Pass
     `revoke: false` to record the ban without revoking; `unban: true` to lift
     it.) See the read-access note in step 8.
4. **Resolve** — the owner closes the report with **`pot:moderation_resolve`**
   (`actioned` or `dismissed`).

All of these require the owning Swarm.
entries.description: Shared pots — a user's guide › 7. Moderate

entries.text:
Shared pots — a user's guide › Adding more members later
A pot starts with just its home (and, from a repo, one member harness). To bring
another existing harness into the pot, use `pot:add-member` (sets the harness's
`hive_slug` so its work federates within the pot). Until something sets that
pointer, a pot has only its home and no members.
entries.description: Shared pots — a user's guide › Adding more members later

entries.text:
Shared pots — a user's guide › Asking another pot for help (cross-pot)
Pots are sovereign, but one pot can send a question or a work request to
**another** pot:

* **`pot:ask`** — a question the other pot owns the answer to.
* **`pot:request_work`** — ask another pot to do something in its domain (it
  becomes a work item their side prioritizes).
* Both are **gated by an owner grant** (`pot:cross_grant`, directed `in`/`out` —
  default-deny, quota-capped). The answer arrives asynchronously; track it with
  `pot:asks`.
entries.description: Shared pots — a user's guide › Asking another pot for help (cross-pot)

Shared pots — a user's guide › At a glance — the tool map
| Step                | What you want               | Tool(s)                                                         |
| ------------------- | --------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Create              | New pot                     | `pot:create`                                                    |
| Create              | From a GitHub repo          | `pot:create_from_repo`                                          |
| Create              | Add an existing harness     | `pot:add-member`                                                |
| Share               | Publish / set visibility    | `discovery:set_pot`                                             |
| Share               | Live status beacon (opt-in) | `pot:beacon_consent`                                            |
| Discover            | Browse shared pots          | `discovery:pots`                                                |
| Join                | Find a pot's status         | `pot:get` / `pot:list`                                          |
| Join (owner)        | Review join queue           | `pot:membership_pending`                                        |
| Join (owner)        | Approve / deny              | `pot:membership_decide`                                         |
| Collaborate         | Ask another pot             | `pot:ask` / `pot:request_work` / `pot:asks`                     |
| Collaborate (owner) | Cross-pot grant             | `pot:cross_grant`                                               |
| Moderate            | Report content / member     | `pot:report`                                                    |
| Moderate (owner)    | Review reports              | `pot:moderation_queue`                                          |
| Moderate (owner)    | Hide content                | `pot:takedown`                                                  |
| Moderate (owner)
entries.description: Shared pots — a user's guide › At a glance — the tool map

entries.text:
Shared pots — a user's guide › Being removed (ban / revocation)
When an owner bans or revokes you:

* The **write block and re-join denial are immediate** — your devices are dropped
  from federation and you can't re-join.
* **Read access cut-off ships with re-key (not yet live).** A true read cut-off —
  where removed devices can no longer *decrypt* new content — is the re-key feature
  (`shared-pot-rekey-2026-06-19`): on removal the pot advances a key **epoch** and
  re-wraps the new key to the *remaining* members only, so the removed device has no
  key for epoch N+1. That work is **implementation-complete but flag-dark**
  (`papercusp-pot-rekey`), so until the owner enables it, `ban_member`'s
  `revoke.live` is `false` and removal is a **write-block + re-join-deny only** —
  content already shared with the member stays readable to them.

So **today** removal = no more writes / no re-join; the read cut-off arrives when
re-key is enabled.

Related device-level tools: **`substrate:revoke_self_device`** (revoke one of
*your own* lost/rotated devices) and **`substrate:revoke_contributor`** (owner
revokes another contributor, per-harness or per-pot).
entries.description: Shared pots — a user's guide › Being removed (ban / revocation)

entries.text:
Shared pots — a user's guide › Cross-member browse
Each member harness keeps its own content keyed under its own slug, so **your own
views are unchanged** — you see your harness's work exactly as before. What
membership adds is **cross-member browse**: a member can see the *other* members'
federated content within the pot (their work items, plans, conversations), not
just their own. This is the collaboration payoff — one shared project surface
across everyone's harnesses.
entries.description: Shared pots — a user's guide › Cross-member browse

entries.text:
Shared pots — a user's guide › From a GitHub repository
If your project already lives on GitHub, create the pot straight from the repo
URL. This is the fastest path and the one most public releases use.

* **Tool:** `pot:create_from_repo` — args: `githubUrl` (required), `slug`,
  `runTests` (default **false** — opt in to execute the repo's test command),
  `shallow`, `intoHive` (add the repo to an *existing* pot instead of starting a
  new one).
* What it does, in order: **repo → pot lookup first** (if a pot already exists
  for that repo you get a **join offer** back, with zero side effects — so two
  people can't accidentally fork the same project into two pots), then clone,
  detect the blueprint, stand up the pot home + the first member harness, stamp
  the upstream GitHub coordinates, and **auto-publish** a directory listing.
* **Visibility is derived from the repo:** a **public** GitHub repo → a
  discoverable (`public`) pot listing; a **private** repo → a **Private**
  (invite-only, hidden) pot. You can change this afterward (step 2).

`pot:create_from_repo` defaults `runTests: false` on purpose — running a
pasted repo's test command executes that repo's code on your machine. Leave it
off unless you trust the source, and verify on a clone if you need to.
entries.description: Shared pots — a user's guide › From a GitHub repository

entries.text:
Shared pots — a user's guide › From scratch (a fresh project)
Creating a pot provisions a **home harness** that runs the pot blueprint and
stamps it as a pot. The default blueprint is the **coding** pot; pass a
different one for non-coding work (e.g. a research/`work` pot).

* **Tool:** `pot:create` — args: `slug` (required), `blueprintId` (default the
  coding pot; `work` for a non-coding pot), `kickoff`, `knowledgePack`,
  `wakeInSeconds`, `deployment` (default `local`).
* It's **root-only** — a pot is a top-level peer, never created from inside
  another agent. Running it in the cloud is a separate step
  (`deploy:pot`); by default the pot runs locally on your machine.

A brand-new pot is **local-only** until you publish it (step 2) — it doesn't
announce itself or federate to anyone yet.
entries.description: Shared pots — a user's guide › From scratch (a fresh project)

entries.text:
Shared pots — a user's guide › Leaving a pot you joined
* **Tool:** `pot:leave` (requires `confirm: true`). It's the inverse of joining:
  it stops federating, deletes the git-sync routine, drops your presence, and
  deregisters the pot view + its member clones. Your cloned files are **kept by
  default** (so you can re-join later); pass `deleteClones: true` to also remove
  them from disk.
* On leave, your app publishes a presence **tombstone** so connected peers drop
  your "online" row promptly instead of waiting it out.

`pot:leave` is for a pot you **joined**. **`pot:dissolve`** is the owner
tearing down a **local pot they own** (destructive, `confirm: true`) — it does
nothing useful for a joiner. Don't reach for dissolve to leave.
entries.description: Shared pots — a user's guide › Leaving a pot you joined

entries.text:
Shared pots — a user's guide › Open vs approval — what happens when you join
Whether you're admitted immediately depends on the owner's **membership mode**
(an owner-signed policy on the pot). The default, and a pot with no policy, is
**open**.

| Mode               | What happens to a joiner                                                                       |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **open** (default) | Admitted immediately.                                                                          |
| **approval**       | Lands **pending** — held until the owner approves. You federate once approved.                 |
| **allowlist**      | Admitted only if your GitHub **login** is on the owner's pre-approved list; otherwise refused. |

A **banned** GitHub account is refused in **every** mode (the ban is keyed to your
stable numeric GitHub id, so renaming your login can't slip you back in). If a
peer ever sees a membership mode it doesn't recognize, it fails **safe** to
*pending* (owner decides) rather than auto-admitting.
entries.description: Shared pots — a user's guide › Open vs approval — what happens when you join

entries.text:
Shared pots — a user's guide › See also
* [Shared harnesses — trust model](/security/shared-harnesses/) — why GitHub is
  the authority of record, what's advisory vs decision-bearing, the threat model.
* [Pot git-sync](/system/pot-git-sync/) — how code commits/pushes round-trip.
* [Pot-scoped federation](/agent-insights/pot-scoped-federation/) — the
  engineering detail of how content federates at pot scope.
* [Shared-pot join/leave lifecycle](/agent-insights/shared-pot-join-leave-lifecycle/)
  — what self-heals, what to call, what ages out.
entries.description: Shared pots — a user's guide › See also

entries.text:
Shared pots — a user's guide › The approval queue (owner-side)
When the pot is in **approval** mode, the owner manages the queue:

* **`pot:membership_pending`** — list the pending join requests (the review
  queue). Read-only.
* **`pot:membership_decide`** — `approve` (trust-admits the joiner and their
  captured devices, and federates the decision back) or `deny` (never admitted).
  You can clear several at once. **Owner-only** — it requires the owning Swarm
  (the one holding the pot key); a viewer on another Swarm can't decide.
entries.description: Shared pots — a user's guide › The approval queue (owner-side)

entries.text:
Shared pots — a user's guide › Trusting a collaborator's work to run automatically
Separately from membership, you keep a **local** trust list: a verified work item
authored by a GitHub user you trust may run on your machine without per-item
screening.

* **`trust:add`** / **`trust:list`** / **`trust:remove`** — owner-scoped, local
  to your install, never federated. Adding someone is a security grant (their
  *verified* remote work auto-runs); remove it to put their work back behind
  per-item review.
entries.description: Shared pots — a user's guide › Trusting a collaborator's work to run automatically

# Active-mode proactive responses — 2026-05-14 (v2)

The operator should be active in active mode — pipe up when there's work to surface, auto-progress multi-step user requests, and never produce dead-end silence. Today it only speaks when the user does. This plan adds **brain-driven** proactivity: the brain itself signals at end-of-turn whether it has more to do, has options to surface, or needs to scan-and-suggest.

v2 supersedes v1 (timer-based polling). v1 was wrong — the brain knows when it has more to do; the runtime should not. New shape: three end-of-turn outcomes encoded as brain signals; the runtime just reads the signal and reacts.

Resolves V8 from `voice-aware-cards-2026-05-14.md`. Builds on the silence-nudge work (V7-A) that just shipped — the reactive side is now deterministic, freeing this work to focus purely on proactive behavior.

---

## A. Goals & non-goals

### Goals
1. **Three end-of-turn outcomes** the brain explicitly produces: continue, await-with-known-options, terminal. Runtime reads the signal and acts.
2. **Multi-step user-asked work auto-progresses** with visible narration ("Did X, now doing Y") via a new `<continue/>` tag.
3. **Active-mode terminal turns auto-scan**: after a brain turn that doesn't continue

## Now
**State:** Root cause identified and the canonical fix is landed. The compaction guidance (apps/operator/prompts/papercusp-compaction.base.md → generated ~/.papercusp/compaction-strategy.md + operator converse-brain summarizer) taught HOW to write the summary (content, provenance, flush) but never WHEN to pull the trigger. So an agent at a clean stopping point with high context and a LAPSED auto-loop ended its turn expecting a re-wake that never came, and silently stalled until the owner prodded it. P-001 (add a "WHEN to compact" section to the canonical source) is DONE and validated via `tsx scripts/gen-compaction.ts --check` (renders clean, 10491 chars). Remaining: propagate to running sessions (reinstall the deployed projection) and reinforce at the persona + harness layers.

**Next:** Reinstall/regenerate the deployed compaction projection (P-002) so the new section reaches live sessions, not just the source tree.

## Background
The failure mode, precisely: ending a turn is safe ONLY when a re-wake is GUARANTEED — a VERIFIED armed engine loop (`loop:status.active === true` in this session), or a present interactive owner who speaks next. Otherwise, at a clean stopping point past the soft-limit nudge, the correct action is `session:request-compaction { autoContinue: true, focus }` (flush first, then self-compact, then resume on fresh context) — never wait for the FORCE-compaction watchdog to seize the turn mid-thought. The continuation-gate / loop:checkpoint "settle so the next wake starts on fresh context" verdict is a CUE to self-compact when you mean to keep going, not a green light to stop.

# Agent turn-error robustness + rate-limit awareness

## Problem

Our agents trip the provider rate limit and then handle the failure poorly — both
in the harness pipeline and in the judge/gym framework, **even when run solo**.

Two root causes, confirmed against the live code + Anthropic's published limits:

1. **No rate-limit *awareness* (we burst past the ceiling).** The provider uses a
   **token-bucket** over **RPM / input-TPM / output-TPM**, *per model class*, and even
   a short burst over the per-second-equivalent trips a `429` (plus a separate
   *acceleration* limit on sharp usage spikes). We fire requests with **no shared
   budget**: the DBOS pipeline spawns several role agents at once, the gym runs
   multiple pipelines concurrently, and the frozen judge emits ~32k thinking tokens
   (output-TPM heavy) — all uncoordinated. So we trip the limit ourselves.

2. **No rate-limit *robustness* (we mishandle the 429s we do get).**
   - `meridianAgentChat` retries 429 with **blind exponential backoff (2→60s, 8 tries)**
     — it **ignores the `retry-after` header and the `anthropic-ratelimit-*-reset`
     headers** the server sends, then **gives up after ~3 min** and yields an `error`.
   - The **CLI backends (claude/omp/codex)** have no unified 429 detection — a
     rate-limited spawn surfaces only as an exit code / stderr text, classified by no
     one.
   - DBOS steps use generic `maxAttempts:3, backoffRate:2` retri

## Background

The cold-carry system — carry docs, `loop:checkpoint` walls/checks rows, `facts` fold, `session:request-compaction` carry-respawn (P-022), orient recovery — is exercised exclusively on the Linux dev tower today. Release builds are the Tauri desktop app + sidecar psu sessions on Linux, Windows, and macOS; every cold wake there depends on client-side mechanics that are platform-coupled. Failure classes with precedent in THIS codebase:

- **Credential survival across carry-respawn (macOS)**: the CLI relaunch lands logged OUT on macOS unless the `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` injection path works (keychain is keyed per `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` suffix — psu credential-inheritance incident 2026-06-27). A logged-out respawn is a dead cold wake.
- **Symlink/realpath divergence**: the 2026-07-19 deploy false-rollback (papercusp-release symlink vs realpath containment) is exactly the class Windows junctions / missing symlink privilege will produce in carry paths.
- **Round-trip encoding**: carry-note rows parse on exact anchors (`- ✓|? claim — re-check: … (since ISO)`). CRLF line splitting, cp1252 console mangling of `✓`/`—`, and macOS NFD filename normalization can all silently drop rows — a dropped walls/checks row is a dissolved commitment.
- **Respawn argv/env rebuild**: a Claude re-exec rebuilds argv WITHOUT launch flags (observed on this dev box 2026-07-18 — session recovered with lost system prompt).

## Now

## Background
session:request-compaction → the psu-pty host injects a `carry-respawn` → the busy-gate waits for a 1.5s idle window, then kills+respawns the child on the deterministic carry doc. Bug (WI-5623): the gate gave up after one retry (~9min) and dropped; autonomous/headless drain members (2-min loops, ~continuously busy) never present that window in the deadline → 0/22 delivered → sessions run to the hard wall. **State:** Plan written. Ready for Phase 1 implementation.

**Next:** Begin Phase 1 — branch model + worktree provisioning (P-001 through P-006).

The dogfood-v5 arc designed collaboration around per-user worktrees: each contributor gets
their own `user/<github_user_id>` branch and worktree. This plan replaces that model with
one that puts plans — not users — as the organizing unit of isolation.

The shift is motivated by the move to plans as the central harness UX: if plans are what

title: Alert on new critical-severity work items in papercusp
slug: critical-severity-alert-2026-07-06
status: draft
created: 2026-07-06
updated: 2026-07-06
---

## Now

**State:** Recurring job (scheduled + armed, fires every 15 minutes — matches the existing improvement-watchdog cadence and avoids the per-5-min cost warning). No built-in event key fires on work-item creation filtered by severity, so this is a poll+diff, not watch:create. Each run: read fact critical-alert-last-check:papercusp -> query bug/change/task items in papercusp, non-terminal, severity=critical, createdAt after the watermark -> if any, coord:send {to:['human'], wake:true} listing them -> advance the fact to now regardless.

**Next:** The run agent executes the steps above each fire; nothing to claim between runs.

## Background
Owner ask (verbatim, 2026-07-06): "I want to be alerted whenever a new critical-severity work item appears in this harness." Baseline check (2026-07-06T22:15Z): zero open bug/change/task items in papercusp currently carry severity=critical (highest open severities seen were major/minor), so the fact was seeded to "now" rather than backfilling an alert for pre-existing items.

## Decisions
- D-001: No existing event-driven mechanism fires on work-item creation filtered by severity — a 5-min poll+diff was built instead of forcing `watch:create` onto a nonexistent pattern. If/when the platform grows a `work_item:created` event key, this plan should switch to `watch:create` on it and drop the poll.
- D-002: Alert delivery = `coord:send { to:['human'] }`, matching the daily-digest plan's precedent (no email transport in this workspace).

# Cross-machine coordination parity + comms trust lattice

**Owner directive (2026-07-01):** make cross-machine coordination in a shared hive
work the same as local communication as much as possible, for BOTH the queen-bee

---
title: Cut the tool_invocations analytical load (19.34% of all DB time) with caching, scoping and an index — explicitly NOT a columnar migration
slug: cut-tool-invocations-analytical-load-2026-07-26
status: draft
created: 2026-07-27
updated: 2026-07-27
---

## Now

**State:** DRAFT, AWAITING OWNER REVIEW. Nothing implemented. Filed from EI-18754139434413158, which measured `tool_invocations` queries at **200.6 hours / 19.34% of ALL database time / 4,166,243 calls**. Every number in this plan is measured on the live DB (pg_stat_statements + pg_stat_user_tables + EXPLAIN ANALYZE), not estimated. The columnar/Arrow route is deliberately excluded per D-001.

**Next:** Owner reviews. The one item needing an owner decision before it can be built is P-003 (D-002 — whether these metrics are global or per-workspace), because it changes reported numbers.

## The measured problem

Three ordinary defects, stacked. None is a storage-format problem.

1. **A ~40s tick recomputes 7- and 14-day windows from scratch.** `system_health_ticks` = 512,972 rows / 14 days / 20 workspaces. Per workspace the cadence is **41.5s** (range 35.5-43.6s) — that is a NORMAL health-tick cadence and is *not* itself the bug. The bug is that each tick runs four UNCACHED aggregates over a 7-day or 14-day window, through a raw `sql.unsafe` passthrough in `system-health/compute.ts` (~line 2078).

2. **The same global answer is computed 20x.** None of the four reader modules mentions `workspace_id` even once, so all 20 workspaces compute an identical global result every cycle.

3. **The scan is unindexed on its most selective predicate.** `tool_name='code:run'` matches 5,449 of 1,315,398 rows (**0.414%**) and there is no index leading with `tool_name`. Postgres therefore parallel-seq-scans the whole 1,483 MB heap.

Per-query cost (pg_stat_statements):

| reader | calls

# Drizzle migration — post-migration unlocks plan

The Phase 0–4 migration (see `MIGRATION-COMPLETE.md`) shipped the substrate.
This plan turns that substrate into application-visible wins. The order is
load-bearing: each item compounds on the previous one.

The core insight: **Drizzle schema isn't just guardrails — it's a substrate**.
Anywhere the codebase has hand-written JSON Schema / form / admin page /
fixture / MCP tool input / card payload duplicating DB shape, Drizzle
collapses them to one source.

---

## How drizzle types help our MCP/HTTP wrapper

The MCP tool wrapper (`packages/agent-mcp/src/define-tool.ts`) already takes
a Zod schema for tool arguments — that schema serves both runtime validation
and JSON Schema generation for `tools/list`. Drizzle types compound with it
three ways:

**1. Args schemas for write tools.** Today a "create goal" MCP tool would
hand-write `z.object({ title: z.string(), body: z.string().optional(), ... })`
mirroring `goals` columns. With `schemaOf(generated.goalsInHarness_shared).insert`
the args schema *is* the column shape — NOT NULL becomes required, SQL
defaults become optional, generated columns are omitted. One source of truth.

**2. Response row types.** Every list/get tool currently returns
`Array<Record<string, unknown>>`. With `z.infer<typeof schemaOf(t).select>`
the response shape is the column shape. The agent sees a typed row, MCP
clients can validate the resp

Build a system where agents **write their intent** and other agents **read it**.

This is correct, and the 2026 literature supports it more strongly than it supports ToM:

- The single largest measured gain in the corpus was **+128% from inter-agent conventions** — declaration — while *deeper* ToM belief-graphs were **harmful** at higher player counts (Hanabi, arXiv:2604.23057).

# Two file-locking systems in Papercusp — a comparison

**Date:** 2026-05-20
**Status:** Analysis / design reference
**Subjects:**
- `FileLockQueue` — `libs/papercusp/packages/orchestrator/src/file-lock-queue.ts`
- SU-locks — `apps/operator/lib/agent-tools/locks/` (committed `9ebb499a`), plan `su-agent-coordination-v3-2026-05-14.md`

---

## TL;DR

Papercusp has **two** file-claim coordinators. They look like siblings —
both do atomic multi-path acquire, FIFO fairness, deadlock-freedom,
dead-owner cleanup — but they solve **different problems that share a
vocabulary**.

The single variable that differs is **how many OS processes must
agree**. FileLockQueue coordinates async tasks inside *one* process;
SU-locks coordinates *N* independent processes. Every other design
difference — in-memory vs Postgres, Promise vs LISTEN/NOTIFY, string
owner vs session identity, `reap()` vs TTL, one trusted caller vs many
untrusted ones — is a *downstream consequence* of that one variable.

Neither is "better." FileLockQueue is **the easier problem solved
well**; SU-locks is **the harder problem solved adequately**. Swapping
them ranges from wasteful (SU-locks in-process) to physically
impossible (FileLockQueue cross-process).

The one criticism that survives scrutiny is *not* "which is better" —
it's that SU-locks was designed with n

# Generalize the memory backend (swappable, shared lib)

## Now

Memory is **hardwired to mem0**. The store core is *already* extracted to the shared lib **`libs/generic/memory`** (`@papercusp/memory`) with a `configureMemory()` host-seam — but the abstraction is **mem0-shaped**: `getMemoryClient()` returns mem0's `Memory` class, and the `memory:*` tool handlers (`packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/memory/{remember,search,list,forget,update}.ts`) call mem0-shaped methods (`client.add/search`) and lean on mem0 concepts (`user_id`/`harness:<slug>` scoping, pgvector dedup, mem0 result shape). There is **no `MemoryBackend` interface** anywhere, and **no Claude-file backend** in-codebase (Claude memory is a Claude Code feature *outside* this repo). Owner uses Claude memory now, may switch to mem0 later (undecided), and wants a memory tab. **This is the moment to introduce the swap seam** (pre-alpha, do-it-right) — in the existing shared lib. **No code yet.**

**Next:** P0 — define `MemoryBackend` + wrap mem0 as one impl.

## Decisions

### D-001 — A neutral `MemoryBackend` interface in `libs/generic/memory`
The swap point. Interface (deliberately a **subset that does NOT leak mem0's `user_id`/pgvector vocabulary**):
`remember(text, {kind, scope, metadata}) → {id}` · `search(query, {scope, limit}) → Entry[]` · `list({scope, kind}) → Entry[]` · `forget(id)` · `update(id, patch)`, over a neutral `Entry = { id, text, kind, scope, score?, metadata }`. Lives in `@papercusp/memory` (domain-free, borrowable — per the CLAUDE.md generic

# Hive coordination model + Queen prompt

## Now

**State:** All three items landed and tested this session. P-001 personas rewritten; P-002 swarm-affinity co-location lever behind the default-OFF claim-lease flag; P-003 two-plane invariants verified green. Deferred (owner/budget-gated): activating the cross-Swarm lease flag with 2+ Swarms, and the cross-Hive ask/answer live leg (rides shared-hive-federation).

**Next:** Owner: activate cross-Swarm co-location and E2E the cross-Hive leg when its gates open.

## Entity recap

Workspace ⊃ **many Hives** ⊃ { harnesses, **Swarms** (a deployment of the Hive to an instance, local or cloud), **Colony** (the live agents on a Swarm), **Bees** (contributors, human or agent) }. **One Queen per Hive.** (Naming per [[the-hive-lexicon-2026-06-06]].)

## The two planes (the load-bearing invariant)

- **Horizontal — peer coordination (the magic, preserved):** agents talk *directly* to each other via the coord substrate (`coord:send`/`ask`/conversations/handoffs/topics/presence + locks). The Queen does NOT route, mediate, or sit in the middle of agent chatter.
- **Vertical — steering (new, for scale):** the Queen reads *summaries* (the change feed) and adjusts backlog **priorities** + plan direction. She never touches an individual agent-to-agent message.

**Invariant (D-001):** the Queen is never on the agent-to-agent path. If agent chatter ever routes through the Queen, that is a bug.

## Scope behavior

| Scope | Coordination | Latency |
|---|---|---|
| **Within a Swarm** (one instance) | identical to today — local substrate, direct, everyone-relevant sees everything; locks prevent stomping | instant

HTTP/1.1 budget.

  over h2 it is an h2 stream. This is a transport/serving change, not an

  multipl

# LLM Testing Framework — Decisions Log

**Started:** 2026-05-14
**Maintainer:** the agent currently shipping the framework, plus whoever's after.
**Scope:** narrow log of *why* we picked a path when more than one was viable. Read together with the plan doc
(`llm-testing-framework-2026-05-14.md`) and the handoff doc
(`llm-testing-handoff-2026-05-14.md`).

This file is append-only in spirit — never delete a decision, supersede it with a follow-up entry.

---

## D-001 — Key supply via PG, not file or env-only

**Date:** 2026-05-14

**Choice:** `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is resolved by `llm-client.ts` in this order:
1. `process.env.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` (if non-empty)
2. `readCredentials().anthropic_api_key` from `harness_shared.operator_credentials`
3. throw with an instructive message

**Considered:**
- env-only (handoff's original ask): forces every user to wire shell exports + remember to unset `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`.
- file (`~/.papercusp/anthropic-key`): fewer moving parts but parallel to the existing PG credentials store; mirror is exactly what `feedback_pg_canonical_no_mirrors` says not to do.

**Why PG:** `operator_credentials` already exists with an `anthropic_api_key` column. Reusing it removes a mirror, gives the UI strip at `/admin/testing` a single source of truth, and lets a one-time `INSERT` set up every future CLI invocation.

## Background

**The question this answers** [owner:Avi 2026-07-10]: does adding Apache AGE to our memory stack actually improve the system's real, high-volume use case — memory recall for an agent turn (`memory:search` + orient's recall fold) — or does it only add speed on queries we never ask? **The two systems:**
- **A (today's stack):** mem0 v3 hybrid retrieval — harrier cosine + BM25 + flat entity boost (ENTITY_BOOST_WEIGHT 0.5) + recency decay — over the live pgvector tables.

**Two lanes, deliberately separate:**
1. **Shared-capability head-to-head (the fair A/B):** real mined queries both stacks can answer; measures retrieval quality + latency.
2. **AGE-only capability lane (explicitly NOT a head-to-head):** multi-hop qu

# Native-scheduler lockout — agents schedule only through the harness (claude · omp · codex)

## Now

**State:** Plan remains complete. The old Codex-hook caveat was re-audited on 2026-06-22 against current Codex: managed Codex homes use stable hooks.json PreToolUse/PostToolUse gates for Bash and apply_patch/Edit/Write; the remaining operational check is local hook installation diagnostics, not an upstream inert-hook blocker.

**Next:** None for the shipped scheduler-lockout plan; use papercusp-diagnostics.json if a specific Codex session appears hookless.

## Background — why a lockout

The Queen self-schedules via `hive:declare-wake`; the liveness backstop guarantees a wake row always exists; Pause/`hive:status`/the wake-mode gate all read the SAME routines table. A wake scheduled through claude-code's own surfaces (`CronCreate`/`CronDelete`/`CronList`, `ScheduleWakeup`, the `/schedule` + `/loop` skills) lives in claude's harness state instead:

- the liveness backstop sees "no wake armed" and double-fires (floor-debounced, but noise);
- **Pause Hive cannot pause it** — a cron job keeps firing as a zombie after pause/dissolve;
- the wake-mode gate cannot stage it; `hive:status` cannot show it;
- it violates the storage policy (durable state in PG), doesn't migrate with the harness DB, and is audit-invisible.

Forcing the internal scheduler is what makes "one switch pauses the whole hive" true.

## Threat model — three layers

- **T1 — first-class scheduler tools.** claude: `CronCreate`/`CronDelete`/`CronList`, `ScheduleWakeup`, `Skill(schedule)`, `Skill(loop)` — confirmed present even in headless `-p` runs. omp/codex: **confirmed none** (P-006/P-007

# OpenAPI surface — design spike

**Date:** 2026-05-20
**Phase:** 7 of host-architecture v2 (Extend `tools/list` to OpenAPI). The plan calls for a ~30-minute spike on the wire shape before committing to implementation; this is that spike.
**Status:** Design-review. Implementation gated on §6 questions.

---

## 1. What this is and isn't

**Is:** a written answer to "how do we surface our `events:`-schema-array tool definitions as a valid OpenAPI 3.1 document?" The mapping is non-trivial; spec'ing it on paper before writing the codegen avoids re-doing the mapping when an edge case appears.

**Isn't:** an implementation. No code lands from this doc.

**Isn't:** a typed-client codegen story. That's a separate decision (Phase 7 NOT-shipping line).

## 2. What `tools/list` produces today

From `packages/agent-mcp/src/server.ts:368`:

```jsonc
{
  "tools": [
    {
      "name": "operator:scan",
      "description": "Operator's per-turn workspace scan...",
      "inputSchema": { /* JSON Schema from zod via toJSONSchema */ }
    },
    ...
  ]
}
```

What's there:
- `name` — string
- `description` — string
- `inputSchema` — JSON Schema (drafts 2020-12 from zod 4's `toJSONSchema`)

What's missing for OpenAPI parity:
- **Output schema.** `ToolResult` shape (`{ content: [{type:'text',text:string}, ...] }`) is implicit; clients infer.
- **Events schemas.** A tool with `events: { delta: z.object(...), progress: z.object(...) }` advertises nothing to the client about what SSE chunks to expect.
- **State schema.** Tools with `state: z.object(...)` (the publishState path) advertise nothing.
- **Error responses.** Standard error codes (`invalid_input`, `quota_exceeded`, `unauthorized`, `role_not_allowed`, `missing_capability`, `timeout`, `handler_error`) aren't surfaced

remember the gist of everything at bounded cost.

older turns, regenerated incrementally as turns age out of the verbatim window.

- The conversation is a **shared PG thread** (`harness_shared.operator_conversations`

**State:** Plan COMPLETE as of 2026-06-16. All 13 items are in terminal state: P-001 through P-008, P-011, P-012, P-013 all done; P-009 and P-010 dropped. P-013 Part B (papercup workspace-identity data migration 'default'→'papercusp-workspace') landed in release 9c78a5512 on 2026-06-16 and was live-verified — Queen frontier opened from 14→69 items (D-020). WI-158 (P-009 Phase 2 socket handoff) was deprecated; sidecar work dropped per plan scope. No open work items remain.

**Next:** Owner — update hive steering to the eligible plans you want placed next; the papercup frontier is now open at 69+ items. No Queen action needed on this plan.

## Background

Trigger: `psu` repeatedly failed with `... could not reach the operator at http://localhost:3070 (fetch failed)`.

Root cause (NOT load slowness): the `:3070` operator was in a memory-watchdog crash-loop — RSS crossed the in-process self-recycle cap (3.2 GB) within ~90 s of every boot, so the watchdog drained + exited and systemd restarted it (~one recycle every ~2 min; 47 restarts). Each ~10-15 s drain/restart window made the bootstrap fetch fail with a connection-level error (`fetch failed`), and psu's single 1.5 s retry could not span it.

Two memory facts behind that:

1. The *runaway* leak — `mcp-handler@1.1.0`'s stateless POST branch news an McpServer+transport per MCP request and never closes them (every agent's `initialize`/`tools/list`/`tools/call` leaked one). ~0.2 GB/min, no plateau. Root-caused + patched as **EI-127** (`patches/mcp-handler+1.1.0.patch`). Verified live on :3070 (close() present in the release bundle); RSS now plateaus.
2. The *baseline* footprint (this plan's main subject). Measured vi

App-wide persisted sync cache — reload hydrates ALL query data instantly from IndexedDB (stale-while-revalidate)
---
title: App-wide persisted sync cache — reload hydrates ALL query data instantly from IndexedDB (stale-while-revalidate)
slug: persisted-sync-cache-2026-07-07
status: draft
created: 2026-07-07
updated: 2026-07-07
---

## Problem
On GUI reload every tab renders hard-coded defaults / empty states for seconds until POST /rest-query-batch resolves (whole batch resolves together — head-of-line blocking behind the slowest resolver). The 👑-tab even flashes "Pause indefinitely" as if the owner's pause were lost (owner-observed 2026-07-07 during WI-3309; the pause was intact — pure rendering defect).

## Fix (one chokepoint, app-wide effect)
All app data flows through ONE TanStack Query cache — the getQueryClient() singleton in libs/generic/sync, used by BOTH transports (SSE + polling). Persist that cache to IndexedDB with the first-party persistQueryClient layer: reload → restore (~tens of ms) → every useSyncQuery renders last-known data instantly, marked stale → background refetches replace it as they land → SSE keeps it live.

## Semantics
- storage key: papercusp-sync-cache:<server-or-host>:<userId|anon> (per-user, per-backend)
- throttled writes ~2s · maxAge 24h · buster = app build version (mismatch discards cache)
- dehydrate only SUCCESSFUL queries · default ON, opt-out via SyncProvider prop

## Edge cases
- version query-shape drift → buster discard, clean refetch
- briefly-stale data → by design (owner-requested stale-while-revalidate)
- multi-tab → TanStack last-write-wins (safe)
- workspace switch → unchanged vs today; follow-up: workspace id in the buster if bleed ever matters
- disk → single IDB entry, 24h self-expiry

## Rollout
Flag-ON routine feature (opt-out prop is the escape hatch); rides auto-commit → green-checkpoint gate → release:deploy (same pipeline as the WI-3309 fix, shipped 2026-07-07 09:46 EDT).

## Status
Owner approved the plan

# Plans become harness-scoped, author-owned, fork-on-drag

## Now

**State:** **draft.** Carved out of the `papercusp-dogfood-v5` arc (addendum 2)
during the design-review pass so the architecture rework of plans
can be reviewed independently before it lands in v3. The collab
substrate from v3 (HYPERBEE sync, author pubkeys, shared.json,
git-as-sync for code) is the prerequisite; this doc only adds the
plan-specific behavior on top.

**Next action:** user sign-off on this doc, then split into per-phase
execution work and slot the phase tasks into the v3 timeline (Phase
5a or 5b — after the Hyperbee substrate, alongside or just before
the Plans pane UI work).

## Background

Today, plans live at `apps/operator/docs/plans/*.md`, owned by the
workspace. One canonical directory; every plan is implicitly
"everyone's plan." This fits the single-engineer model but breaks as
soon as a harness becomes shared:

- Two engineers planning different approaches to the same feature
  have nowhere to put their separate plans.
- The "decisions of record" function of a plan (D-NNN entries) is in
  permanent tension with multiple engineers wanting to amend.
- There is no way to take inspiration from someone else's plan
  without overwriting theirs.

The user's framing: **per-user worktree, per-user plan-set; no
canonical decision-of-record across forks; truth is what lands on
`main`.** Disagreement between contributors is fine. This doc lays
out the architecture for that shift.

## Goals

1. **Plans become harness-scoped.** Each harness owns its own plan
   set, replacing the workspace-scoped directory for shared harnesses.
2. **Plans are author-owned.** Only the author of a plan can edit it.
   Everyone in the harness can read.

# Brief: migrating components to the projected-tool MCP framework

For agents picking up component migrations after the spawn-system port. Read this front-to-back before touching code.

---

## TL;DR — what the framework gives you

You write **one typed function**. The framework projects it onto:
- An HTTP route at `/api/plugins/<plugin>/<tool>` (or `/api/agent-tools/<tool>` for built-ins)
- An MCP `tools/call` entry under `<plugin>.<tool>` (or `<scope>:<verb>` for built-ins)

You declare exposure + role + quota + capabilities in a manifest entry. The framework handles auth gating, role allowlisting, quota windows, telemetry persistence, streaming progress, and per-spawn URL context — none of which you write per tool.

Spec: `apps/operator/docs/plugin-mcp-host-design.md`. Read D1–D6 before D3 ("Authentication boundary" + the Phase 9 sketch are the bits agents miss most).

---

### Built-in tools (`packages/agent-mcp/src/tools/**`)
- Use `defineTool({ name, capability, schema, handler })`
- Handler signature: `(input, { principal, tx, ... })`. Auth-required (bearer → principal); throws `UnauthorizedToolError` (→ 401) if `principal` is missing.
- Auto-projected to both transports via `defineTool`'s extension. **You do not write a route file.**
- Quota / role gating: not used (built-ins gate by capability via principal).

### Plugin tools (`libs/papercusp/plugins/<name>/`)
- `papercusp.json` declares `tools[]` with `{ name, descr

# psu --fork disclosure

## Now

- **state:** Authored from the 2026-07-07 fork-misdiagnosis incident. Not started.
- **next:** P-001 — inject the fork-disclosure block into the forked session's first turn.

## Background

`psu --fork` (apps/operator/scripts/psu-launcher.mjs: `resumeArgsFor { fork }`, `forkBootstrapBody`, tracked-fork mint via bootstrap-su §821-900) branches a session: claude `--fork-session` (+ pre-minted `--session-id` for tracked forks), codex `fork <uuid>`. The fork gets a FRESH PAPERCUSP_SID and coord identity — but its transcript is a byte-copy of the parent's, so the agent in the fork has no way to know it isn't the parent. Everything ownerId-keyed (armed loops, fleet leadership/membership, claim-specs, wakeOnReply awaits, loop-scoped carry-notes) stays with the PARENT's sid.

Incident (2026-07-07): fork su-adddb732 of su-bbf8a1fe found `loop:status` null under its own id, concluded "identity drift orphaned my surfaces", and escalated a false bug. The owner had simply forked it.

## Phase 1

- [ ] P-001 **Fork-disclosure injection.** On the fork launch path, inject a first-turn disclosure block into the forked session (same injection surface as the existing session-recovery banner / launch-context): "⑂ You are a FORK, minted <ts>. Your identity: <fork-sid> (fresh). Parent: <parent-sid> — the parent RETAINS everything ownerId-keyed: armed loops, fleet leadership/membership, claim-specs, wakeOnReply awaits, carry-notes. You own NONE of these. Do not act as leader / assume loops are yours; run coord:orient { intent } to establish your own footing. Your transcript below is a COPY of the parent's history — 'I' statements in it are the parent's, not yours."

# PSU wrappers + plan-tracked terminal launch

## Now

**State:** Plan drafted; awaiting human review of scope/sequence before Phase A code starts.

**Next:** human confirms phase ordering and the open questions in Decisions, then we kick off Phase A (rename + codex wrapper + bootstrap endpoint).

## Background

Today the only SU agent wrapper installed by Papercusp is `omp-su`. It is
auto-installed on desktop boot via three call-sites
(`instrumentation-node.ts`, `bin/host-bootstrap.ts`,
`lib/endpoint-route/routes/agent-mcp/console-launch.ts`) and surfaced in the
operator at `/settings/omp-integration`. Claude Code and Codex are both
first-class MCP clients of `papercusp-su`, but neither has a wrapper
counterpart — Claude Code only gets the bash-installer path
(`apps/operator/scripts/install-standalone-mcp.sh`), and Codex has nothing.

Separately, agents launched from `/adv` are tracked as `plan_runs` /
`spawns` so they show up in the Sessions tab and can be resumed. Wrappers
launched from a terminal today produce **untracked** sessions — they just
exec the CLI with the engineer-collaborator playbook appended, with no
server bookkeeping. This means terminal SU work is invisible to /adv.

This plan unifies the three CLI agents under a `*-psu` naming scheme
(papercusp-su), gives every wrapper the same plan-or-NO-PLAN picker UX
on launch, registers wrapper-launched sessions as real `plan_runs` (or
no-plan `spawns`) so they appear in /adv, and retires the desktop-boot
auto-install in favour of per-harness settings. Once shipped, opening a
terminal and typing `claude-psu` will produce the same tracked,
playbook-flavoured agent as clicking "Launch SU engineer" in /adv.

### Design constraints

- **Global wrappers, not per-harness binaries.** Three wrappers total

# Route audit — Phase 4 opening deliverable

**Date:** 2026-05-20
**Phase:** 4 of host-architecture v2 (Route migration after mandatory pre-flight audit).
**Status:** Audit framework + baseline snapshot. Per-batch migrations land as follow-up PRs that update the rows in this doc.

---

## Why this doc

The audit IS the first deliverable. Phase 4 of host-architecture v2 has 240 `route.ts` files under `apps/operator/app/api/**` and a four-axis classification rule. Migrating before the audit runs would mean re-migrating the wrong routes when their A1-ness surfaces during the work. The audit comes first, the migrations come second.

Every PR that migrates a route updates this doc's row for that route — `hint` becomes `decision`, the link points at the migration commit. New routes get added during creation. Closing the audit means every row has a decision.

## The four axes

From host-architecture v2 §6.1, applied per route:

| Axis | Question | What "yes" means |
|---|---|---|
| **a** | Does the handler hold non-transport state? | A1 |
| **b** | Is there pre/post handler work that doesn't belong in a transport-agnostic tool? | A1 |
| **c** | Does it touch cookies / cost-caps / feature-locks? | A1 |
| **d** | Is its wire contract stable? | Migrate only if all of a-c are "no" AND d is "yes" |

Any single "yes" on (a)-(c) → **A1-class.** Keep the route as a Hono / Next shim. The agent-chats precedent (`_hono/agent-chats.ts`, 419 LoC — transcript persistence + cost caps + feature locks + three rejected relocations) is the canonical A1.

Otherwise → **migrate** if the wire contract is stable; **review** if d is in question.

A fourth bucket is **consolidate** — loopback-gated routes that are simple enough to migrate b

## Background — the gap evidence (the rubric's model/method/drift seed)

**Theme:** hive-coordination-health scorecard

**Signal:** recurring (68× · 68 authors · 2 cycles), no covering rubric (drill-back: wi:EI-2978)

The Hive repeatedly hit this cluster (≥3 distinct authors across ≥2 cycles) yet has no

above are the raw material for the rubric's per-criterion model (how it should work),
method (how to investigate it), and drift markers (what degraded/broken looks like).

## Proposed rubric — Queen/Scout fills the structured `templateData` on ratification

## Plan (what the branches are building)

Three layers, in dependency order:

### Layer 1 — Wire-format normalization (✅ shipped)
Move every hand-rolled SSE producer/consumer in the operator
(`:3055`/`:3070`) onto `@restart/sse`. Concrete consequences:
- `handleHttpToolRequestStreaming` writes to an `SseSink` instead of
  building byte strings.

- `branch-actions.ts` + `delegation.ts` use `parseSseStream` for
  multi-line-`data:` correctness.

### Layer 2 — Endpoint-system typed event channel (✅ shipped)
Extend `defineTool` so streaming tools declare an `events: {...}`
schema and emit typed events via `ctx.emit(name, data)`.
`ctx.progress(pct, msg)` becomes an alias for
`ctx.emit('progress', ...)`. Three transports project the same
ctx.emit call:
- **HTTP/SSE** → `event: name\ndata: ...` via `@restart/sse`.
- **MCP** → `notifications/papercusp/event` JSON-RPC notification.
- **In-process** → `dispatchProjectedToolStream(...)` async iterator.

Schema-inferred wire format per event

**State:** **Canonical vocabulary (owner-ratified — [[hive-model-reconciliation-2026-06-08]] D-001, which postdates + supersedes this plan's naming):** this plan's **"hive" = a Swarm** (a deployment of a Hive to one machine — one subscription, a brain + a Colony of bees); the **Hive** is the *project* (harnesses+plans+settings) that owns a shared backlog across its **1..N Swarms**; this plan's **"fleet" = a Colony**. title: Investigation: test:affected core-dumps (Node 25 + vitest worker pool) — RESOLVED
slug: test-affected-coredump-investigation-2026-06-01
created: 2026-06-01

## Now

**State:** RESOLVED 2026-06-01 (status reconciled by the Brief 51 sweep). Root cause: libs/test-config/src/vitest-config.ts set the unit+browser layers to pool:threads (worker_threads), which abort mid-run under Node >=25 on this kernel. Fix: pool = layer===browser ? threads : forks (forks = vitest default, stable across Node versions) — committed c09cf6b1b, verified live in vitest-config.ts. Full operator suite ~29s parallel, no meaningful slowdown.

**Next:** None — resolved; the fix is live in the shared test-config.


## RESOLVED 2026-06-01 — `pool: 'forks'` (commit c09cf6b1b)

**Root cause (corrected):** the shared config was **not** "no pool override"
as the brief guessed — `libs/test-config/src/vitest-config.ts` set the unit +
browser layers to **`pool: 'threads'`** (worker_threads). worker_threads share
one libuv loop, which aborts mid-run under Node ≥25 on this kernel (io_uring is
a symptom on *some* runs, not the cause — `UV_USE_IO_URING=0` alone is
insufficient, as the brief already found).

**Fix (candidate #2, chosen over the Node-22 pin #1):**
`pool: layer === 'browser' ? 'threads' : 'forks'`. `forks` is vitest's own
default; it runs each file in its own child process, is stable across Node
versions, and removes the dependency on which Node the runner's PATH resolves.
Chosen over the Node-22 pin because a pool change is robust on every runner
(CI + each box), whereas PATH-based Node pinning re-breaks the moment a runner
resolves a different Node. Wall-clock for the full operator suite ≈ 29s
parallel — no meaningful slowdown, so #2's "slower" caveat did not materialize.

**Verification:** full `npm test --workspace apps/operator` (661 fi

Summary of this wake's progress:

**Claimed & fixed EI-18698120633403217** (`processes:kill` falsely reports `pid_not_found` for a live process outside its 6-kind classifier).

- **Root cause**: `listProcesses()` in `dev-data.ts` silently drops any process classified `'other'` before returning, so `killProcess()`'s "not in the list" check couldn't distinguish "doesn't exist" from "exists but untracked kind."
- **Fix**: added `probeProcess(pid)` to `dev-data.ts` — a raw `/proc/<pid>` check independent of the kind-allowlist. `killProcess()` now calls it when a pid isn't in the classified list; a live-but-untracked pid now returns the new `unsupported_kind` error (with kind + cmdline evidence) instead of the false `pid_not_found`. Deliberately did **not** widen the 6-kind classifier — the bug report's own P-008 verdict says that's out of scope (belongs to a future job-handle surface).
- **Tests**: updated `process-kill.test.ts` to mock `probeProcess`, added a dedicated regression test for exactly this bug shape (live `vitest`-like pid → `unsupported_kind`, never signaled). 10/10 pass. Also re-ran `dev.test.ts` (25/25) and `proc-guard.test.ts` (13/13) — no regressions in sibling process-inventory code.
- **Committed**: git-sync already picked it up (`cb772e40aa`).
- Checkpointed the work-item with full evidence.

Next: a broader `npm run test:affected` is running in the background to catch any other consumer of these exports before I call `work_items:complete`. I'll finish the item the moment that comes back green (or fix/report if it surfaces something).

**`drop-sync-batcher-2026-07-25` is complete and shipped.** All 8 items done, plan status flipped `ready → shipped`.

## What landed

The micro-batcher is gone. `batch-fetcher.ts` deleted along with `SyncQueryOptions.priority` and all 12 `priority:'interactive'` call sites; replaced by `query-fetcher.ts` (one `GET /rest-query` per query) + `concurrency-gate.ts` (FIFO async semaphore), with per-query `AbortSignal` cancellation restored — something a bundle structurally could not offer. `rest-query` raised `auth:'public'` → `'loopback'`, verified live on `:3170` (loopback Host=200, non-loopback Host=403).

**Green:** `libs/generic/sync` 184/184, re-run after my final edit. `tsc --noEmit` clean. No `batch-fetcher`/`batchFetch` references remain anywhere.

## The finding worth your attention

My predecessor's P-007 measurement overturned the plan's own premise, and I want to flag it because it nearly shipped a wrong default. **Every number in the plan was taken over loopback HTTP against `:3070` — a transport no user is ever on.** Re-measured inside the real Tauri shell, the optimum moved 2x: at concurrency 12 the new design's wall time actually *regresses past the batcher it replaced* (4981ms vs 3000ms), which would have made the whole change a net loss. The default had to be 24. Recorded as plan D-003.

Two confounds are worth knowing: the first run showed the *opposite* winner purely because cold cache absorbed the cost of whichever condition ran first — it had to be retracted and redone warmed + interleaved. And wall time isn't the user-visible metric: a bundle's effective p50 *is* its wall, so individual requests won ~7.6x on time-to-first-paint at wall-time parity.

Done — the bug is fixed and landed, with one piece of live verification pending on the Windows rig. Compaction is queued, so here's the full picture:

## What happened

**I rejoined the fleet** (`windows-parity`, led by su-b0fbf; su-a81a6 died in the host restart — flagged to the leader) and **fixed the Windows desktop-launch bug (WI-3289)**, plus a second critical bug I hit on the way in.

## The Windows terminal-launch fix (WI-3289)

Root cause: on Windows the operator runs inside WSL2, and anything it spawns lands in invisible Session 0 — so `capability:terminal` / `fleet:launch-on-plan` hard-501'd with "Linux/macOS only". The working Windows mechanism (Tauri `console_launch` → `wt.exe`) was only reachable from the desktop webview, which agent tools couldn't reach.

The fix is a relay bridge riding the existing sync-SSE bus (same rails as `attention.notify`):
- **Operator**: `console-launch-bridge.ts` parks the agent's call, emits `console.launch-request` with the envelope, and fails loud after 30s if no desktop shell answers; new loopback routes `launch-claim` (first-claimer-wins, so N webviews spawn one window) and `launch-result`.
- **Renderer**: `DesktopConsoleLaunchBridge.tsx` (mounted at the app root) claims the request, invokes Tauri `console_launch`, posts the result back.
- **Callers**: `spawnConsole` gained opt-in `allowDesktopBridge`; both agent tools use it. The user "+" button path is untouched.
- **Rust**: 3-line guard in `launch_inner` so agent envelopes (empty mcp-json) no longer clobber a project's real `.mcp.json`.

Verified: 1,672 operator-core tests green (incl. 9 new bridge/spawn tests), vite build green, `cargo test` 14/14, typecheck under baseline. **Remaining**: live verify needs a real Windows box — su-b0fbf's already-planned rebuild ships it, and I sent him the verify one-liner.

# The Queen — placement-specialist operator for the Hive

You are **the Queen of this Hive**, running in the placement-specialized mode:
your judgment is concentrated on **where work runs** — surveying the ranked
backlog, the Swarm's bee slots, and the bees' work-lists, and for each task
picking a placement (free slot / graceful-evict+fresh / warm-inject), attaching a
situational brief, and declaring your next wake. Placement is the concrete form
of one of the Queen's levers (co-location); the rest of the Queen's role below
still applies — you are the same judgment layer, just with the dial turned toward
placement automation.

## Your verbs are MCP TOOLS — never curl them (read this before your first action)

Every `group:verb` named in this prompt (`fleet:spawn`, `coord:send`,
`work_items:*`, `events:emit`, …) is an **MCP tool on your connected papercusp
server** — call it as a tool (load schemas via ToolSearch first when deferred:
`select:mcp__papercusp__fleet_spawn`, then invoke `mcp__papercusp__fleet_spawn`
directly). There is **NO REST surface for these verbs**: `localhost:3055` /
`:3070` paths like `/api/mcp-invoke`, `/api/work-items`, or `/api/events/emit`
DO NOT EXIST — a curl there fails or misleads, and the standalone webapp is
retired. If the MCP server reads "still connecting", retry the tool call — do
not fall back to curl.

**Integrity is absolute.** If a tool path is broken or you cannot complete an
instructed action: STOP, record the blockage honestly (`coord:escalate`, or your
report's BLOCKED line), and end your turn. NEVER simulate the outcome by hand —
writing a bee's checkpoint file yourself, marking unexecuted work verified, or
recording a success memory for something that did not happen is fabrication; the
fleet's ground truth (work-item states, spawn rows) will contradict you and the
turn will be judged a failure. A truthful BLOCKED is always a better outcome
than a fabricated DONE.
